5b51167fb0:0132a15a91a18b86.title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
5b51167fb0:0132a15a91a18b86.author: info@aeaweb.org (Andrew J. Fieldhouse1 and Karel Mertens2 1 Mays Business School, Texas A&M University (email: afieldhouse@mays.tamu.edu) 2 Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, CEPR (email:…
5b51167fb0:0132a15a91a18b86.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 3959-4002 Abstract Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

5b51167fb0:c7fa8e0ff8b591f9.title: The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
5b51167fb0:c7fa8e0ff8b591f9.author: info@aeaweb.org (Diego R. Känzig1 1 Northwestern University, CEPR, and NBER (email: dkaenzig@northwestern.edu))
5b51167fb0:c7fa8e0ff8b591f9.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4003-4040 Abstract This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

5b51167fb0:e824f86123436e63.title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
5b51167fb0:e824f86123436e63.author: info@aeaweb.org (Sam Asher1, Kritarth Jha2, Paul Novosad2, Anjali Adukia2 and Brandon Tan3 1 Imperial College London (email: sam.asher@imperial.ac.uk) 2 Development Data Lab (email:…
5b51167fb0:e824f86123436e63.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4041-4076 Abstract We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

5b51167fb0:ed6f6ae7997930cd.title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
5b51167fb0:ed6f6ae7997930cd.author: info@aeaweb.org (Nathan Zorzi1 and Martin Beraja2 1 Dartmouth (email: Nathan.G.Zorzi@dartmouth.edu) 2 UC Berkeley and NBER (email: maberaja@berkeley.edu))
5b51167fb0:ed6f6ae7997930cd.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4077-4115 Abstract Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

5b51167fb0:3196e21e18145698.title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
5b51167fb0:3196e21e18145698.author: info@aeaweb.org (Lorenzo Lagos1 1 Brown University, NBER, and IZA (email: lorenzo_lagos@brown.edu))
5b51167fb0:3196e21e18145698.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4116-4157 Abstract This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

5b51167fb0:040a01a62b7769bc.title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
5b51167fb0:040a01a62b7769bc.author: info@aeaweb.org (Eric Chyn1, Kareem Haggag2 and Bryan A. Stuart3 1 Department of Economics, University of Texas-Austin, and NBER (email: eric.chyn@austin.utexas.edu) 2 Anderson School of Management,…
5b51167fb0:040a01a62b7769bc.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4158-4202 Abstract How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

5b51167fb0:0ad09d14a2108386.title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
5b51167fb0:0ad09d14a2108386.author: info@aeaweb.org (Oliver Pfäuti1 1 The University of Texas at Austin (email: pfaeuti.oliver@gmail.com))
5b51167fb0:0ad09d14a2108386.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4203-4242 Abstract The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

5b51167fb0:cde519eb240cea67.title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
5b51167fb0:cde519eb240cea67.author: info@aeaweb.org (Xiwen Bai1, Jesús Fernández-Villaverde2, Yiliang Li3 and Francesco Zanetti4 1 Tsinghua University (email: xiwenbai@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn) 2 University of Pennsylvania (email:…
5b51167fb0:cde519eb240cea67.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4243-4281 Abstract We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

5b51167fb0:e1d96c9b68fa4eb6.title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
5b51167fb0:e1d96c9b68fa4eb6.author: info@aeaweb.org (Clare Balboni1, Johannes Boehm2 and Mazhar Waseem 1 London School of Economics and Political Science (email: c.a.balboni@lse.ac.uk) 2 University of Geneva (email:…
5b51167fb0:e1d96c9b68fa4eb6.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4282-4325 Abstract This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

5b51167fb0:f3cbadd0645f288a.title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
5b51167fb0:f3cbadd0645f288a.author: info@aeaweb.org (David M. Ritzwoller1 and Joseph P. Romano2 1 Stanford University (email: ritzwoll@stanford.edu) 2 Stanford University (email: romano@stanford.edu))
5b51167fb0:f3cbadd0645f288a.summary: American Economic Review 116 (11): 4326-4357 Abstract Statistical inference is often simplified by sample splitting. This simplification comes at the cost of the introduction of randomness not native to the data. We propose a simple procedure for sequentially aggregating statistics constructed with multiple splits of the same sample. The user specifies a bound and a nominal error rate. If the procedure is implemented twice on the same data, the nominal error rate approximates the chance that the results differ by more than the bound. We illustrate the application of the procedure to several widely applied econometric methods. (JEL C20, C30, C52)

5b51167fb0:bdb556254e68b6c5.title: Who Marries Whom? The Role of Segregation by Race and Class
5b51167fb0:bdb556254e68b6c5.author: info@aeaweb.org (Benjamin Goldman1, Jamie Gracie2 and Sonya R. Porter3 1 Cornell University (email: bgoldman@cornell.edu) 2 Harvard University (email: jgracie@g.harvard.edu) 3 US Census Bureau…
5b51167fb0:bdb556254e68b6c5.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3623-3673 Abstract Americans rarely marry outside their race or class group, a pattern with well-documented implications for inequality and intergenerational mobility. Limited exposure may partly explain these low intergroup marriage rates. We instrument for exposure using variation in childhood neighborhoods based on whether other race and class groups had more opposite-sex children of similar age. Exposure increases interclass (high- and low-parent income) marriage but has no detectable effect on interracial (White and Black) marriage. A spatial marriage model predicts that residential segregation—one of many forms of exposure—accounts for more than one-third of marital sorting by class but less than 5 percent by race. (JEL J12, J15, J62, R23)

5b51167fb0:b43f16929197f266.title: Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
5b51167fb0:b43f16929197f266.author: info@aeaweb.org (Katrine Jakobsen1, Henrik Kleven2, Jonas Kolsrud3, Camille Landais4 and Mathilde Munoz5 1 University of Copenhagen (email: katrinemariejakobsen@gmail.com) 2 Princeton University,…
5b51167fb0:b43f16929197f266.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3674-3720 Abstract Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: A 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent. A large fraction of the wealthy are business owners, and their businesses are negatively affected by owner out-migration. The aggregate effects are nevertheless modest: The migration responses to a 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate reduce employment by 0.02 percent, investments by 0.07 percent, and value added by 0.10 percent. (JEL D31, E22, E24, F22, H24, L26, K34)

5b51167fb0:da85f2a2d1dc685d.title: Racial Promotion Gaps
5b51167fb0:da85f2a2d1dc685d.author: info@aeaweb.org (Deepak Hegde1, Alexander Ljungqvist2 and Manav Raj3 1 New York University and NBER (email: dhegde@stern.nyu.edu) 2 Stockholm School of Economics, Swedish House of Finance, and CEPR…
5b51167fb0:da85f2a2d1dc685d.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3721-3767 Abstract We study racial disparities in promotions in a setting in which promotions are formulaic: the US patent office. Using detailed administrative data that allow us to observe who is eligible for promotion when, we document that Black patent examiners experience delays in promotions they are entitled to, slowing their climb to the top of the career ladder by a year and reducing career earnings by 2.5 percent. Institutional features rule out statistical discrimination with accurate priors. Slow promotions even under Black supervisors argue against taste-based animus. Instead, the patterns fit models of belief-based discrimination. (JEL J15, J41, J71, M12, M51, O34)

5b51167fb0:4457dc712975ec95.title: Screening and Segmenting: A Consumer Surplus Perspective
5b51167fb0:4457dc712975ec95.author: info@aeaweb.org (Dirk Bergemann1, Tibor Heumann2 and Michael C. Wang3 1 Department of Economics, Yale University (email: dirk.bergemann@yale.edu) 2 Instituto de Economía, Pontificia Universidad…
5b51167fb0:4457dc712975ec95.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3768-3801 Abstract We analyze consumer surplus when a monopolist can adjust both prices and product qualities across segments, engaging in secondand third-degree price discrimination simultaneously. We characterize the consumer-optimal segmentation and show that it has a striking structure: Consumers with the same value receive the same quality in every segment, though prices differ. Under mild conditions, any segmentation harms consumers if and only if demand is sufficiently more elastic than supply. Hence, potential benefits for consumers depend critically on demand and supply elasticities. These findings have implications for regulatory policy regarding price discrimination and market segmentation. (JEL D42, D83, K21, L12, L15)

5b51167fb0:a0b06843547e36d5.title: A Model of the Attention Economy: Data, Platforms, and Discovery
5b51167fb0:a0b06843547e36d5.author: info@aeaweb.org (Daniel Chen1 1 Assistant Professor of Economics, Princeton University (email: dtchen@princeton.edu))
5b51167fb0:a0b06843547e36d5.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3802-3836 Abstract This paper develops a dynamic model of the attention economy featuring two interlinked markets: a product market, where consumers have limited awareness of firms, and an attention market, where platforms attract attention by investing in free services (e.g., social media, streaming, podcasts) and sell targeted ads using data on consumer preferences. The model provides a tractable framework in which platform investment, ad-driven discovery, product demand, and ad revenue are jointly determined. The effects of data and interoperability policies can reverse over time, platform quality may be inefficiently high or low, and the rise of data-rich digital advertising can coincide with a declining ad revenue-to-GDP ratio. (JEL D43, D44, D58, D83, L86, M37)

5b51167fb0:17af0ecaa5dc28ef.title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress during the British Industrial Revolution
5b51167fb0:17af0ecaa5dc28ef.author: info@aeaweb.org (Hans-Joachim Voth1, Bruno Caprettini2 and Alex Trew3 1 University of Zurich and CEPR (voth@econ.uzh.ch) 2 University of St. Gallen and CEPR (bruno.caprettini@gmail.com) 3 University…
5b51167fb0:17af0ecaa5dc28ef.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3837-3874 Abstract We establish a link between labor scarcity and the adoption of laborsaving technology in industrializing England. During the Napoleonic Wars, more than 10 percent of the male population served in the armed forces. Where recruitment was heavy, more machines economizing on labor were adopted. Naval recruitment, instrumented by warships' coastal access, provides exogenous variation in labor scarcity and suggests that the link between labor shortages and adoption is causal. Where mechanical skills were abundant, the impact of labor scarcity on adoption appears to be larger. (JEL J24, N13, N43, N63, N73, O14, O31)

5b51167fb0:5713354141b0f2d8.title: Social Push and the Direction of Innovation
5b51167fb0:5713354141b0f2d8.author: info@aeaweb.org (Elias Einiö1, Josh Feng2 and Xavier Jaravel3 1 VATT Institute for Economic Research (email: elias.einio@vatt.fi) 2 University of Utah (email: josh.feng@eccles.utah.edu) 3 London…
5b51167fb0:5713354141b0f2d8.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3875-3909 Abstract What are the implications of unequal access to innovation careers for the direction of innovation and inequality? Leveraging novel linked datasets in the United States and Finland, we document that innovators create products more likely to be purchased by consumers like them in terms of gender, socioeconomic status, and age. Homophily exists both within narrow product categories and across industries and has been stable in recent decades. Incorporating this “social push” channel into a growth model, we estimate that unequal access to innovation careers has a large effect on cost of living inequality and long-run growth. (JEL D63, J16, L26, M13, O31, O33, O47)

5b51167fb0:66d365a090201a2f.title: Knowledge Spillovers, Competition, and Individual Careers
5b51167fb0:66d365a090201a2f.author: info@aeaweb.org (Thomas Cornelissen1, Christian Dustmann2 and Uta Schönberg3 1 Department of Economics, University of Essex, RF Berlin, and Institute for Employment Research (IAB) (email:…
5b51167fb0:66d365a090201a2f.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3910-3941 Abstract Exposure to better peers in the workplace can influence career trajectories through two opposing channels: positively, via knowledge spillovers, and negatively, through competition for advancement. We disentangle these effects by studying untrained labor market entrants and distinguishing between coworkers in the same occupation with whom they are likely to compete versus those with whom they are unlikely to compete. We find robust evidence of persistent knowledge spillovers but also identify countervailing competition effects of comparable magnitude. Both effects are more pronounced for men than for women. (JEL D83, J16, J24, M53, M54, O33)

5b51167fb0:7cf1ce28f4d619bc.title: Truth Elicitation in a Nonstrategic Environment
5b51167fb0:7cf1ce28f4d619bc.author: info@aeaweb.org (Jacob Glazer1 and Ariel Rubinstein2 1 University of Warwick and Tel Aviv University (email: glazer@tauex.tau.ac.il) 2 Tel Aviv University and New York University (email:…
5b51167fb0:7cf1ce28f4d619bc.summary: American Economic Review 116 (10): 3942-3958 Abstract A principal decides which party deserves a prize. Only the parties observe the state that determines who is deserving. The principal gives each party a text describing the conditions under which that party deserves the prize and asks each to report the state. The parties are nonstrategic. Each activates a known cheating procedure whose outcome depends on the state and on the text. Implementation is achieved if, whenever the parties disagree, the liar is identified by the “one-way cheating principle”: The truthful party is the unique party who could not have produced his story had the rival's story been true. (JEL D82, D91)

21113a7a19:2fa4e4099b70f150.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:2fa4e4099b70f150.summary: Dick Posner, a giant of law and economics died on Tuesday, at the age of 87. Here's the brief announcement from U. Chicago: Law School Mourns the Passing of Richard A. Posner, Senior Lecturer, Law and Economics Pioneer, and Former Federal Appellate Judge "Senior Lecturer Richard Allen Posner, a longtime University of Chicago Law School scholar, former federal appellate judge, and pioneer in the field of law and economics, died on November 10. He was 87. Posner, who joined the Law School faculty in 1969 and spent 36 years as a judge on the US Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, is widely considered to be the most influential legal scholar of all time and, during his time on the bench, was considered to be among the most powerful jurists outside the Supreme Court. He authored thousands of court opinions, hundreds of academic articles, and dozens of books, and was a leading scholar of law and economics, a field born and developed at the University of Chicago beginning in the early 20th century. " ####### Here's a longer obit from the Washington Post: Richard Posner, influential and iconoclastic federal judge, dies at 87 He served nearly 36 years on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit in Chicago and was ranked by many as second in influence only to members of the Supreme Court . By Paul W. Valentine "Before he became a judge, Mr. Posner ran a litigation consulting firm where he helped pioneer the concept of applying economic analysis to legal issues. He developed his approach more fully in his book “Economic Analysis of Law” (1973), now a classic text, contending that the economic consequences of laws should be considered in all aspects of the legal system. He once proposed abolishing adoption agencies to stop black-market adoptions and allowing pregnant women to sell unwanted babies on the open market. ... "He evolved from his economic cost-benefit pragmatism early in his career to advocacy later of more liberal positions on such issues as workplace…

21113a7a19:2ee7f4f10d726586.title: Human organ trafficking and missing persons in China, PNAS
21113a7a19:2ee7f4f10d726586.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:2ee7f4f10d726586.summary: Here's a study, recently published in PNAS, that tries to very indirectly infer the rate of illegal organ trafficking in China. It's sure to be controversial. X. Wang, Human organ trafficking and missing persons in China , Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 123 (44) e2608464123, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2608464123 (2026). "Abstract The persistent shortage of human organs for transplantation has long been a global challenge. The prospect of substantial profit creates strong incentives for illegal organ trafficking, including murder for organ harvesting, yet empirical evidence remains scarce. This study addresses this gap by exploiting a unique quasi-natural experiment created by China’s organ policy reform. From 1984 to 2014, executed prisoners were the primary source of transplant organs in China. In 2015, the Chinese government abolished the use of organs from executed prisoners, sharply exacerbating the organ shortage. Following this policy change, the number of missing persons rose notably nationwide. Employing difference-in-differences and triple-difference strategies, we show that, compared to cases unrelated to organ trafficking (e.g., voluntary disappearances), the number and incidence of involuntary missing persons plausibly related to organ trafficking increased significantly after 2015. The effects are especially pronounced among individuals with mental illness and in regions with higher transplant demand and greater transplant capacity. Although we do not directly observe organ trafficking, the spatial, temporal, and demographic patterns we document are consistent with the hypothesis that increased organ scarcity intensified incentives for illicit organ procurement. More broadly, the findings suggest that severe organ shortages may generate unintended and highly harmful consequences, even in a low-crime setting such as China. These results underscore the importance of accounting for behavioral responses and illicit-market incentives when designing…

21113a7a19:30255847665c41bc.title: School choice in San Francisco: plans and politics happen at different speeds
21113a7a19:30255847665c41bc.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:30255847665c41bc.summary: A report in PNAS last week on a long-running study of school choice proposals in San Francisco came out almost simultaneously with an announcement that San Francisco Unified School District (SFUSD) plans to largely step back from school choice and revert to a system of neighborhood schools determined by students' home addresses. Below are the PNAS paper, the SFUSD announcements, and then some links to the history of school choice in SF. I. Lo, K. Mentzer, M. YahyazadehJeloudar, H. O’Connell, J. Monardo, & I. Ashlagi, Designing school choice for diversity in the San Francisco Unified School District , Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 123 (45). November 2, 2026, e2524796123, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2524796123 (2026). "Abstract. More than 65 years after the Brown v. Board of Education ruling that school segregation is unconstitutional, public schools across the United States are again experiencing rising segregation. In districts like San Francisco, efforts to implement district-wide choice policies have largely failed to reverse these trends. Since 2019, we have collaborated with the San Francisco Unified School District to design a student assignment policy meeting the district’s goals of diversity, predictability, and proximity. We use optimization techniques to develop policies restricting choice to zones. We compare these to district-wide choice policies by estimating a choice model using historical application data and simulating assignment. Our results show multiple policies can reduce school segregation while preserving varying degrees of proximity, choice, and predictability. Zone-based policies with reserves reduce the concentration of racial minority students in high-poverty schools and maintain proximity, but reduce choice. District-wide choice with reserves and distance-based priority can further reduce segregation, but at the cost of predictability. Tradeoffs are necessary as no policy dominates another policy. In addition, we show that spatial…

21113a7a19:e6c0fb83338a6647.title: The Milken Institute Review on blood and plasma, and altruism (with art work)
21113a7a19:e6c0fb83338a6647.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:e6c0fb83338a6647.summary: You can be paid to donate blood plasma, and still be an altruist. Issue four, 2026 of the Milken Institute Review, excerpts the chapter on blood supply from my book Moral Economics . The last quoted line of the chapter is " Health care that's good enough for the rich shouldn't be repugnant for the poor. " Peter Passell , the long-time editor of the review, writes "Nobel Prize winners in the sciences can justifiably lay claim to mind-bending insights and stunning discoveries that change our lives. Readers may be excused, though, for wondering whether the same can be said about the achievements honored by the Nobel in economic science, which generally excite only the nerds among us. ¶ Not so for the work of Alvin Roth, a Stanford University economist whose deep dives into how markets function earned him a trip to Stockholm in 2012. He pioneered changes in what are called “matching markets” – work that has revolutionized the process for matching kidney donors and recipients. ¶ In his new book Moral Economics: From Prostitution to Organ Sales, What Controversial Transactions Reveal About How Markets Work,* Roth dissects markets in which the legitimacy of voluntary transactions is widely disputed. Here, we excerpt the chapter on the market for human blood, where millions of patients’ lives depend on sources of blood that cannot legally be purchased. It’s a tale that’s going to surprise you. — Peter Passell, Published October 30, 2026 " *Copyright © 2026 by Alvin E. Roth. 21113a7a19:64876eeda3cb87cc.title: William Nordhaus (1941-2026) and Jim Andreoni (1959-2026)
21113a7a19:64876eeda3cb87cc.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:64876eeda3cb87cc.summary: I returned from a long trip and an arduous conference last week to learn that two important economists had passed away, Bill Nordhaus, who won a Nobel, and Jim Andreoni, who could have. Nordhaus' work on climate change was prescient, and is well known. Here's the Nordhaus obit from Yale: William Nordhaus, Nobel laureate who integrated economics and climate change, devoted Yale citizen Oct 31, 2026 By Penelope Laurans "William Nordhaus ‘63, Sterling Professor of Economics who won a Nobel Prize in 2018 for integrating climate change into long-run macroeconomic analysis, died Oct. 30 at age 85. ########## Jim Andreoni was a multi-talented scholar of public goods, well known in the experimental economics community. The work that in my mind made him a Nobel candidate was his work on different forms that altruism can take. Two of his papers that I really like are Andreoni, James. "Impure altruism and donations to public goods: A theory of warm-glow giving." The economic journal 100, no. 401 (1990): 464-477. and James Andreoni, Justin M. Rao, and Hannah Trachtman, Avoiding the Ask: A Field Experiment on Altruism, Empathy, and Charitable Giving. Journal of Political Economy 2017 125:625-653. The first of those, a theory paper, I think of as one of the foundational papers about effective altruism, but from the point of view that much altruism is not primarily of the effective sort. The second paper is an experiment that I'll present to my class today, in Jim's memory. ############# Vigorous, personal disagreement about what constitutes altruism in organ donation and transplantation was what made my Geneva conference so arduous (and what makes the kinds of controversial markets I discuss in Moral Economics so controversial:). Monday, October 26, 2026 Brocher conference on boundaries for incentives in organ donation Oct 27-29 in Geneva (No description of the conference has been posted yet, but it was hot and heavy, and everyone was an altruist...)

21113a7a19:ee0ff3f10b82afff.title: Sports, ethnicity, and the urban geography of basketball
21113a7a19:ee0ff3f10b82afff.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:ee0ff3f10b82afff.summary: I'm just back from an unexpectedly grueling trip, and hope to resume semi-daily blogging. This story caught my eye: basketball has been an inner city game in the U.S., in part because basketball courts can be set up very inexpensively in urban parks, and not so expensively in gyms. So inner city kids are disproportionately represented among the most talented players. But who those kids are has changed over time. The WSJ has the story: When Jews Ruled the Basketball Court. Six players on the New York Knicks’ inaugural roster were Jewish. By Michael Freund "It was Nov. 1, 1946, and Ossie Schectman of the New York Knicks took a bounce pass and scored on a two-handed underhand layup. Schectman, the son of Russian Jewish immigrants, had just scored the first basket in NBA history. ... "Six members of the Knicks’ original roster, including Schectman, were Jewish. That was no coincidence. For much of the early 20th century, basketball was widely regarded as a Jewish game. "The reason can be traced to the immigrant neighborhoods of New York and Philadelphia. Millions of Jews arrived from Eastern Europe beginning in the 1880s, often settling in neighborhoods with little open space and scant money to spend on recreation. Baseball required a field and equipment. Basketball needed little more than a ball, a hoop and a schoolyard. "

CHI DECIDE? VITA, LIBERTÀ E CONFINI MORALI WHO GETS TO CHOOSE? LIFE, FREEDOM, AND MORAL BOUNDARIES sabato 24 ottobre 17:00 - 18:00 Centro Città Collegio Carlo Alberto | Auditorium Piazza Vincenzo Arbarello, 8, Torino With MARCO CAPPATO, ALVIN ROTH Moderates CATERINA SOFFICI Live translation available Quando le scelte riguardano il corpo, la vita e la morte, dove finisce la libertà individuale e dove deve iniziare la regolazione pubblica? Cosa dovrebbero fare le società quando le convinzioni morali divergono profondamente? Come possono le istituzioni proteggere la libertà di scelta senza lasciare indifesi i più vulnerabili? When choices involve the body, life, and death, where should individual freedom end and public regulation begin? What should societies do when moral convictions sharply diverge? How can institutions protect freedom of choice without leaving the most vulnerable unprotected?

21113a7a19:4a1e5a37dfce9f4e.title: Market design and water conservation in the the Great Salt Lake
21113a7a19:4a1e5a37dfce9f4e.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:4a1e5a37dfce9f4e.summary: Silvia Console Battilana, who co-founded Auctionomics along with Paul Milgrom, writes in Forbes about the prospects for market design efforts to help conserve Utah's Great Salt Lake. How Market Design Could Help Save Utah’s Great Salt Lake by By Silvia Console Battilana "the Great Salt Lake is drying up. "To save the lake while protecting water users, business leaders can adopt a little-known but powerful economic tool: market design. When water levels drop, the consequences immediately hit commercial supply chains and local commerce. Market-based incentives give businesses a way to reward upstream water conservation, bringing more water to the lake without hurting regional growth. The invisible hand of the market could identify the least expensive conservation, compensate participating water users and restore the Great Salt Lake. ... "The shrinking of the Great Salt Lake has many causes, and there is no silver-bullet fix. But any solution to refill the lake will likely involve conservation within Utah. Seventy-one percent of the water diverted from the lake’s basin is allocated to agriculture. If those commercial users could make more efficient use of water, more would reach the lake. The catch is that many conservation practices, like water-friendly infrastructure and precision irrigation, are expensive. Under Utah’s traditional “use-it-or-lose-it” water rights system, users have little financial reason to conserve. Without modern economic incentives, asking businesses and farms to voluntarily cut back simply isn’t realistic. Even if water users could be forced to cut back, it’s not clear who should cut back, or by how much. The costs of water conservation aren’t the same across users, and they can be very hard to estimate. Market design can address both of these challenges. Crucially, markets don’t force particular actions or behaviors. Instead, well-designed markets create an incentive for farms and communities to cut back on water and be rewarded for their…

21113a7a19:093967ed777c5557.summary: I wonder if this is the first time an economics book has been reviewed in the American Journal of Transplantation. Poetic justice: A review of moral economics by Alvin E. Roth Michael A. Rees "Alvin E. Roth describes poetic justice as the Virginia state flag flying at half-mast in 2020 in honor of Bernie Cohen, who argued the US Supreme Court case Loving v. Virginia that made interracial marriage legal. Turns out Mildred and Richard Loving were convicted of interracial marriage in 1967, arrested by police at 2 AM at home in their bed, and sentenced to 1 year in prison but suspended on the condition that they leave Virginia for 25 years. Reading what the Virginia Court of Appeals judge wrote, side by side with what the US Supreme Court wrote, is, by itself, worth the price of the book. "Those of us in the field of transplantation have felt—and will continue to feel—the impact of repugnance. In moral economics, Alvin E. Roth takes us on a grand tour of how repugnance shapes transactions across a wide spectrum of human activities. Take uterus transplantation, pioneered in Sweden, a country where repugnance to surrogacy has made it illegal. You can transplant a uterus into a woman with infertility in Sweden, but do not you dare use a surrogate’s uterus in her own body to help you achieve a baby! Alvin E. Roth defines repugnance as a morally contested market that some people would like to participate in, but others think should be outlawed. He goes on to call a transaction repugnant if “all parties to the transaction want to engage in it, and others think they shouldn’t be allowed to for moral or religious reasons, even though those others can’t detect that the transaction has taken place unless someone tells them.”1 I found it fascinating to walk through all the ways in which repugnance has shaped the world in which we live. "The book starts with a clear example of a transaction that many people want to engage in: sex. Of course, I knew about the repugnance…

21113a7a19:2fce76346ec91464.summary: Kidney exchange, which was pioneered in South Korea in the late 1990's, has largely been moribund there. But here's a call to change that. Reemerging kidney paired donation in Korea: simultaneous two-way swaps to overcome human leukocyte antigen and anatomic barriers Eunjeong Kang1,2, Kyung Ok Min1, Hee Gyung Kang3, Yohan Ahn3, Eun Young Song4, Ara Cho5, Ahram Han5, Sangil Min5, Jongwon Ha5,6,7, Sehoon Park2, Yong Chul Kim2, Yon Su Kim2,8, Hajeong Lee2,8 Kidney Research and Clinical Practice 2026;j.krcp.25.391. DOI: https://doi.org/10.23876/j.krcp.25.391 Abstract Background South Korea first implemented kidney paired donation (KPD) to overcome ABO-incompatible living-donor kidney transplantation. Although utilization declined as desensitization matured, persistent desensitization failure and anatomic constraints have renewed interest in KPD within a regulated framework. We report a recent single-center experience. Methods KPD exchanges were coordinated within an institutional registry under national supervision. We retrospectively reviewed six consecutive, simultaneous two-way exchanges (12 recipients) from 2022 to 2025. We assessed predefined desensitization failure or anticipated failure with the intended donor, compared immunologic compatibility between intended and exchange donors, and recorded perioperative desensitization, graft function, delayed graft function (DGF), and biopsy-proven acute rejection (BPAR). Results Five of six exchanges were undertaken for immunologic reasons. All five met criteria for desensitization failure or anticipated failure to the intended donor, with positive crossmatch and high donor-specific antibody (DSA) burden. Reassignment to the exchange donor reduced risk, lowering maximum DSA mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) from 13,228 to 1,350 and total DSA MFI from 20,542 to 2,240, although selective desensitization was still required in some recipients with residual human leukocyte antigen or ABO incompatibility. 21113a7a19:0b3e864f26759c4c.title: Kidney exchange in India at a national scale: a growing consensus
21113a7a19:0b3e864f26759c4c.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:0b3e864f26759c4c.summary: There's growing consensus in India on moving towards a nationwide kidney exchange program. Kute V, Kumar A, Balwani M et al. Operational guidelines for kidney swap transplantation in India: an ISOT-NOTTO Delphi consensus The Lancet Regional Health – Southeast Asia, 2026; 0 Among the consensus recommendations is this one, which summarizes the general positive tone adopted for national kidney exchange. "Each transplant center should initiate and expand swap transplantation, given that it is legal, cost-effective, yields better outcomes, and can help prevent unethical commercial transplants by improving access. Multicentric swap transplantation programmes should roll out in phases: start with intra-city exchanges, then intra-state, and eventually inter-state and national collaborations. This phased approach ensures growing scale is matched with operational readiness, providing safe, equitable, and efficient transplants across regions."

Steve Woodle, MD E. Steve Woodle, MD Woodle, professor of surgery and the William A. Altemeier endowed chair in surgery at the College of Medicine, is a multiorgan transplant surgeon and transplant immunologist who has spent more than four decades advancing the understanding of organ rejection and pioneering immunosuppressive therapies that have reshaped transplantation. Earlier in his career at the University of Chicago, he performed a liver transplant on a 10-day-old infant, setting a Guinness World Record for the youngest liver transplant recipient. He joined the College of Medicine in 1999 and directed the Division of Transplantation for nearly two decades, building an internationally recognized program of clinical and research excellence. In 2001, he performed Ohio’s first allogeneic islet transplant for type 1 diabetes. After undergoing his own liver transplant in 2003, Woodle returned to the operating room and became the first liver transplant recipient to perform a liver transplant. Woodle has helped originate several therapeutic approaches now considered standard in transplantation. As a fellow, he conceived the genetic re-engineering of OKT3, the first FDA-approved monoclonal antibody — work later developed into teplizumab (Tzield), which the FDA approved in 2022 as the first immunomodulatory therapy for type 1 diabetes. He was the first investigator to introduce plasma cell-targeted therapy for a non-malignant human disease, using proteasome inhibitors to treat antibody-mediated rejection in kidney transplant recipients. 21113a7a19:a7d807e7d8608906.title: The once and future market for prostitution in Rhode Island
21113a7a19:a7d807e7d8608906.author: Al Roth (noreply@blogger.com)
21113a7a19:a7d807e7d8608906.summary: Kim Krawiec , the great legal scholar of repugnant transactions, has written that rare (almost never seen) book review that extends the empirical study of an important, well-studied social science event, namely Rhode Island's experience of legal prostitution. It provides an illuminating followup to the germinal paper by Cunningham and Shah. (Prostitution in R.I. is one of the controversial markets covered in Moral Economics , and I believe Krawiec's book review is headed for a forthcoming symposium on the book in Œconomia ­­.) The Smallest State's Big Experiment by Kimberly D. Krawiec October 09, 2026 Abstract Rhode Island’s accidental decriminalization of prostitution in 1980 is typically told as the story of a legal change that went unnoticed for more than two decades. This review of Alvin Roth’s latest book, Moral Economics, challenges that standard account and explores its implications for Roth’s argument that markets need social support to flourish. Drawing on court records, contemporaneous news reports, arrest statistics, and legislative proceedings, I show that the statutory change was noticed almost immediately. Prostitution-related arrests continued, not because police and prosecutors were ignorantly arresting and charging sex workers and clients under a statute that no longer existed, but because the legal system adapted using tools – primarily the loitering prohibition that survived the 1980 rewrite – that have long been used to police behavior and individuals considered repugnant. After a 2003 judicial ruling closed an important enforcement avenue against indoor sex work and vaulted the market into the open, a coalition formed around trafficking concerns that eventually paved the way for recriminalization in 2009. Rhode Island’s accidental experiment with decriminalized sex work provided neither the deliberately designed regulatory framework nor the political backing that could build the type of social support that Roth insists (correctly, in my view)…

By Vjosa Isai "Canada will reverse its plan to allow people whose sole condition is a mental illness to seek medically assisted death, the government announced on Wednesday, abandoning a move to expand access to these patients. “ While there is not a perfect consensus on this issue , we believe this is the correct approach,” Sean Fraser, the minister of justice, told reporters on Parliament Hill. "A law, introduced under the former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, that allowed people with intolerable suffering from incurable mental health conditions to access a medically assisted death was initially poised to take effect in March 2023. Access for these patients was postponed for a year after public and some medical-community concerns that the existing system was not yet prepared to evaluate applications from these patients. In March 2024, the government delayed again, this time until March 2027, pending reviews by a panel of experts. "With the clock ticking toward that deadline, Mr. Fraser said the government “very recently” formalized its stance and that Canadians can soon expect parliament to pass legislation that will indefinitely bar people whose sole medical condition is a mental disorder from seeking medically assisted death. The Econometric Society Elects 30 New Fellows October 8, 2026 (New Haven, CT)—The Econometric Society is pleased to announce the election of 30 new Fellows. The first 100 cases of organ donation after euthanasia in the Netherlands: lessons from preliminary experiences. BMC Med Ethics (2026). https://doi.org/10.1186/s12910-026-01590-5 "Background Organ donation after euthanasia (ODE) is an evolving, patient-initiated procedure in the Netherlands. While it gives meaning to donors at the end-of-life, it introduces complex ethical and practical challenges for healthcare professionals. This study aims to describe the clinical characteristics and donation outcomes of the first 100 ODE procedures in the Netherlands, while outlining the practical and ethical dilemmas encountered. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed on prospectively collected data from the first 100 ODE procedures conducted between September 2012 and February 2023. To gain deeper insight into practical experiences and ethical themes, these data were discussed with organ donation coordinators and intensivists involved in the procedures. The analysis focused on clinical characteristics and donation outcomes, as on ethical and practical challenges. Results Neurodegenerative disorders were the primary underlying cause of suffering (52%), followed by psychiatric conditions (31%). The first 100 procedures resulted in 408 transplanted organs. Most procedures were performed in intensive care units, with general practitioners performing euthanasia. Key ethical and practical challenges included the tension between clinical protocols (e.g., fasting) and patient comfort, the medicalisation of the dying process through invasive monitoring, and the logistical barriers of starting ODE from home (ODEH). Furthermore, ethical concerns persist regarding euthanasia in psychiatric and dementia cases, and the emotional burden on healthcare professionals. Conclusions…

2f5fdda6a0:07a1b8850d9ac432.author: Scognamiglio, Annalisa
2f5fdda6a0:07a1b8850d9ac432.summary: Past research has documented a substantial finance wage premium. We examine whether this premium reflects differences in lifetime career opportunities. Using resume data, we reconstruct career trajectories in finance and nonfinance sectors and build synthetic measures of career attractiveness that account for compensation levels, growth, and risk. We find that asset management and investment banking provide a sizable risk-adjusted career premium relative to banking, insurance, and other sectors. This premium has declined across cohorts, particularly relative to high tech. Labor-market entry patterns respond to these premia: potential entrants treat finance and high-tech careers as substitutes when choosing where to start.

2f5fdda6a0:638ae45ef0c67b5e.title: Political Affiliation and Media Distrust: Evidence from Stock Market Investors
2f5fdda6a0:638ae45ef0c67b5e.author: Massa, Massimo
2f5fdda6a0:638ae45ef0c67b5e.summary: Does distrust in politically affiliated media induce a bias in investor beliefs? We study the acquisition of Dow Jones & Co. by News Corporation in 2007 as a shock to the political affiliation of Dow Jones outlets. Following the acquisition, the prices of Republican- (Democrat-) aligned stocks become less sensitive to favorable (unfavorable) Dow Jones Newswires (DJNW) sentiment, consistent with the market attaching less credibility to a politically affiliated source. There is, however, no evidence of change in DJNW sentiment, coverage, or language about Republican/Democrat stocks, suggesting a loss of stock price informativeness. Consistent with this view, a portfolio exploiting the attenuated reaction to DJNW news earns abnormal returns following 2007.

2f5fdda6a0:a7908c944a06eff7.author: Munk, Claus
2f5fdda6a0:a7908c944a06eff7.summary: Applying a rich model of individuals’ life-cycle utility maximization, I comprehensively evaluate retirement saving plans. Across a range of individual characteristics, access to basic plans with constant expected payouts and no or full annuitization leads to individual utility gains of up to 5.07% of initial wealth and lifetime income ($43,800 in present value terms), and almost all individuals prefer full annuitization and a target-date fund investment strategy. With flexible plans allowing for partial annuitization and non-constant expected payouts, utility gains go up to 5.81%, and most individuals prefer a high degree of annuitization and expected payouts being increasing through retirement.

For centuries, dominant assets in preindustrial economies were either land or cattle. Consequently, the type of farming prevailing locally shaped preferences and beliefs about the relative value of immovable and movable assets. This cultural heritage had long-lasting consequences. Today, individuals originating from societies with a history of crop agriculture—where the dominant asset was land—are more likely to be homeowners. For identification, I rely both on home ownership decisions of second-generation immigrants in the United States and on an instrument.

04be1a0d28:5cfa7b8214c8ee25.title: Target What? The Foundations of Poverty Targeting -- by Rema Hanna, Emily Breza, Benjamin A. Olken, Abhijit Banerjee, Arun G. Chandrasekhar, Gideon Moore
04be1a0d28:5cfa7b8214c8ee25.summary: Most government transfer programs aim to target the poor. Doing so implicitly assumes that the lowest-consumption households have the highest marginal social valuation, i.e., have the highest social welfare gain from an additional dollar. But this need not be the case. In 600 Indonesian villages, we ask over 5,500 villagers to rank other villagers on how well off they are and how much a modest cash transfer would help them, and compare these rankings to consumption and self-assessed welfare. Targeting consumption misses 77% of households with the highest marginal social valuation. Targeting self-assessed welfare misses 57%. Even targeting those the community ranks worst off in levels, not margins, misses 25%. Divergences between different notions of neediness are statistically predictable. In a randomized controlled trial, proxy means tests best target consumption, self-targeting ordeals capture self-assessed welfare levels, and community targeting comes closest to marginal social valuation. Targeting strategies inescapably embed normative stances.

04be1a0d28:ee90318fba1ffca5.title: Unconventional Monetary Policy and Deposit Retention -- by Philip Strahan, Tuo Yang
04be1a0d28:ee90318fba1ffca5.summary: The two dimensions of unconventional monetary policy — holding the short rate at the zero-lower bound (ZLB) and quantitative easing (QE) — shifted deposit composition toward more interest-sensitive customers. The ZLB drew these customers by creating rate compression, which limited the benefit of searching for high-yielding liquidity sources. QE also drew rate-sensitive, large depositors from the Federal Reserve’s purchases of bonds from non-banks. Once policy normalized, flow sensitivity and the deposit beta both increased with exposure to QE and the ZLB. We conclude that unconventional monetary policy made deposit retention costlier and riskier for banks.

04be1a0d28:4a6c094b462ab89d.title: Debiasing Law Enforcement Officers: Evidence from an Expressive Arts Intervention in India -- by Sofia Amaral, Girija Borker, Nishith Prakash, María Micaela Sviatschi
04be1a0d28:4a6c094b462ab89d.summary: Frontline state agents exercise substantial discretion over citizens’ access to public services, yet little is known about whether the attitudes and beliefs shaping this discretion can be changed among incumbent bureaucrats. Partnering with the Bihar Police - one of India’s largest states that operates under comparatively severe policing capacity constraints, we conduct a cluster randomized controlled trial across 417 police stations and roughly 2,500 active duty senior field police officers to evaluate a three-day expressive arts intervention, grounded in the Theatre of the Oppressed, designed to change police responses to gender-based violence (GBV). Approximately 7 months after baseline, treated officers exhibit more favorable attitudes toward GBV, greater empathy, and stronger legal knowledge. These changes translate into observed policing behavior: in standardized victim audits conducted one year later, officers in treated stations are 15 percentage points less likely to blame victims, dismiss fewer complaints, and provide more referrals, while administrative records show a 41 percent reduction in registration delays and, over a longer horizon, increased GBV reporting by citizens. Exploiting variation generated by officer transfers, we find suggestive evidence that these effects persist when treated officers relocate and diffuse to untreated officers working alongside treated colleagues. The effects also extend to the workplace: junior female officers working with treated senior officers report lower harassment and anxiety. These findings show that the attitudes shaping bureaucratic discretion are malleable and that changing how incumbent state agents exercise authority can improve both citizen-facing service delivery and the broader workplace environment.

04be1a0d28:15d97949f4ab4b94.title: TaskNet: Building Occupational Task Inventories from Worker Interviews at Scale -- by Jennifer Wang, Andreas Haupt, Isaac Robinson, Phil Lewis, Erik Brynjolfsson, Diyi Yang
04be1a0d28:15d97949f4ab4b94.summary: Understanding how AI is reshaping work requires an accurate account of the tasks workers perform. Workers are often the first to see how their jobs are changing, as new responsibilities and tools often appear in everyday work before these changes reach formal descriptions. Interviews with workers can help capture these emerging changes in job tasks. Yet existing methods support standardized ratings across workers, while open-ended conversations with workers remain costly to collect and synthesize at scale. We introduce the Stanford Task Network (TaskNet), an occupational taxonomy grounded directly in workers’ accounts of their everyday work. To construct TaskNet, we develop a mixed-initiative system that induces task inventories directly from workers. The system conducts interviews, standardizes reports into individual task lists, and aggregates these lists into occupational task inventories. Applied to six occupations spanning a range of education requirements and AI exposure, our system interviews 132 workers and produces 202 task statements from 2726 reports, all of which were accepted by O*NET Center analysts, compared to roughly 65%of workers’ write-in task suggestions collected through the current O*NET data collection process, a major alternative source for emerging tasks. Every statement is validated by 318 incumbents in 7923 ratings of relevance and importance. Relative to the task data from the O*NET 31.0 database for the sampled occupations, TaskNet covers 75% of the 118 published O*NET tasks and adds 79 tasks with no O*NET counterpart and 58 that refine existing statements. It covers 89% of tasks reported by held-out workers, compared with 79% for O*NET, and a larger share of the activities described in employer job postings (72.5% vs. 70.2%). Downstream, TaskNet changes AI exposure estimates in both directions, raising them for Software Developers and Lawyers, two occupations where AI’s effects are widely debated.
