40c94f9b29:b100efc723d36b59.title: Hubris, Humility, and the AI Revolution (with Walter Isaacson)
40c94f9b29:b100efc723d36b59.summary: The people building artificial intelligence worry there’s a real chance it could doom us all. So why do they keep building anyway? Walter Isaacson , biographer extraordinaire, talks with EconTalk’s Russ Roberts about why the AI innovators feel trapped in a race none of them can pause. Drawing on The Builders, a new podcast he’s launched, Isaacson explains why so many of these innovators see humility and empathy as handicaps rather than virtues, and why he worries they’re pouring their talent into autonomous agents that leave humans out of the loop. Isaacson traces today’s AI debate back to the rival visions of Alan Turing and Ada Lovelace, reveals why Elon Musk once told him his empathy was really vanity, and recalls Benjamin Franklin’s surprising lesson about faking humility. Plus: a Marie Curie story involving a secret affair and a second Nobel Prize. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:150ea9598763b2ab.title: Revisiting the China Shock (with Joseph Francis)
40c94f9b29:150ea9598763b2ab.summary: What if the results of one of the most influential economics papers of the past 25 years are unreliable? The “China shock” narrative–that a surge of Chinese imports destroyed American manufacturing jobs and the communities that depended on them–became conventional wisdom in Washington and beyond. But economic historian Joseph Francis argues that the claim is much weaker than it looks. Listen as he tells EconTalk’s Russ Roberts how a 2022 correction to the paper’s research design cut its estimate of lost jobs in half and erased its findings on wages and living standards. He and Russ then look at what this affair reveals about economics as a field, including the incentives that reward dramatic results, and the problems with peer review. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:132b72ffa2674c2c.title: The Fusion of Commercial Civilization
40c94f9b29:132b72ffa2674c2c.summary: In his new book The Civilization of Commerce ( Encounter Books, October 2026 ), American Institute for Economic Research president Samuel Gregg explores the requirements, benefits, and positive features of a commercial society, which isn’t merely trading and exchanging goods but a civilization of growth in knowledge, specialization, networks, and institutions that is built on tradition, virtue, and law. Moving beyond the usual arguments for free markets, Gregg doesn’t base his case on personal liberty, economic growth, efficiency, and technological sophistication. While these elements are present, Gregg grounds his case in the virtues, traditions, institutions, habits, and mindset of a commercial civilization. The book draws on the case made by Friedrich Hayek and Adam Smith for what they both called “the Great Society.” This commercial society is built on a certain approach to knowledge, dynamism, institutions, and virtue that drives individual and social improvement, all of which contributes to opulence, defined by Smith as “overcoming deprivation.” Such a trajectory also requires a steady adherence to, and a continued building of social and moral capital that no one rationally designed, but that many in the past and present have contributed to and shaped. In this argument, we can trace Hayek’s beliefs and his views as a central figure in the Austrian School of Economics , aspects of the American founding and the nineteenth-century republic, Tocqueville ’s musings on democratic society, and most significantly, the influence of the Scottish Enlightenment . Gregg observes that much of the case for understanding commercial civilization turns on what leading Scottish thinkers identified in their developing society in the eighteenth century: a new type of economic and social ordering that broke with a largely static and, in many cases, impoverished existence. He demonstrates how Friedrich Hayek and Adam Smith’s Great Society liberated people “from economic stagnation…

40c94f9b29:dab670eec04342c8.title: The Invisible Shackle: How Bureaucracy Stifles the Economy and Constrains Our Freedom
40c94f9b29:dab670eec04342c8.summary: For millions of entrepreneurs , the greatest barrier to generating wealth is no longer market competition but the relentless expansion of regulations and administrative procedures. While governance is ostensibly designed to ensure order, modern bureaucracy has morphed into a formidable “invisible shackle.” Rather than functioning as a neutral tool of oversight, excessive red tape treats a citizen’s inherent right to produce as a conditional concession granted by the state through endless, discretionary hurdles. The sixth edition of the Index of Bureaucracy 2026, developed at the Adam Smith Center for Economic Freedom at Florida International University, offers an empirical diagnosis of this administrative drain. Analyzing 27 countries—20 from Latin America and the Caribbean (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guyana, Honduras, Jamaica, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, and Venezuela), representing 94.4% of regional GDP, and 7 from Europe (France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom), accounting for 59% of Europe’s GDP—the study maps the complete administrative burden cycle across three milestones of the business life cycle: opening, running, and closing. The findings offer an unvarnished look at how bureaucratic overload distorts economies, punishes small businesses, and destroys productive potential. The Relevance of Measuring Bureaucracy Quantifying bureaucracy is not a mere academic exercise; it is an urgent economic necessity. Historically, administrative complexity has been treated as an unavoidable cost of doing business. However, scholarly frameworks from public choice theory, institutional and neo-institutional economics, and modern studies of governance show that government rules and procedures tend to expand because of political incentives, institutional fragmentation, and the tendency of legislators to answer every social…

40c94f9b29:2702ebc51439ad37.title: How Your Situation Shapes You (with Angela Duckworth)
40c94f9b29:2702ebc51439ad37.summary: Sure, you can use willpower or grit to break bad habits and build new ones. But maybe the key to success is simpler: change your situation. Psychologist Angela Duckworth explains to EconTalk’s Russ Roberts why the people and places around us shape our behavior more than we realize–and why we’re hard-wired to resist that idea. Listen as they discuss the three-box framework for understanding human behavior, why creating friction to avoid temptation is itself an act of agency, and how the cultures we choose to join end up shaping who we become. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:34e4107222a28b61.title: Sam’s Links: September Edition
40c94f9b29:34e4107222a28b61.summary: Sam Enright works on innovation policy at Progress Ireland , an independent policy think tank in Dublin, and runs a publication called The Fitzwilliam . Most relevant to us, on his personal blog , he writes a popular link roundup ; what follows is an abridged version of his Links for August. Blogs and short links Notes from my talk at Invisible College in Cambridge about the intellectual history of proportional representation voting systems. The latest Fitzwilliam essay investigates the design of the Irish sovereign wealth fund and finds it lacking . Ben Yeoh writes about my favour auction . He also links to me linking to him linking to me linking to him . A new record for the number of layers of recursion featured on the blog. Within the first generation of settlement, British Australians were enjoying something like the living standards of Britain itself. Being a convicted criminal is apparently not enough to entirely exclude you from the benefits of legal occupational licensing: Before the arrival of solicitors who were also free settlers, legal representation was sometimes…

40c94f9b29:83e72c7055498ecf.title: Lives Wasted and Well-Lived: David Wolpe on The Death of Ivan Ilyich
40c94f9b29:83e72c7055498ecf.summary: What if you did everything right and discovered on your deathbed that you’ve wasted your life? Rabbi and author David Wolpe talks about Tolstoy’s “The Death of Ivan Ilyich” with EconTalk’s Russ Roberts . Weaving Rabbi Wolpe’s own brushes with mortality and his years at the bedsides of the dying into Tolstoy’s masterpiece, they talk about the lies we tell ourselves about death, our longing for honesty and human touch at the end, and the way that death forces us to take a clear-eyed look at life. They conclude by offering advice on how we can avoid Ivan’s regrets. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:1f07dabd4e53cb32.title: The Liberty Fund Prize for Advancing Economic Liberty Presented by The Neal and Jane Freeman Foundation
40c94f9b29:1f07dabd4e53cb32.summary: Senator Phil Gramm and Professor Donald Boudreaux have been named the inaugural recipients of The Liberty Fund Prize for Advancing Economic Liberty, presented by The Neal and Jane Freeman Foundation. Through decades of teaching, writing, and public discourse, both honorees have deepened the public’s understanding of how competitive markets sustain a free society. The prize was presented during a ceremony at Liberty Fund headquarters in Carmel, Indiana, on Monday, October 12, 2026. Established to honor those who have illuminated the foundations of free markets and advanced them in the wider world, the prize reflects a principle long held by Liberty Fund and shared by Neal B. Freeman: That competitive markets are not merely instruments of material progress but expressions of human liberty itself, and that their defense requires both clarity of thought and steadfastness of purpose. Freeman, chairman of The Neal and Jane Freeman Foundation, served as Washington editor of National Review and was the founding producer of Firing Line . Across a long career in journalism and broadcasting, he has been a prominent voice in the public conversation about economic freedom and individual liberty. Together, the two recipients are honored for lifetimes of work that have shaped how the world understands economic liberty. Senator Phil Gramm began his career as an economist, spending more than a decade at Texas A&M University teaching and writing on monetary theory, private property, and the economics of natural resources. Over a long career in public service, he became a prominent advocate for fiscal restraint, competitive markets, and economic freedom while serving in the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate. He continues to write and speak on economic policy as a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Professor Donald Boudreaux has devoted his career to helping his students and the broader public better understand the principles of economics. Through…

40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.title: A Nobel for Microfoundations
40c94f9b29:0c24df0751808b58.summary: This year, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, colloquially called the Nobel Prize in Economics , went to Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University for their work in “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization.” Those five words do not adequately describe their contributions. Hall and Woodford are macroeconomists whose major works emerged when macro was in crisis. Old school Keynesian economics had dominated economic policy discussions since the 1940s. Generally speaking, Keynesians advocated fiscal policy tools (specifically taxes and spending) to stabilize the economy. For about 20 years, those tools seemed to work. But starting in the late 1960s and through the 70s, the macroeconomic relationships broke down. A seemingly impossible confluence of rising inflation and high unemployment characterized this period. Keynesian spending policies were becoming impotent. Critics of Keynesianism rose, and macroeconomics called out for new theories. It was during this period that macroeconomics began to explore more microfoundations. That is, rather than treating the economy as a series of aggregates and their relations to one another, economists started to explore how aggregate macroeconomic factors were the results of individual behavior, institutions, and expectations. Stabilization policy could not be simply levers pulled or pushed by the policymaker. Rather, stabilization policy had to include theories on how people will react to such changes, as well as their expectations about the future. Models such as rational expectations, adaptive expectations, and the permanent income hypothesis were developed during this period as a means to explain why these Keynesian stabilization policies failed. One of the models that came out of this period was Milton Friedman’s Permanent Income Hypothesis. The basic idea is that people base their consumption decisions not just on current income…

40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.title: The Great Fertility Collapse (with Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde)
40c94f9b29:a780bf86d4a4f4b9.summary: For the first time in human history, we’re not having enough children to keep the world’s population from falling. And fertility is collapsing fastest not in rich nations but in places like Colombia, Thailand, and Guatemala, upending decades of economic wisdom. Economist Jesus Fernandez-Villaverde tells EconTalk’s Russ Roberts that falling fertility has accelerated sharply over the past decade and defies easy explanation. Declining religiosity, smartphones and social media, soaring housing costs, and changing gender norms are popular, but unconfirmed, theories. Fernandez-Villaverde offers his own speculative answer, that modern life makes a third child costly and childlessness easy, but admits the puzzle is unsolved. What’s clearer is why it matters: as retirees become the dominant voting bloc, spending on pensions and health care crowds out roads, schools, and defense. Shrinking economies make public debt harder to service, and fewer births mean fewer scientists, artists, and inventors. (1 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.title: Debt and Profit
40c94f9b29:a54c6f82e5753273.summary: An ordinary person can earn a paycheque, pay her taxes, cover living costs and mortgage payments, and perhaps even add to her savings — and at the end of the day she will still owe most of her mortgage. This is a normal state of affairs, and nobody finds it puzzling. Yet when a company reports profits alongside large amounts of debt, the reaction is often to question whether it’s really making money. After all, if a company is “truly” profitable, why is it in debt? The short answer is that debt is not the opposite of profit. Loss is the opposite of profit. This imagined contradiction is easier to resolve once we recognize that profit is a flow and debt is a stock. According to the SEC’s guide to financial statements, the income statement records revenues, expenses, and profit over a period, while the balance sheet records assets and liabilities — such as debt — at a point in time. In fact, debt and profit are entirely unrelated concepts. Imagine a firm borrows money to purchase a machine. When the loan arrives, the firm’s cash and debt rise by the same amount. When the purchase is made, the firm simply exchanges one asset (cash) for another (the machine). Neither transaction creates a profit or a loss. Over time, the machine may be used in productive activities that raise revenue. By the same token, depreciation in the machine’s value can lower profit over its useful life, and interest — the cost of managing debt — adds to expenditures for as long as the debt is outstanding. The best way to think about debt is as a contract that moves purchasing power across people and time. Savers give up control over their resources today, while borrowers promise principal and interest later in exchange for controlling those resources now. Banks and bond markets pool and match funds from many people, letting a single firm undertake a factory, railway, or phone network without first accumulating the cash itself. As Frédéric Bastiat put it, credit institutions “can make it easier…

40c94f9b29:b79d2bc5c55e544a.title: Addiction, Faith, and the Limits of Willpower (with Meghan O’Gieblyn)
40c94f9b29:b79d2bc5c55e544a.summary: Why do we keep doing things we know we shouldn’t? And is that really a failure of will? Author Meghan O’Gieblyn spent years trying to answer that question, first in response to her struggle with alcoholism and her loss of faith, and then by means of Simone Weil, William James, and Iris Murdoch, who argue that the will is powerless over the things we want to change most. Listen as she speaks with EconTalk’s Russ Roberts about her new memoir, Will and Attention , which explores why paying attention does what effort alone can’t, why we can reason ourselves into doing destructive things, and why the choices that most shape our lives are the “choices in between the choices,” or the ones we barely notice making at all. (0 COMMENTS)

40c94f9b29:e8f93f2515871ba5.title: Prices as a Map for Minds That Can’t Know Everything
40c94f9b29:e8f93f2515871ba5.summary: Reading Dean Ball’s recent essay “ On the Loose ” has me thinking about an old idea in a new light. Ball asks us to imagine a world containing “self-sovereign” AI agents. These are not simply chatbots we rent by the month. They are agents capable of operating independently, acquiring the computer they need to keep running, moving across infrastructure, and interacting economically without a human owner making each decision. Some might be productive. Some, Ball worries, might be rogue. Whether or not you find the whole scenario plausible, it forces an interesting economic question. If such an agent existed, how would it find its way around an economy? It cannot read the minds of the millions of strangers whose choices determine what is valuable. It does not automatically know that a mine flooded yesterday, that a restaurant has empty tables tonight, or that a particular programmer suddenly has three free hours. What can it see? The answer, I think, is the same thing you and I look at: prices. In 1945, Friedrich Hayek published “ The Use of Knowledge in Society .” His starting point was humility about how little any single mind can hold. A modern economy needs to make use of knowledge about who needs tin, which mine just flooded, and what resources happen to be sitting idle in one particular place. This information is not sitting in a central file. It is scattered across millions of people, most of whom know only their own small corner of the world. Hayek emphasized the importance of knowledge of the particular circumstances of “time and place.” The person standing beside an underused machine knows something that a central planner does not. Hayek’s insight was that the price system allows people to act on some of this knowledge without possessing all of it. When tin becomes scarce, its price rises. The people who use tin do not need to know why. It could be a flooded mine or a war in a country they cannot find on a map. They only need to know that tin is more…

26e942feef:ef6e72d6845e0735.title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
26e942feef:ef6e72d6845e0735.author: Van Reenen, John
26e942feef:ef6e72d6845e0735.summary: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

26e942feef:8d1962f98ebcc65f.title: Earnings Dynamics under Firm Heterogeneity
26e942feef:8d1962f98ebcc65f.author: Timo Virtanen
26e942feef:8d1962f98ebcc65f.summary: We develop a permanent–transitory earnings process in which permanent shocks depend on a latent firm type and workers’ exposure to firm types is persistent. Persistence can substantially slow the finite-horizon attenuation of earnings skewness and excess kurtosis over the life cycle relative to an iid mixture benchmark. We estimate the model from matched employer-employee data, first grouping firms based on the distribution of residual earnings changes and then using worker transitions across groups to estimate persistence. Finnish data reveal heterogeneity in permanent-shock variances and persistent exposure to firm groups. Although skewness and excess kurtosis are not targeted in estimation, over ages 35–50 the extended model accounts for 49 percent of average empirical skewness and 39 percent of average excess kurtosis, compared with 4 percent and 3 percent under the iid benchmark. Quantitative exercises show that persistence increases the life-cycle cost of earnings risk and affects saving behavior.

26e942feef:fc419420556e8540.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
26e942feef:fc419420556e8540.author: Ana Popovici
26e942feef:fc419420556e8540.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

26e942feef:58acf291ef954ec1.title: Tariffs, Employment and the Balance of Trade
26e942feef:58acf291ef954ec1.author: Sweder van Wijnbergen
26e942feef:58acf291ef954ec1.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

26e942feef:9e86f65dc1557311.title: The Transparency Tax : Discouraging Firm Ownership via Tax Havens
26e942feef:9e86f65dc1557311.author: Bajaña, Alex
26e942feef:9e86f65dc1557311.summary: Tax havens weaken tax enforcement by obscuring firm ownership and facilitating offshore evasion. This paper studies a reform in Ecuador that imposed a corporate tax surcharge on firms with owners in tax havens, using a newly available ownership registry. Comparing haven-owned firms to other foreign-owned firms, the analysis finds that the reform reduced haven ownership by 12 percentage points, largely through disclosure of non-haven individual owners. Exposed firms reduced transactions with tax havens and increased corporate tax payments, with no detectable effects on investment or firm size. The results suggest that ownership transparency can meaningfully improve tax compliance at limited efficiency cost, even through unilateral action.

26e942feef:16426232dae6b9e2.title: Measuring Shipping Disruptions with Satellite Data
26e942feef:16426232dae6b9e2.author: Ricardo Marto
26e942feef:16426232dae6b9e2.summary: A new measure using satellite vessel-tracking data reveals how much potential U.S.-bound shipping capacity was reduced by disruptions such as port congestion, canal bottlenecks and rerouting.

26e942feef:aa9c38191ba05627.title: Which types of education raise firm productivity? Evidence for managers and workers in the UK
26e942feef:aa9c38191ba05627.author: Hall, Tessa
26e942feef:aa9c38191ba05627.summary: This paper estimates the firm productivity returns to degree field, institution quality, and degree level, and compares them with wage returns. I link a LinkedIn panel from Revelio Labs to Orbis financial accounts for over 20, 000 UK firms over 2015?2024. Within firms, a bachelor's degree raises a worker's productivity by around 20%; a top-20 institution adds a further 10% and a postgraduate qualification 6%. The returns differ by organisational role. A bachelor's degree raises productivity for managers and non-managers alike. Specialist credentials - a STEM field, an elite institution - raise productivity for non-managers but not for managers, whose premium loads instead on postgraduate qualifications, above all MBAs. Managers also contribute around 26% more than otherwise identical non-managers, a premium that education does not explain. Averaged over the workforce, wage premia are close to productivity premia for each type of degree. However, the average conceals two wedges of opposite sign: STEM-trained non-managers are paid below their relative productivity, and degree-holding managers above it. Finally, for a subset of firms matched to the World Management Survey, workforce education accounts for around a quarter the well-documented correlation between management practices and productivity.

26e942feef:d6ebf535151fd830.title: Business networks and the persistence of entrepreneurship: evidence from China
26e942feef:d6ebf535151fd830.author: Lee, Neil
26e942feef:d6ebf535151fd830.summary: This paper investigates the long run association between business networks and entrepreneurship and regional development in China. We focus on chambers of commerce, bodies which facilitated networking between businesses until private firms were banned by Mao. Our results suggest that the pre-Mao chamber system is associated with long-lasting patterns of business creation and economic output in China, with this influence surviving until the post-1978 return of the market economy. The associations are strongest in the early reform period but weaken over time. We show evidence that historic chambers density is correlated with later social capital, despite major political change.

26e942feef:800932119aa7f871.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
26e942feef:800932119aa7f871.author: Xu, Yaling
26e942feef:800932119aa7f871.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

26e942feef:33a508e98ad79509.title: What is an AI worker? Evidence from Matched Vacancy-Hires
26e942feef:33a508e98ad79509.author: Hellsten, Mark
26e942feef:33a508e98ad79509.summary: Despite growing policy interest in AI workforce development, surprisingly little is known about what defines these workers, or indeed if they differ from their occupational peers. Using a novel matched vacancy-hire dataset linking Swedish job postings to the individuals hired to fill them, drawn from register data on the entire Swedish population, I study the characteristics of workers who develop and apply AI. Observable traits including high cognitive ability, a tertiary degree in STEM subjects, and a recent migrant background largely explain occupational sorting. Of these, only higher education, prior AI experience, and a science degree set them apart within occupation. I then use earnings as a window onto unobservable differences: AI workers earn approximately 5% more than their peers, entirely explained by firm-level wages. However, AI workers with a doctorate degree stand out sharply in both traits and earnings, indicating that AI workers split into segments that differ by the complexity of their skills and tasks. Taken together, these results point to two distinct policy levers: the supply of average AI workers, termed AI integrators, can be expanded via STEM education participation, while the elite AI developers are supplied by researchers moving to the private sector.

26e942feef:e6c6f5dddcb85506.title: Tracking management practices over time: Response rates and survey design choices behind the UK Management and Expectations Survey
26e942feef:e6c6f5dddcb85506.author: Wickersham, Tom
26e942feef:e6c6f5dddcb85506.summary: This paper uses three waves of the ONS Management and Expectations Survey (2016, 2020 and 2023) to examine how management practices evolve over time and to understand response behaviour in a voluntary business survey. We track management scores for firms responding across multiple waves and assess the extent to which changes in management practices reflect genuine managerial improvements or responder biases captured by the responder’s occupation. Firms that responded in 2020 were 24.9 percentage points more likely to respond in 2023 when controlling for firm characteristics. Where the individual responding on behalf of the firm was a senior official, such as a director, the respondent provided faster and more consistent responses across waves than firms responding with junior staff. Firms responding in all three waves report higher and improving management practices on average, particularly in employment practices. However, this difference is associated with observable firm characteristics, such as firm size. These results highlight the importance of understanding response patterns when interpreting survey results. We recommend maintaining continuity by retaining firms that responded in all three waves, encouraging responses from senior staff, and applying longitudinal weights to address non-response. The findings support improved survey design for future MES waves and strengthen the use of management practices as a measure of organisational capital in productivity research.

26e942feef:bc3e8394a1ddef62.title: The Geoeconomic Footprint of Chinese Acquisitions: Micro-Evidence on Target Firms
26e942feef:bc3e8394a1ddef62.author: Sjöholm, Fredrik
26e942feef:bc3e8394a1ddef62.summary: Chinese acquisitions of Western firms have become central to debates over technology transfer, national security, and investment screening. Understanding their economic consequences requires evidence on how acquired firms perform and reorganize under Chinese ownership. Using linked Swedish firm and worker registers for 1997–2021 and a matched, stacked difference-in-differences design, we examine majority acquisitions by Chinese and other foreign owners. Other foreign acquisitions raise labor productivity by about 6 percent and employment by about 14 percent on average, alongside increases in total factor productivity, workforce skills, and trade intensity. They also reshape management, strengthen trade links with the acquirer’s home country, and increase workers’ mobility to multinational enterprises. For Chinese acquisitions, we find no statistically detectable improvements in firm performance or comparable evidence of management restructuring, worker mobility, or trade integration. Chinese acquisitions are also rare in industries classified as security-sensitive. These findings provide a detailed account of the economic footprint of Chinese ownership in an advanced host economy. The pattern is consistent with acquisitions seeking assets valuable to the parent group rather than gains through restructuring the target.

26e942feef:42da307b91160128.title: Representation over Rents: Sorting in a Market for Lemons
26e942feef:42da307b91160128.author: Pieter Gautier
26e942feef:42da307b91160128.summary: Search frictions normally raise the bar for sorting: both random and directed search require complementarities strictly stronger than the supermodularity that suffices in Becker's (1973) frictionless model. We introduce private information into this setting: firms post wages without observing worker productivity, while better workers have better outside options, creating a market for lemons (Akerlof 1970). We show that this information friction pushes sorting the other way: attracting high-productivity workers without attracting low-productivity ones requires a higher wage paired with a lower job-finding probability, so vacancies fill faster. This strict ranking of vacancy filling rates sorts the market positively whenever output is complementary in worker and firm quality. Becker's condition therefore suffices once more, and private information makes positive sorting easier to sustain than complete information does.

26e942feef:cfa2403e9f8860ee.title: Returns to Private Debt in Emerging and Developing Economies
26e942feef:cfa2403e9f8860ee.author: Moelders, Florian
26e942feef:cfa2403e9f8860ee.summary: Private debt is an important form of corporate financing in emerging markets, but its investor returns are not well understood. This paper uses loan-level cash flow data from the International Finance Corporation to provide the first systematic evidence on realized returns across 4, 109 loans over more than 20 years, totaling about US$115 billion in 127 countries. Post–global financial crisis loans outperform both the JPMorgan Corporate Emerging Market Bond Index and U.S. Treasuries, with public market equivalents of 1.02 and 1.10, respectively, rising to 1.05 and 1.14 over the latest five years. Over 2002–24, the corresponding public market equivalents are 0.98 and 1.07, respectively, with global financial crisis–era vintages posting weaker performance relative to the JPMorgan Corporate Emerging Market Bond Index. Overall, returns are competitive with public markets. The paper also assesses financial performance more specifically within the most challenging markets: very low-income countries and fragile and conflict-affected states. Although default rates are higher in these markets, returns relative to public-market alternatives are statistically indistinguishable from those of the overall portfolio, suggesting that the International Finance Corporation priced default risk appropriately even in these markets.

26e942feef:7d35b3deb708c512.title: Minimum Wages and Cost-Push Inflation: Economy-Wide Evidence from Germany
26e942feef:7d35b3deb708c512.author: Maximilian Priem
26e942feef:7d35b3deb708c512.summary: We provide the first estimates of minimum wage effects on the aggregate price level using data on the near-full German consumer basket across four national reforms, 2015-2024. Drawing on a structural model of pricing under imperfect competition, we utilise minimum wage cost shocks rather than the commonly used firm-level ‘bite’ that we show to be biased under strategic complementarity. Labour cost pass-through is 83-94 percent, at the higher end of estimates for other cost shocks. The implied macro-price elasticity is 0.024. The largest increase in October 2022 to €12 raised the aggregate price level by 0.39 percent.

26e942feef:0b2ff47be3072c71.title: Moving Out: Geoeconomic Policy and the Relocation of Foreign Affiliates
26e942feef:0b2ff47be3072c71.author: Stefano Verzillo
26e942feef:0b2ff47be3072c71.summary: Governments increasingly use trade and industrial policy to reshape where multinationals produce, yet standard measures of this geoeconomic pressure are aggregate and cannot detect origin-specific discrimination. We build a bilateral, directional index of relative protectionism that measures how restrictive a destination is toward a given origin. We combine it with bilateral geopolitical risk indices and global ownership links over the period 2010-21, and estimate a gravity-type Poisson-Pseudo Maximum Likelihood model with three-way fixed effects. Our results show that where bilateral protectionism is greater, foreign-affiliate presence is markedly smaller: a 1 percentage point increase in the index is associated with 1.3% fewer subsidiaries than that origin-destination pair would otherwise have. The main mechanism runs through an operational hostility channel (e.g. discriminatory subsidies, procurement exclusion), which outweighs an offsetting tariff-jumping channel and concentrates in non-tradable sectors, where serving the market requires local presence. The estimates show no evidence of anticipation and are robust to longer lags and sample splits. Bilateral geopolitical risk enters with the same negative sign, adding a smaller but complementary layer of fragmentation risk to the effect of geoeconomic policy.

26e942feef:28297616f008c815.title: The Production Network Amplification of Retaliatory Tariffs
26e942feef:28297616f008c815.author: Jacob Short
26e942feef:28297616f008c815.summary: We develop a framework to quantify how tariff changes on imported goods affect sectoral and aggregate consumption prices through direct and production-network channels. Using Canada's input-output matrix and administrative firm-good import data for the universe of Canadian firms, we estimate price elasticities for tariffs on U.S.-imported goods. Tariffs on machinery and equipment and transport equipment generate the largest effects on final prices, reflecting their widespread use as intermediate inputs. On average, two-thirds of the total price response stems from higher intermediate input costs passing through domestic supply chains. Applying the framework to Canada's 2025 counter-tariffs, we estimate consumption price increases of 1.56 and 0.72 percentage points for the pre- and post-September 2025 phases, respectively; alternative packages of equal import value could reduce aggregate price effects by three to seven times. A hypothetical CUSMA breakdown reverting to MFN tariffs would raise final-good prices by 0.64 percentage points.

26e942feef:f8f5a1c2dbabd23e.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
26e942feef:f8f5a1c2dbabd23e.author: Collin B. Raymond
26e942feef:f8f5a1c2dbabd23e.summary: We study how firms choose among incentive contracts and how accurately managers predict their effects. Using a survey of managerial beliefs and a large-scale field experiment, we randomly assign agents at the market level to several widely used, expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes. In the field, the best-performing contract increases agent output and firm revenue by over 20% relative to the status quo, despite being ranked lower by managers, whereas the worst-performing contract performs as predicted. Managers correctly identify underperforming contracts but systematically underestimate top- performing ones. We document the sources of performance di!erences—labor supply responses rather than selection or pricing and the determinants of managerial predictability: contract complexity and managerial hierarchy. Our results highlight the importance of contract design for firm performance and reveal systematic limits to managerial cognition in shaping incentives.

26e942feef:334d09e6e7f7fdb7.title: The Investment Channel of Monetary Policy: Disentangling Firm Heterogeneity
26e942feef:334d09e6e7f7fdb7.author: Laura Pilossoph
26e942feef:334d09e6e7f7fdb7.summary: To study monetary policy transmission at the firm level, researchers typically consider heterogeneity along a small number of firm characteristics, such as size or leverage. We instead estimate the full distribution of firms’ investment responses to monetary policy, using a clustering regression framework. Our novel approach captures multidimensional and unobservable heterogeneity across firms and time. We find that investment by most firms in most time periods responds little to monetary policy. Only about 5% of firm-time observations are associated with a strong response. We then investigate the sources of heterogeneity ex post. We find that most of the variation in investment sensitivity arises within firms over time. Although several firm characteristics predict responsiveness to monetary policy, the majority of heterogeneity remains unexplained by firm observables. We demonstrate that our empirical estimates provide new targets for disciplining structural models of firm heterogeneity.

26e942feef:c11ab353728739f8.title: Taxing Entrepreneurial Wealth: Evidence from Norway, 2021–2025
26e942feef:c11ab353728739f8.author: Marius A. K. Ring
26e942feef:c11ab353728739f8.summary: Whether imposing higher taxes on business owners adversely affects business activity by constraining investment and inducing capitalist flight is a central question in the ongoing debate on how to tax the ultra wealthy. To shed new light, I exploit a series of related Norwegian reforms during 2021–2024 that increased dividend tax rates, removed migration-related capital gains tax loopholes, and nearly doubled the effective marginal tax rate on business wealth. These reforms spurred international debate and, allegedly, an “exodus” of Norwegian billionaires (Financial Times, 2023). While I document clear effects on migration, these responses are concentrated among the top 0.1% of the wealth distribution and mostly confined to 2022 and 2023. My results indicate that at most 100 individuals left due to the reforms. I find no evidence of significant outmigration or reduced inflows of startup founders or inventors. I estimate that absent any outmigration, wealth tax revenues would have increased by 75% from 2021 to 2024. Reform-driven outmigration lowers the revenue gain to 71.5%. My findings further show that outmigrating owners’ firms remain economically active and do not reduce investment. In a broader set of analyses, I examine whether business outcomes are affected, regardless of whether owners outmigrate, since firms may reduce investment both due to liquidity constraints or distortions to owners’ savings decisions. I compare firms owned by Norwegian individuals subject to the wealth tax with firms owned by foreigners and other tax-exempt entities. By merging historical ownership data from Orbis with the Norwegian shareholder register, I perform these analyses on both Norwegian and foreign-domiciled firms. Across settings, I find no evidence that Norwegian-owned firms pay out more dividends or invest less after the reforms, nor is there any evidence that the reform induced more bankruptcies. These findings indicate that the short-run economic costs of wealth…

26e942feef:29ebb44ed7b384e0.title: When Does Bad News Stick? Topic-Level Asymmetry in Narrative Dynamics
26e942feef:29ebb44ed7b384e0.author: Eswar S. Prasad
26e942feef:29ebb44ed7b384e0.summary: When does bad news stick? This paper shows that the persistence of media sentiment depends not only on whether news is good or bad, but also on what the news is about. Using the complete Wall Street Journal archive from 1990 to 2025, we construct monthly positive and negative sentiment indices for twelve economic topics and estimate topic-specific sentiment dynamics. Bad-news innovations generate larger cumulative responses than positive-sentiment innovations in every topic, indicating that negativity asymmetry is a broad feature of media sentiment. But the size of this asymmetry varies sharply across topics. The bad-minus-positive persistence gap is largest in security and human rights, firms and corporate strategy, health and public safety, and real estate and financial stability. Bad-news persistence is also sizable in data-rich topics such as financial markets, real estate, and corporate news, suggesting that frequent information arrival does not necessarily lead narratives to revert quickly. These findings show that aggregate sentiment indices mask substantial topic-level heterogeneity in the asymmetric dynamics of narratives, with potential implications for how persistent negative sentiment shapes expectations, asset prices, and real economic outcomes.

26e942feef:833c47310195d6e4.title: Integration versus Outsourcing with Vertical Linkages
26e942feef:833c47310195d6e4.author: Gaetano Alfredo Minerva
26e942feef:833c47310195d6e4.summary: I propose a mechanism for the coexistence of vertical integration and outsourcing within an industry. In a monopolistically competitive model with incomplete contracts, final-good producers under either organizational form combine labor and differentiated inputs to produce fixed capital. Since its unit cost depends on the industry price index, distinct zero-profit conditions can hold, sustaining a mixed free-entry equilibrium. The forms differ in fixed-capital cost per unit of contribution to the price index; this ranking determines comparative statics and whether local stability is possible. I derive a sufficient condition ensuring stability whenever the mixed equilibrium exists. In numerical parameterizations using empirically standard elasticities of substitution, the condition holds throughout the admissible range of vertical-linkage intensity. Within the stable region, larger markets raise the integrated share without changing output prices or supplier bargaining terms. Relative firm size depends on governance costs and upstream bargaining share, so the model imposes no uniform ranking.

26e942feef:412b5df697ac2708.title: Avoiding Regulation: Evidence from Nursing Homes
26e942feef:412b5df697ac2708.author: Riley League
26e942feef:412b5df697ac2708.summary: We study strategic responses by firms to threshold-based regulations. We document extensive bunching in response to additional staffing requirements for California nursing homes with at least 100 beds. To estimate the regulation’s effect on staffing, we develop a novel treatment effects estimator for threshold-based regulations under precise manipulation, by decomposing firms into response types based on counterfactual and realized staffing and size, separating causal effects from selection. We estimate that higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely due to selection, with low-staffing facilities manipulating their size to avoid the regulation. These size distortions limit access, particularly for disadvantaged patients.

26e942feef:efbecc19f108fc0e.title: Regulating a Monopolist through Capacity Control
26e942feef:efbecc19f108fc0e.author: Dihan Zou
26e942feef:efbecc19f108fc0e.summary: We study monopoly regulation when capacity is contractible but subsequent output is not. A firm privately observes its production cost before installing costly capacity and then choosing output, while the regulator cannot use transfers. We provide sufficient conditions under which a single capacity floor implements an optimal mechanism with full participation. The floor raises output by changing investment while leaving utilization to the firm after installation costs are sunk. Under additional conditions, the allocation has three regions: laissez-faire, full utilization of the floor, and underutilization. High-cost types knowingly install capacity they will not fully use, yet produce more than under laissez-faire. This physical waste is a necessary evil of optimal regulation that expands service. We also show that underutilization can persist in optimal regulation with capacity-contingent subsidies or a common entry fee.

26e942feef:dd05b757bdca93b4.title: Financing the AI Buildout
26e942feef:dd05b757bdca93b4.author: Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh
26e942feef:dd05b757bdca93b4.summary: Artificial intelligence is driving a large expansion in data center capacity, power infrastructure, and specialized computing equipment. We estimate that a 1 GW AI campus costs about $41 billion. A 188 GW U.S. buildout completed by 2032 would require total investment of nearly$9 trillion and amount to annual investment of 3.2 percent of GDP over 2025–2032. As hyperscaler capital expenditures outgrow internal cash flow, financing is shifting toward leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, securitization, and special-purpose vehicles. These structures expand funding capacity but also raise asset-level leverage, obscure contingent obligations, and expose investors to tenant concentration, technological obsolescence, execution delays, and uncertain residual values.

26e942feef:50e9468ebde11262.title: Which Workers Left the Labor Force Post-COVID Recession and Why?: Filing, Tax Credit Take-Up, and Labor Force Engagement by Occupation
26e942feef:50e9468ebde11262.author: Michael Stevens
26e942feef:50e9468ebde11262.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp initial rise in unemployment, followed by an unexpectedly tight labor market. Using a panel of tax data containing newly assembled information on worker occupation, we document persistent labor force exit, especially among low-income and low-skill workers. Low-skilled unmarried men are by far the most likely to exit, reinforcing recent concerns regarding the economic and social engagement of this group. Contrary to prevailing theories, we find little evidence that school closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments, or unemployment benefits explain these exits. Nor is the exit explained by additional upgrading of occupations or firm quality. Individuals who leave the labor force do not (on average) make up the missing income; however, self-employment income replaces roughly a quarter of the lost W-2 income. The facts suggest that the willingness to work for low pay decreased and preferences for leisure and job flexibility increased among a large set of workers who have found ways to get by with less income. These results have implications for tax policy, fiscal projections, and labor market dynamics in the post-pandemic economy.

26e942feef:3bfb18e406fc8d9c.title: Same Destination, Different Eyes: FDI and Trade Responses to Media Coverage of Geopolitical Risk
26e942feef:3bfb18e406fc8d9c.author: Yasuyuki Todo
26e942feef:3bfb18e406fc8d9c.summary: Existing measures of geopolitical risk are country-level and assume that all investors face the same risk in a given destination. This paper constructs a directional, bilateral geopolitical risk index that captures how the domestic media of each source country report on geopolitical conflicts involving each destination country. Using GDELT news data, the index covers more than 200 source and destination countries at a monthly frequency. We combine the index with project-level data on greenfield FDI and product-level trade data, and exploit variation across source countries for the same destination and period while controlling for destination-specific shocks. Source countries whose media place greater emphasis on a destination's geopolitical risk subsequently announce more greenfield projects there: a one-standard-deviation increase in the index is associated with a 7% increase in new projects. This suggests that firms may read such coverage as a signal of future market-access frictions and localize production in advance. Consistent with this interpretation, the association is concentrated in projects serving the host market and in sectors that depend on local demand, and is absent among politically aligned country pairs. By contrast, higher risk coverage is followed by a short-lived decline in imports, driven by severe conflicts, while exports do not respond.

26e942feef:8f4b54a02b7d1905.title: Tax Planning and Multinational Behavior
26e942feef:8f4b54a02b7d1905.author: Juan Carlos Suárez Serrato
26e942feef:8f4b54a02b7d1905.summary: We use newly linked IRS data to study how US multinationals use tax-planning structures that exploit mismatches between US and foreign tax laws. In 2016, these structures accounted for 36% of foreign profits despite being adopted by only 18% of firms. We develop and estimate a structural model using adoption patterns and changes in foreign effective tax rates, domestic and foreign investment, and global R&D following adoption. The model implies substantial heterogeneity in adoption costs and benefits and shows that restricting tax planning creates tradeoffs between tax revenue and economic activity that are amplified by global R&D linkages.

26e942feef:e0f0f748cc34a0ff.title: How Low Can You Go? Validating Administrative Union Records for Substate Estimates of US Union Membership
26e942feef:e0f0f748cc34a0ff.author: Eric Thai
26e942feef:e0f0f748cc34a0ff.summary: Unions are important economic and political actors at the local level, but the primary source on US union membership, the Current Population Survey (CPS), is unreliable below the state level. Researchers have therefore turned to union-reported membership in federal "LM" filings, geolocating unions and aggregating their reported membership to estimate union density for counties, commuting zones, and congressional districts. We ask whether this practice is sound. We develop and defend multilevel regression with poststratification (MrP) on the CPS as a benchmark, then validate LM-based estimates against it from the state level down. LM, CPS, and MrP are highly correlated at the state level, but this correlation is roughly halved at the congressional-district, commuting-zone, and county levels. The breakdown is driven in part by reporting "lumpiness, " which produces improbable values, including union densities exceeding 100%. Missing public sector union members explains only a small part of this divergence. These issues are substantively consequential: in a standard commuting-zone "China shock" regression, swapping density measures changes the import-exposure coefficient enough to alter its magnitude, significance, and sign. We conclude that LM records remain a rich resource for studying unions as organizations, but aggregating LM-reported membership is not a reliable way to measure union density at fine geographic resolution.

26e942feef:8688237e1e389ed0.title: Social push and the direction of innovation
26e942feef:8688237e1e389ed0.author: Jaravel, Xavier
26e942feef:8688237e1e389ed0.summary: What are the implications of unequal access to innovation careers for the direction of innovation and inequality? Leveraging novel linked datasets in the United States and Finland, we document that innovators create products more likely to be purchased by consumers like them in terms of gender, socioeconomic status, and age. Homophily exists both within narrow product categories and across industries, and has been stable in recent decades. Incorporating this “social push” channel into a growth model, we estimate that unequal access to innovation careers has a large effect on cost-of-living inequality and long-run growth.

26e942feef:b61055ddfe888fe0.title: The Effects of a Shorter Workweek on Employment, Output, and Productivity
26e942feef:b61055ddfe888fe0.author: Nina Roussille
26e942feef:b61055ddfe888fe0.summary: Do shorter workweeks generate work-sharing and productivity gains, as intended by policymakers? We study France’s pay-preserving reduction in the workweek from 39 to 35 hours, bundled with employer payroll tax cuts. We first exploit the staggered implementation by firm size to identify the impact of the reform package. We then use differential exposure to the hours cut and tax cut to separate their effects. We combine matched employer-employee, balance-sheet, and survey data to study worker, firm, and local labor market effects. The reform package left employment unchanged. This zero masks large offsetting effects: absent the tax cuts, the shorter workweek would have reduced employment by 3.8%. The effects are skill-biased, raising employment among managers and professionals while reducing it among other employees. Finally, shorter hours raised total factor productivity by 2%, limiting the output decline to 1% despite a 6% fall in total hours. Surveys point to work intensification and organizational changes as potential drivers of productivity gains.

26e942feef:2343dc858220bf3a.title: The Impact of Electrification on Quality and Productivity: Evidence from Japanese Cotton Spinning
26e942feef:2343dc858220bf3a.author: Yoichi Sugita
26e942feef:2343dc858220bf3a.summary: Conventional productivity estimation treats unobserved heterogeneity as a single efficiency term, conflating product quality with physical output efficiency. This paper shows that unobserved quality and quantity-based productivity (TFPQ) can be separately identified from panel data on prices, quantities, and inputs when the two latent variables exhibit differential persistence. A constructive nonparametric identification argument based on transformation models is developed, alongside a parametric estimator for implementation. Applied to Japanese cotton spinning (1914-1920), instrumenting for electric motor adoption with geographic variation in electricity grid access, quality increased by 1.5 percent per percentage point increase in electric motor share while TFPQ remained unchanged. Full electrification raised quality by nearly 60 percent relative to no adoption.

26e942feef:77831564fc762ade.title: Firms' Investment and the Real Transmission of the Global Financial Cycle
26e942feef:77831564fc762ade.author: Diego J. Perez
26e942feef:77831564fc762ade.summary: We study how global financial conditions transmit to firms’ investment. We document that increases in risk premia are followed by large investment contractions, particularly among firms with higher default risk. We develop a quantitative heterogeneous-firm open-economy model where firms finance investment with defaultable debt priced by risk-averse global investors. We identify a strong risk channel linking changes in the global price of risk to financing costs through firms’ quantity of risk—the sensitivity of debt repayment to global shocks. This introduces a risk dimension to stabilization policy: smoothing cash flows reduces firms’ quantity of risk and dampens international financial transmission.

26e942feef:6c9d3daa0af4d18a.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
26e942feef:6c9d3daa0af4d18a.author: Christopher T. Stanton
26e942feef:6c9d3daa0af4d18a.summary: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

26e942feef:0a4d43d328c522c7.title: AI Adoption by Firms: Insights from the Literature and the German Innovation Survey
26e942feef:0a4d43d328c522c7.author: Czarnitzki, Dirk
26e942feef:0a4d43d328c522c7.summary: This paper provides an overview of evidence on firmsâ€™ adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI). We revisit the main conceptual drivers of AI uptake discussed in the literature and summarize global trends in AI diffusion. We then examine the firm characteristics associated with adoptionâ€”including the distinction between in-house development and external acquisitionâ€”and highlight how patterns differ between general AI and generative AI technologies (GenAI). Next, we review the emerging literature on the productivity effects of AI, distinguishing non-experimental firm-level studies from recent experimental and quasi-experimental evidence on task-level impacts. As a case study, we draw on recent firm-level data from the German Innovation Survey to investigate how adoption decisions correlate with firm size, age, R&D intensity, human capital, location, and strategic orientation, and how these patterns vary across stages and types of AI adoption.

26e942feef:ce41107cf49fb624.title: Training Your Replacement: Worker Incentives and the Pace of Automation
26e942feef:ce41107cf49fb624.author: Peter Landry
26e942feef:ce41107cf49fb624.summary: Firms ask workers to train AI systems that will replace them. We model this with a worker who can shirk, cooperate with training, or obstruct training while maintaining productivity. Because training ends the job but only cooperation completes training, dismissal becomes a weaker penalty for shirking. The firm must raise the worker’s rent, and the worker gains from their replacement. AI can create jobs paying more than they produce and eliminate jobs it never automates. Firms paying only wages may slow training. A credible completion bonus equal to the worker’s rent without AI removes both the gain and the slowdown.

26e942feef:e14cca2f8057bbf4.title: How Shocks Travel: The Cross-Border Impact of Natural Disasters in Firm Networks
26e942feef:e14cca2f8057bbf4.author: Alviarez, Vanessa, Cevallos Fujiy, Brian, Espinoza Escobar, Angel De Jesus
26e942feef:e14cca2f8057bbf4.summary: Do the boundaries of the multinational firm shape how shocks propagate through global production networks? We link U.S. Bill of Lading microdata, geocoded natural disaster records, and cross-border ownership data to trace the transmission of exogenous supply disruptions from foreign suppliers to U.S. importers. Exploiting the quasi-random timing and location of natural disasters in a staggered event-study design, we document that disasters abroad generate sharp, persistent export declines at affected suppliers, shocks that propagate downstream, reducing the growth rate of U.S. importers total purchases by up to 25 percentage points. Transmission, however, is far from uniform: non-MNC buyers contract roughly twice as much as importers belonging to global corporations, and intra-firm relationships contract about a third less than arms-length ones. These patterns point to the internal networks of multinational firms as shock absorbers that attenuate and redirect supply-side disruptions, suggesting that firm boundaries are not merely organizational choices but also determinants of macroeconomic resilience.

26e942feef:7894de5cb170eaa3.title: From Power Shortages to Reliable Electricity: Grid Upgrading and Firm Performance in Nepal
26e942feef:7894de5cb170eaa3.author: Dâ€™Maris Coffman
26e942feef:7894de5cb170eaa3.summary: Reliable electricity is critical for firms in developing economies, yet improvements in electricity infrastructure may not translate immediately into better firm performance. This study examines whether grid upgrades were associated with changes in electricity reliability and firm performance in Nepal. We combine three waves of the World Bank Enterprise Survey (2009, 2013, and 2023) with city-level information on major grid upgrades and predetermined industry electricity intensity from the 2006/07 Census of Manufacturing Establishments. Using a difference-in-differences-in-differences (DDD) framework, we exploit variation across time, upgraded and comparison cities, and firmsâ€™ predetermined industry electricity intensity. The baseline estimates suggest that a one-standard-deviation increase in electricity intensity is associated with a 32.3-percentage-point larger decline in outage incidence and approximately 14.1 fewer hours of monthly outage exposure in upgraded cities relative to comparison cities. However, statistical significance is sensitive to model specification, and the outage-exposure estimate depends substantially on the composition of the comparison group. We find no statistically significant effects on real sales, employment, or labor productivity, while the positive estimates for total factor productivity provide only suggestive evidence of improvement. Pre-treatment placebo tests reveal no statistically significant differential changes, although the limited pre-treatment observations constrain their interpretation. Overall, the findings suggest that grid upgrading may improve electricity reliability, but the evidence is sensitive to identification and inference choices, and its implications for broader firm performance remain uncertain.

26e942feef:e657a5cc3fc9e22a.title: Industrial Policy via the IPO Market
26e942feef:e657a5cc3fc9e22a.author: Wang Renxuan
26e942feef:e657a5cc3fc9e22a.summary: This paper studies how China uses access to public equity markets as an instrument of industrial policy. We find that policy-favored status, rather than industry Tobin's Q, predicts IPO activity, in contrast to the United States. The effect is economically large: our estimates imply that favored industries had 287% more IPOs and 148% higher IPO proceeds than non-favored industries over 2002 to 2022. We develop a framework to interpret these findings: the government shapes the number of listing opportunities available across industries, while market forces determine which firms obtain these opportunities based on firm fundamentals. Consistent with our framework, policy favor also predicts a valuation premium which persists after listing.

26e942feef:36af80aa9fca3397.title: Who Can Control Our Firms? National Security and Foreign Ownership Regulation
26e942feef:36af80aa9fca3397.author: Olivier Kooi
26e942feef:36af80aa9fca3397.summary: Governments invoke national security to regulate foreign acquisitions of domestic firms. Why is ownership regulation a distinct policy margin beyond standard tools, like production subsidies and trade taxes? We show that contractual frictions make multinational firm boundaries central to geoeconomic policy. Within firms, ownership allocates residual control that affects outcomes through non-contractible decisions. Between governments, the absence of enforceable agreements makes the economic costs of conflict shape geopolitical bargaining. Foreign ownership depends on private returns to foreign control, but also determines national exposure to geopolitical conflict. It can increase foreign dependence, technology transfer, or sabotage scope. If such margins were contractible, the government could regulate them directly. When they are not, ownership regulation is the second-best tool that changes control rights and, thus, geopolitical outcomes. Consistent with our mechanism, U.S. regulation emphasizes the national-security risks of foreign control over firm decisions, has tightened with rising geopolitical tensions, and is tighter in sectors with higher exposure to defense demand and contractual frictions.

26e942feef:85417c17e0d7f564.title: Sorting in a Market for Lemons
26e942feef:85417c17e0d7f564.author: Gautier, Pieter
26e942feef:85417c17e0d7f564.summary: Search frictions normally raise the bar for sorting: both random and directed search require complementarities strictly stronger than the supermodularity that suffices in Becker's (1973) frictionless model. We introduce private information into this setting: firms post wages without observing worker productivity, while better workers have better outside options, creating a market for lemons (Akerlof 1970). We show that this information friction pushes sorting the other way: attracting high-productivity workers without attracting low-productivity ones requires a higher wage paired with a lower job-finding probability, so vacancies fill faster. This strict ranking of vacancy-filling rates sorts the market positively whenever output is complementary in worker and firm quality. Becker's condition therefore suffices once more, and private information makes positive sorting easier to sustain than complete information does.

26e942feef:06e5dcccb70a32dd.title: Employer Concentration and Minimum-Wage Employment Effects: Evidence from China's Transition
26e942feef:06e5dcccb70a32dd.author: Duan, Wenjing
26e942feef:06e5dcccb70a32dd.summary: How do local labour markets shape the employment effects of minimum wages? We evaluate this question using comprehensive manufacturing firm data and over 28, 000 hand-collected county-level minimum wages during China's market transition (1998-2007). We find that, consistently with monopsony models, the employment response to higher minimum-wage exposure becomes less negative as local employer concentration increases, with positive point estimates arising in highly concentrated markets in some specifications, particularly among domestic private firms. Higher minimum-wage exposure may also be associated with lower reported training expenditure and greater firm exit. Our findings indicate that the employment effects of minimum wages can depend critically on local market structures, highlighting the importance of geographical and institutional heterogeneity when assessing labour regulation in transitioning economies.

26e942feef:c8ff045703ee1359.title: Which Employers Alter Offers of Health Insurance in Response to Minimum Wage Increases? Evidence From the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey - Insurance Component
26e942feef:c8ff045703ee1359.author: Emma Wohl
26e942feef:c8ff045703ee1359.summary: Offers of health insurance vary significantly across firm and establishment characteristics, including firm size, workforce sex, and workforce age (Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, 2024, Table I.A.2; Abraham et al., 2016). Low-wage workers in particular are less likely to receive health insurance from their employer, and employers tend to roll back benefits as minimum wages rise (Meiselbach and Abraham, 2023; Marks, 2011). This study aims to identify the effects by employer and workforce characteristics of minimum wage increases on employer-provided benefits using restricted-use data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey-Insurance Component (MEPS-IC). I use a two-way fixed effects approach, exploiting state legislation variation, to identify changes in the rates of employers offering health insurance and employer and employee characteristics associated with changes in health insurance offers. I study employer and employee characteristics for which minimum wage responses may differ due to differences in health insurance costs, impacts of the Affordable Care Act and other policies and legislation, and employee preferences for health insurance. I find that establishments alter offers of health insurance in response to the minimum wage differently based on firm size and workforce gender and age. Small firms drive reductions in health insurance offers as the minimum wage increases, and reductions are smaller among workforces with a greater share of female or older workers, who more highly value employer-provided health insurance.

26e942feef:f9ab40548e1cd195.title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
26e942feef:f9ab40548e1cd195.author: Baozhong Yang
26e942feef:f9ab40548e1cd195.summary: Using generative AI, we extract managers’ economic expectations from over 120, 000 corporate conference call transcripts. The resulting AI Economy Score predicts GDP growth, production, employment, and wages five or more quarters ahead, beyond survey forecasts and other existing measures. Industry- and firm-level scores capture sector- and firm-specific activity, and a composite of firm, industry, and macroeconomic expectations further improves forecasting power and horizon. Predictability concentrates among historically more accurate, less biased managers, consistent with an information rather than a noise channel. Managerial expectations thus offer incremental insights into economic activity, with implications for macro- and microeconomic decision-making.

26e942feef:a83505cbb88689da.title: How Knowledge Crosses Borders: Evidence from Semiconductor Manufacturing
26e942feef:a83505cbb88689da.author: Jeff Thurk
26e942feef:a83505cbb88689da.summary: We show that cross-border learning is an important feature of modern semiconductor manufacturing and that several important channels – such as knowledge sharing along global supply chains, the movement of engineers within multinational firms, and foreign direct investment – operate through market mechanisms rather than anonymous technological spillovers. These findings have significant policy implications. When cross-border learning is mediated by purposeful economic relationships, access to frontier knowledge is neither automatic nor guaranteed. Firms and governments can facilitate - or restrict - the international diffusion of technology, implying that policies to foster domestic technological upgrading are likely to be most effective when coupled with continued access to global sources of frontier knowledge.

26e942feef:f3304a8de5a84c26.title: Vertical Mergers, Foreclosure, and Rivals’ Exit: The Role of Fringe Firms
26e942feef:f3304a8de5a84c26.author: Javier D. Donna
26e942feef:f3304a8de5a84c26.summary: We analyze vertical mergers when the upstream and downstream markets each have a dominant firm and a competitive fringe. Adding a fringe at each stage of the successive monopoly model of Spengler (1950) generates the anticompetitive mechanisms of the post-Chicago literature. The merger eliminates double marginalization but creates incentives for input foreclosure, customer foreclosure, and fringe exit. Our main result links customer foreclosure to input foreclosure. When the merged firm sources internally, independent suppliers with high operating costs can exit. Their exit reduces the supply available to downstream rivals and, relative to retaining that capacity, raises the input price rivals pay and the merged firm’s foreclosure wedge. In an equilibrium construction, consumer prices remain below the pre-merger level. With atomless participation, consumer harm is ruled out under stated conditions; with indivisible downstream participation, it can arise. We derive implications for merger review under Section 7 of the Clayton Act.

26e942feef:e945114a8d42403f.title: Coasian Stakeholder Theory
26e942feef:e945114a8d42403f.author: Rob Wuebker
26e942feef:e945114a8d42403f.summary: Stakeholder theory asks who is in, who is out, and who gets what. Existing work illuminates important dimensions of firm–stakeholder relationships but does not supply a common, transaction-level rule connecting these questions. We use the Coase theorem to develop such a rule. A Coasian stakeholder is an actor with shutdown power, defined as the de facto capacity, within the relevant time horizon, to prevent, materially delay, or substantially reduce the expected joint value of a focal value-creating transaction. If all such actors are identified and bargaining and enforcement are costless, value-maximizing transactions proceed, although rights and bargaining positions may affect who captures value. When transaction costs are positive, however, identification, bargaining, coalition formation, and enforcement can delay, distort, or suppress those transactions. Across six propositions, we explain how shutdown power is identified and acquired, how complementarity and bargaining conditions shape value capture, how firms reshape stakeholder sets through coalition costs and governance design, and why consolidated opposition can sometimes preserve transactions that fragmented claims would suppress.

26e942feef:d614266d4a023d82.title: Access to Capital and the IPO Decision: An Analysis of US Private Firms
26e942feef:d614266d4a023d82.author: Gregory Weitzner
26e942feef:d614266d4a023d82.summary: We analyze firms’ IPO decisions using detailed financial data on US private firms. Firms with higher external capital needs are more likely to go public. Following the IPO, firms increase investment and debt issuance, leaving their leverage ratios un-changed from pre-IPO levels. Finally, newly public firms borrow from an expanded pool of lenders on improved terms, and the within-firm dispersion in banks’ private risk assessments declines. Our analysis suggests that firms go public to improve their access to capital, which is facilitated by reduced asymmetric information, and that the benefit extends beyond the IPO itself to new sources of debt.

26e942feef:b9bbf921637d04ec.title: Global Entrepreneurial Talent Flows: Widely Funded, Selectively Successful?
26e942feef:b9bbf921637d04ec.author: Henry Woo
26e942feef:b9bbf921637d04ec.summary: Immigrant founders of US venture-backed startups exit successfully more often than native founders. Does this hold worldwide? Using career histories for 913, 226 founder-firm pairs in 213 countries (1990–2026), we compare founders who build abroad (expats) or return home after foreign experience (returnees) with comparable local founders in the same country. Both expats and returnees raise early funding more often globally. Expats' success premium, however, concentrates in the US (18 percent) and UK (26 percent), especially among those entering the US through graduate school, work, or direct founding. Returnees rarely show such a premium. Capital follows mobile founders across borders, but success follows them selectively.

26e942feef:0baa06fbd06986fa.title: The Occupational Ladder: Implications for Life-Cycle Wage Dynamics
26e942feef:0baa06fbd06986fa.author: Guido Matias Cortes
26e942feef:0baa06fbd06986fa.summary: Some occupations pay higher wages than others, even conditional on worker characteristics, implying that occupations can be ranked on a ladder. We develop a simple decomposition to study the role this occupational ladder plays in average wage growth and in the fanning out of wages over the life cycle. We present three main findings. First, the distribution of employment shifts towards higher-paying occupations as workers gain experience.
