This contributes modestly to average life-cycle wage growth, with greatest impact in early career. Second, this upward movement in the occupational employment distribution is not accompanied by increasing dispersion; thus, the occupational ladder does not directly contribute to the fanning out of wages. Third, early-career workers who are well-positioned on the occupational ladder tend to earn wages far below the occupational average. However, by mid-career, workers’ relative wages within occupations (their positions on the job ladder) no longer depend on their occupation. This change in the covariance between individuals’ positions on the job and occupational ladders is a major contributor to the fanning out of wages over workers’ careers.

26e942feef:932f405c3b6deab8.title: Vertical Integration in Uncompetitive Markets: Evidence from the Acquisition of North Star Air by the North West Company
26e942feef:932f405c3b6deab8.author: Raymond Morgan
26e942feef:932f405c3b6deab8.summary: Canadaâ€™s remote northern communities have some of the highest food prices and food insecurity rates in the world and rely on a small number of retail and transportation firms. In 2017, the largest retailer in the region, the North West Company (NWC), acquired a regional airline and started transporting its own air freight to some of the â€œfly-inâ€ communities it serves. Using a difference-in-difference design, we evaluate the effects of vertical integration on prices and shipment quantities of perishable foods. We find that after the acquisition, communities with vertically integrated retail-air freight experienced approximately 3.9% lower prices and 9.5% higher shipment quantities relative to comparison communities. Effects are qualitatively similar in communities where the acquisition changed firm boundaries without changing routes or upstream competition (Ontario) versus communities where it created new routes and competition (Manitoba and Nunavut). Estimated price reductions are larger in communities where NWC accounts for a smaller baseline share of subsidized shipments, while total shipments increase significantly in high-share communities. A theoretical model suggests that this could be due to greater â€œbusiness-stealingâ€ and lower share of sales exposed to marginal cost reductions in more competitive communities, and evidence from retailer-level shipments supports this interpretation. Our findings show that vertical integration can benefit consumers in markets with limited competition but that the size and nature of these benefits is sensitive to upstream and downstream market structure.

26e942feef:1effde76ac62f6c2.title: Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand
26e942feef:1effde76ac62f6c2.author: Vincent Yao
26e942feef:1effde76ac62f6c2.summary: How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures? Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market. As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers. Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month. Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs. First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers’ capabilities have expanded. Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products. Third, switching rises around major model releases. Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure. Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes. Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers’ pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services.

26e942feef:1b719694277b6c33.title: Population Aging, Firms, and Worker Composition
26e942feef:1b719694277b6c33.author: Takahiro Hattori
26e942feef:1b719694277b6c33.summary: Population aging changes the composition of workers in the labor force. We develop a framework to understand how worker composition affects productivity in an economy with heterogeneous establishments and apply it to Japan. Reallocating workers to the optimal composition of experience and skill increases output by 8.5%. Strong complementarity between workersâ€™ skill and establishment productivity implies differential hiring strategies across establishments and heterogeneous effects of population aging on wages and market concentration. We find evidence consistent with these predictions using Japanese data. Despite large potential gains from reallocation, we find that further aging in Japan has only modest impacts on worker productivity.

26e942feef:178b0fc65481b9a0.title: Coordinated R&D Programs and the Creation of New Industries
26e942feef:178b0fc65481b9a0.author: Maria P. Roche
26e942feef:178b0fc65481b9a0.summary: Large, mission-oriented R&D efforts sometimes generate substantial technological advances, but their commercial impacts vary. This paper uses one such effort—the U.S. World War II radar program—to explore how the outputs of such programs may contribute to later commercial development. Using archival records together with data on firm entry, patenting, and technical labor flows, we reconstruct the organization and outputs of wartime radar R&D, document the rapid postwar growth of a civilian industry, and evaluate which outputs were used in subsequent commercial activity. Codified knowledge (in publications and patents) diffused broadly, embodied knowledge (trained personnel) diffused more locally, and the component-system industrial architecture of the wartime program was mirrored in firms' postwar commercial positions. The evidence points to specific channels through which coordinated technology development programs can give shape to emerging high-tech industries.

26e942feef:eaceff4099e2fd59.title: Manufacturing Renaissance Meets Time-Inconsistent Tariffs
26e942feef:eaceff4099e2fd59.author: Wei Xiang
26e942feef:eaceff4099e2fd59.summary: We analyze optimal tariffs in a dynamic version of the Venables (1987) framework with a time-to-build lag in firm creation. In this environment, trade protection is driven by the desire to increase firm creation at home at the expense of the foreign trade partner. When firm creation takes time, the benefits of protection accrue in the future, whereas the costs in the form of higher consumer prices occur immediately. Under certain parameterizations, a policymaker that can commit to a full time path of tariffs leaves trade unrestricted at date 0, and announces high tariffs coming on at a pre-specified future period. But there is a time inconsistency: the policymaker's short-run incentive is not to impose contemporaneous tariffs due to the adverse effect on prices. Thus, lack of commitment to future tariffs can preserve free(er) trade and derail a manufacturing renaissance.

26e942feef:c4efd2b756df36e6.title: Public R&D and the Automation of Manufacturing: Evidence from the Space Race
26e942feef:c4efd2b756df36e6.author: Jingyuan Zeng
26e942feef:c4efd2b756df36e6.summary: This paper examines how public research and development shaped the direction of technological change during the Cold War–era Space Race and its consequences for US manufacturing. While prior research has documented the effects of public R&D on innovation and economic growth, less is known about whether mission-oriented public investment directed innovation toward automation and how this affected labor markets. We exploit variation in exposure to NASA's Space Race investments across industries and locations to estimate the effects of public R&D on innovation and manufacturing outcomes from 1947 to 1992. Combining newly developed measures of automation in full-text patent data with historical evidence on government involvement in patenting, we show that NASA-sponsored patents are systematically more automation-intensive than non-NASA patents within the same technological classes. Industries and locations more exposed to Space Race activity experienced persistent declines in labor share, consistent with the diffusion of labor-saving technologies developed for space applications. In contrast, we find little evidence of systematic changes in skill composition. These findings show that mission-oriented public R&D can shape the direction of technological change and have lasting distributional consequences.

26e942feef:05c44408261ce49d.title: Opening Hours and Consumer Behavior: Evidence from GPS Data and Deregulation
26e942feef:05c44408261ce49d.author: André Trindade
26e942feef:05c44408261ce49d.summary: In 2019, North Dakota repealed its Sunday closing law, which had required most non-grocery stores to close between midnight and noon. Using this policy change and consumer GPS data, we study the impact of opening hours on shopping behavior and welfare. We compare visits before and after the repeal in North Dakota and neighboring states using difference-in-differences and event-study designs. The repeal caused a large increase in Sunday morning visits, originating partly from intertemporal, store-type, and cross-border substitution. The closing law’s welfare loss is equivalent to increasing the travel distance to affected stores by about 1.4 miles per consumer.

26e942feef:e4be92bafef89f33.title: The Global Office: How Globalisation’s Frontier is Shifting from Factories to Offices
26e942feef:e4be92bafef89f33.author: Richard Baldwin
26e942feef:e4be92bafef89f33.summary: This paper argues that globalisation’s frontier has shifted from manufacturing GVCs to services GVCs: from the Global Factory to the Global Office. While the Factory remains larger in gross trade, the Office is growing much faster. A heatmap of trade in intermediates shows that the Factory is bloc-shaped and dominated by China, whereas the Office is star-shaped and dominated by America. Gravity estimates show that distance matters less for Office exports, but time zones matter more: each hour of time-zone separation reduces Office exports by roughly 4%, while having no effect on Factory exports. Importantly, all of the world’s export-linked net job creation between 2008 and 2022 occurred in digitally delivered services rather than manufacturing, and trade-linked service jobs command higher average pay globally. The Factory-to-Office shift is also reshaping development. Most emerging economies have seen export-led growth tilt towards services, but their service exports are not yet large enough to drive overall GDP growth the way manufacturing did historically. The big picture is that globalisation’s second unbundling is running out of steam even as its third unbundling is powering ahead. The paper, which raises more questions than it answers, closes with the conjecture that the future of trade is services.

26e942feef:bc05df375d05c686.title: Saving for the Machines
26e942feef:bc05df375d05c686.author: Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
26e942feef:bc05df375d05c686.summary: When machines can perform a growing share of tasks, growth depends on two margins: how the task structure affects the returns to accumulating machines, and how strongly capital accumulation responds to those returns. I argue that, in a standard task model, capital supply governs the size of the growth boom associated with automation, while the task structure sets the duration of this growth boom and the evolution of wages. I document how the same technology path that generates 11.7% annual growth when households choose their saving rate optimally delivers only 2.2% when the saving rate is fixed at the calibrated U.S. 2025 level of 23%. Therefore, slow growth might reflect too little capital accumulation instead of a technological bottleneck. Also, the saving rate rises mainly because automation raises the capital share, not because households become thriftier. Long yields price the growth boom: the ten-year real yield jumps from 5.1% to 13.6% on impact. In my benchmark calibration, hand-to-mouth households lose the equivalent of two-fifths to two-thirds of their consumption, while keeping them on trend temporarily costs at most a fifth of GDP.

901dc0be66:100290962a2d20d6.title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany1
901dc0be66:100290962a2d20d6.summary: Abstract Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.

901dc0be66:c821b678b270ddb9.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets*
901dc0be66:c821b678b270ddb9.summary: Abstract This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

901dc0be66:43f09410481a8c5a.title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors*
901dc0be66:43f09410481a8c5a.summary: Abstract People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

901dc0be66:87624d0624dfeff6.title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data*
901dc0be66:87624d0624dfeff6.summary: Abstract We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

901dc0be66:7f4e1ec616e57a61.title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches*
901dc0be66:7f4e1ec616e57a61.summary: Abstract Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning*
901dc0be66:726c580558eff521.summary: Abstract This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals ’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard*
901dc0be66:a03b417b94c31fd5.summary: Abstract Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

901dc0be66:62a3a5dec33f1007.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty*
901dc0be66:62a3a5dec33f1007.summary: Abstract People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. To improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts people to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36%–60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s effect on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

At the top, balanced on their heads, was a gold tripod and bowl that held offerings to Apollo’s sanctuary in Delphi. The tripod was stolen around 100 years later. Whitehead, a student at McGill, was aware of the world-renowned magician’s boast that he could withstand any man’s punch. Catching him off guard in his dressing room at the Princess Theatre in Montreal, he delivered a combination of knockout blows to the escape artist’s abdomen. Houdini, splayed on a couch, didn’t tense in time. Two days later, his appendix ruptured. He died from an infection just over a week later, on Halloween, exactly 100 years ago. fc4853f6ed:e8ae4b8718a04b5a.author: Max Carter
fc4853f6ed:e8ae4b8718a04b5a.summary: An 1881 painting by Claude Monet of Alice Hoschedé, whom he would marry in 1892 after the death of her husband in 1891. By Max Carter P ublishers are rarely mentioned in book reviews, but an exception ought to be made for Thames & Hudson and their growing collection of artists’ letters. In 2020, there was Van Gogh: A Life in Letters . Selected, illustrated, and contextualized with intelligence and care, it fulfilled the subtitle’s promise, giving the measure of Vincent’s inner life and aesthetic philosophy. Their task was aided by his drawings, which complement and enliven the text, and by what he called his “irresistible passion for books.” Vincent’s references are wide and keenly felt, from the Bible and devotional literature to Aeschylus, Shakespeare, Victor Hugo, Charles Dickens, and Harriet Beecher Stowe. Now its septuagenarians have been evicted, too By Wendell Jamieson N ew York has three major press clubs for the city’s legions of journalists, whether working, retired, or somewhere in between: the Deadline Club, the New York Press Club, and the Society of the Silurians. The last one is the oldest and its members skew oldest, a reputation they enthusiastically lean into—the Silurian period occurred roughly 400 million years ago and marked the first time invertebrates walked on land. When they started the club in Greenwich Village in 1924, the founders chose the name to show they’d been around for a while. Early members (it was initially men only) included William Randolph Hearst, Lincoln Steffens, and John Steinbeck. fc4853f6ed:b9dacccc141d398d.summary: Jamaica’s Montego Bay in the early 1950s, before the explosion of all-inclusive resorts. All-inclusive resorts and private compounds now control more than 99 percent of the country’s world-famous beaches. Ordinary Jamaicans are fed up By Ben Ryder Howe A decade ago, while working for a travel magazine, I got into a conversation one day with a few colleagues about which countries, for moral reasons, we would never write about. One person said Saudi Arabia, until it allowed women to drive. Another mentioned Uganda, or any country that persecuted gays. I wouldn’t have said Jamaica back then; in fact, that year I visited Jamaica and wrote a short, positive piece about one of its hotels. However, today if I had to pick a country whose economy I refuse to support, it would be Jamaica, the island nation long defined by beaming smiles, party music, and the all-inclusive resort model, which it invented. At a four-table restaurant on Rwanda’s Lake Ruhondo, Rick Owens’s former private chef is putting African cuisine on the global culinary map By Christine Muhlke S hortly after sunrise on the tip of a peninsula in Rwanda’s Lake Ruhondo, Dieuveil Malonga walks from his house to the water’s edge. The 35-year-old chef boards a kayak to meet the fishermen who have caught perch and crayfish for the day’s menu. Soon, boats carrying his 39-person team will arrive from the mainland. Together, they carry supplies up the hill to his restaurant, Meza Malonga. ( Meza is the Bantu word for table .) Inside the bright, spacious kitchen, featuring full views of green hills and the snow-ringed volcanoes beyond, the young men and women begin the intricate work of preparing the day’s meal. READ ON

An exclusive excerpt from Frank Capra By Sam Wasson S ince returning from the war, Frank Capra had begun to think that maybe what they had said about him was true—he was Pollyanna, he made manipulative, facile, sentimental shit. “Perhaps I had put too much faith in the human race—you know, in the pictures I had made,” he reflected. “Maybe they were too much as things should be.” But then, how could Frank Capra, who had lost his faith in man to be and do good above all, make a Frank Capra movie? fc4853f6ed:e43fac85e52bfb6e.author: Elena Clavarino
fc4853f6ed:e43fac85e52bfb6e.summary: Ahead of the midterms, a new book of photographs by Jean-Pierre Laffont captures two decades of American defiance By Elena Clavarino P erhaps only a first-generation immigrant can truly understand America. “We are outsiders,” explains Eliane Laffont, wife of the French photographer Jean-Pierre Laffont. “Whether we like it or not. You know, we are not your typical Americans, so it’s very easy for us to see what’s good and what’s bad and what’s ugly …” Few have had a better vantage point than Jean-Pierre Laffont. Since his arrival in New York, in 1964, Laffont has photographed America at its most restless, rebellious, and unruly, capturing the civil-rights movement, anti–Vietnam War protesters, hippies turned Rajneeshees in Oregon, the gay-liberation movement, gangs in the Bronx, and the street culture that gave rise to hip-hop. He insists politics have never entered into it. READ ON

dc01c62177:2aa232ce43926070.title: Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets
dc01c62177:2aa232ce43926070.author: Ann
dc01c62177:2aa232ce43926070.summary: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of selective consumers, who search costlessly, and casual consumers, who incur positive search costs. Selective consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; casual consumers, concealment. With both types, the equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition. The post Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:275a82589c9dd579.title: Is the Customer Always Right? Customer Taste-Based Discrimination and Competition
dc01c62177:275a82589c9dd579.author: Ann
dc01c62177:275a82589c9dd579.summary: Does competition always mitigate the impact of discrimination on racial wage gaps? This paper examines the impact of product market competition on customer-driven taste-based discrimination in a service economy characterized by homophily. I develop a novel equilibrium model of both product and labor markets in which heightened product market competition tends to exacerbate labor market discrimination in customer-facing occupations. The post Is the Customer Always Right? Customer Taste-Based Discrimination and Competition appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:815731a64c87a3a4.title: The Roles of Borrower Private Information and Mortgage Relief Design in Foreclosure Prevention
dc01c62177:815731a64c87a3a4.author: Ann
dc01c62177:815731a64c87a3a4.summary: I study frictions that prevent financial institutions from granting debt relief to struggling borrowers in the U.S. residential mortgage market. I contribute to a growing literature on selection markets in industrial organization by exploring how asymmetric information, transaction costs, and aid generosity associated with granting debt relief affect mortgage foreclosure outcomes. The post The Roles of Borrower Private Information and Mortgage Relief Design in Foreclosure Prevention appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:d22543eed07d7e43.title: Taxing Homeowners Who Can’t or Won’t Borrow
dc01c62177:d22543eed07d7e43.author: Ann
dc01c62177:d22543eed07d7e43.summary: Using high-frequency administrative data covering millions of US homeowners, I document three novel facts about homeowner responses to property tax increases driven by rising home values. First, non-migrating homeowners cut consumption, exhibit financial distress, and do not borrow against their higher home values. The post Taxing Homeowners Who Can’t or Won’t Borrow appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:45976742fbd79e99.title: From Design to Disclosure
dc01c62177:45976742fbd79e99.author: Ann
dc01c62177:45976742fbd79e99.summary: We study the role of hard information in contractual and market settings in which the receiver can flexibly adjust allocations and transfers in response to the sender’s disclosure. These settings include monopoly pricing, insurance contracting, and policy negotiations. The post From Design to Disclosure appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:92729d0373c75c8d.title: Fertility and Family Leave Policies in Germany: Optimal Policy Design in a Dynamic Framework
dc01c62177:92729d0373c75c8d.author: Ann
dc01c62177:92729d0373c75c8d.summary: I develop and estimate a life-cycle discrete-choice model of fertility and female labour supply to study the optimal design of a range of child-related policies. First, I examine two German reforms that introduced wage-contingent parental leave payments and expanded access to low-cost public childcare. The post Fertility and Family Leave Policies in Germany: Optimal Policy Design in a Dynamic Framework appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:7b76784f15498c8e.author: kacper.krasowki

dc01c62177:5b62c27ea9582e98.title: Meritocracy and Homophily in Collegial Organizations
dc01c62177:5b62c27ea9582e98.author: Ann
dc01c62177:5b62c27ea9582e98.summary: In collegial organizations, homophily jeopardizes the recruitment of the most talented (“meritocracy”). We analyze the dynamics and welfare properties of an organization whose incumbent members coopt new ones in a forward-looking manner. The post Meritocracy and Homophily in Collegial Organizations appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:e6673aeeca2588ad.title: The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output
dc01c62177:e6673aeeca2588ad.author: Ann
dc01c62177:e6673aeeca2588ad.summary: Commercial real estate accounts for about 20% of the U.S. capital stock and is highly regulated. Yet relatively little is known about how these regulations affect economic activity or consumer welfare. This paper develops a spatial general equilibrium model of the U.S. economy with commercial real estate regulations and congestion effects, the latter providing a rationale for such regulations. The post The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:55b3e51d84fdc6ae.title: Optimal Bailouts in Diversified Financial Networks
dc01c62177:55b3e51d84fdc6ae.author: Ann
dc01c62177:55b3e51d84fdc6ae.summary: Widespread default involves substantial deadweight costs which could be countered by injecting capital into failing firms. Injections have positive spillovers that can trigger a repayment cascade. But which firms should a regulator bailout so as to maximize total firm value for a given amount of cash? The post Optimal Bailouts in Diversified Financial Networks appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:85c854bd6bd168e1.title: Competition in Markups: A Theory of the Lerner Index in Networks and General Equilibrium
dc01c62177:85c854bd6bd168e1.author: Ann
dc01c62177:85c854bd6bd168e1.summary: What determines demand elasticities and markups in production networks, where firms’ demand and pricing are interdependent? I propose competition in markups, an equilibrium concept in which firms choose markups, taking other firms’ markups as given. In partial equilibrium with vertical structures, it links upstream demand elasticities to downstream characteristics without backward induction and ties pass-through to the curvature of final demand. The post Competition in Markups: A Theory of the Lerner Index in Networks and General Equilibrium appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:67e7bad29e054020.title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
dc01c62177:67e7bad29e054020.author: Ann
dc01c62177:67e7bad29e054020.summary: We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. The post Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:b3bce3a82418275f.title: Structured Payment in Pawnshop Borrowing: Mandates vs. Choice
dc01c62177:b3bce3a82418275f.author: Ann
dc01c62177:b3bce3a82418275f.summary: Pawn loans offer borrowers a substantial degree of repayment flexibility in exchange for a harsh penalty in case of default: forfeit of collateral worth more than the loan amount along with any payments made toward recovery. Using a large RCT conducted in Mexico City, we document key stylized facts about pawn lending and explore the merits of replacing flexibility with structured repayment contracts in this important but understudied form of credit. The post Structured Payment in Pawnshop Borrowing: Mandates vs. Choice appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:ff1b30a7b61a4643.title: When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE?
dc01c62177:ff1b30a7b61a4643.author: Ann
dc01c62177:ff1b30a7b61a4643.summary: In this paper I revisit the interpretation of the linear instrumental variables (IV) estimand as a weighted average of conditional local average treatment effects (LATEs). I focus on a situation in which additional covariates are required for identification while the reduced-form and first-stage regressions may be misspecified due to an implicit homogeneity restriction on the effects of the instrument. The post When Should We (Not) Interpret Linear IV Estimands as LATE? appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:18b31a90bf30de54.title: Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information
dc01c62177:18b31a90bf30de54.author: Ann
dc01c62177:18b31a90bf30de54.summary: Decisions are typically made by drawing on multiple sources of information, yet the correlation among these sources is often hard to assess. We study robustly optimal strategies — those that maximize the worst-case payoff guarantee across all correlation structures. With two states and two actions, the robustly optimal strategy is strikingly simple: use only the best information source and ignore the rest. The post Robust Aggregation of Correlated Information appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:4d563343f0796d66.title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
dc01c62177:4d563343f0796d66.author: Ann
dc01c62177:4d563343f0796d66.summary: Economists and historians have long debated how open-access areas, frontier regions, and customary landholding regimes transformed into private property. This paper analyzes decentralized enclosure processes using the theory of aggregative games, examining how population density, enclosure costs, potential productivity gains, and local governance capacity, including the power to demand compensation, jointly determine the mix of property regimes. The post A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:d21547d3a9c0ac9e.title: Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets
dc01c62177:d21547d3a9c0ac9e.author: Ann
dc01c62177:d21547d3a9c0ac9e.summary: Quality regulation seeks to ensure quality and foster competition by reducing vertical differentiation, but it may also have adverse effects on market structure. We study this trade-off in the context of pharmaceutical bioequivalence, which is the primary quality standard for generic drugs. The post Quality Regulation and Competition: Evidence from Pharmaceutical Markets appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .

dc01c62177:56e5c174bcbeb690.title: Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews
dc01c62177:56e5c174bcbeb690.author: Ann
dc01c62177:56e5c174bcbeb690.summary: The advent of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities to conduct qualitative interviews at scale, with thousands of respondents, thereby bridging qualitative and quantitative methods. We develop a simple, versatile approach for researchers to run AI-led qualitative interviews, including voice interviews. The post Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews appeared first on The Review of Economic Studies .
