f965d2251a:62a3a5dec33f1007.title: Retrieval Failures and Consumption Smoothing: A Field Experiment on Seasonal Poverty*
f965d2251a:62a3a5dec33f1007.summary: Abstract People may fail to recall and use information they already know when making decisions. We empirically investigate whether such “retrieval failures” distort consumption-smoothing behavior among Zambian farmers, who derive their income from one annual harvest and spend it over the course of the year. We document that individuals underestimate upcoming spending by 50%, creating scope for undersaving. To improve recall, we randomize an intervention that prompts people to think through their future expenses associatively in categories—without providing any external information or guidance. Treated individuals increase “remembered” expenses by 36%–60%; as predicted by the memory literature, effects are concentrated among small, irregular, and stochastic items. Immediate spending drops and, six weeks after the intervention, treated households hold 15% higher savings. They subsequently enter the hungry season—the final months of the year when consumption typically declines sharply—with one additional month of savings, leading to a flatter spending profile over the year. Households use the increased savings to self-finance additional farm investment, resulting in a 9% increase in the next year’s crop revenue. We replicate the intervention’s effect on beliefs among low-income Americans, suggesting that retrieval failures generalize across settings and populations.

f965d2251a:c79bdfba8535da03.title: Busing to Opportunity? The Impacts of the Metco Voluntary School Desegregation Program on Urban Students of Color
f965d2251a:c79bdfba8535da03.summary: Abstract School assignment policies are a key lever for expanding access to high-performing schools and promoting racial and socioeconomic integration. For over 50 years, the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity (METCO) has bussed students of color from Boston, Massachusetts, to relatively wealthier and predominantly white suburbs. I estimate the effects of attending a high-performing suburban school by comparing applicants who receive enrollment offers with applicants who do not. A two-stage least squares approach exploits waitlist assignment priorities and controls for a rich set of characteristics from birth records and application data. Attending a suburban school boosts math and English test scores, reduces dropout, and increases on-time high school graduation. Four-year college aspirations, enrollment, and graduation increase along with earnings in adulthood. Students whose parents did not attend college and boys experience the largest effects. The evidence points to several mechanisms, including access to higher value-added schools, higher-achieving peers, and schools with stronger college-going norms. Participants are more likely to be tracked into lower-performing classes, implying that effects could be larger with access to more advanced coursework. District value-added estimates suggest that students’ educational trajectories shift at least as much as they would from growing up in the suburban districts.

f965d2251a:7e3356847366fb7c.title: Bringing Work Home: Flexible Work Arrangements as Gateway Jobs for Women in West Bengal*
f965d2251a:7e3356847366fb7c.summary: Abstract There is a large latent workforce in developing countries that consists of hundreds of millions of women who prefer to have paid work and yet are out of the labor force. Often, available job opportunities are incompatible with traditional gender roles that encourage women to stay at home. In a randomized experiment with 1,670 households, we partner with a jobs platform to offer short-term data work to women who are out of the labor force. We find three main results. First, flexible work-from-home jobs are highly effective at bringing women into paid work. Job flexibility more than triples take-up from 15% for an office job to 48% for a job that women can do from home while multitasking with childcare. Second, these jobs can act as a stepping stone to less flexible work. Trying paid work from home increases take-up of less flexible jobs two to three months later among women without previous work experience. “Gateway jobs” are especially important for women from more traditional households: their labor supply is more likely to be marginal to flexibility, and in turn, work experience shifts their attitudes to become less traditional. Third, from the labor demand side, remote work comes with trade-offs in worker performance. Working from the office increases accuracy by 3% and speed by 18%. However, these performance drawbacks of work-from-home arrangements may be outweighed by the increase in available workers.

f965d2251a:e4c5cce8c2a59ace.title: Fairness Across the World
f965d2251a:e4c5cce8c2a59ace.summary: Abstract This article provides the first comprehensive global evidence on people’s fairness and efficiency preferences, beliefs about the sources of inequality and the efficiency cost of redistribution, and policy attitudes toward redistribution. Using a globally harmonized consequential experiment with more than 65,000 individuals across 60 countries, we show that the source of inequality plays a substantially larger role for inequality acceptance than the efficiency cost of redistribution. At the global level, implemented inequality increases by 85% when inequality is caused by merit rather than luck, compared with a 14% increase when redistribution entails a 50% efficiency cost. We document substantial heterogeneity in fairness views and beliefs within and across societies. The meritocratic fairness view is most prominent in many richer Western societies, while libertarian and egalitarian fairness views are widespread in many other parts of the world. Globally, people are more likely to believe that inequality reflects luck rather than merit, while beliefs in large efficiency costs of redistribution are relatively weak. Fairness preferences and beliefs are strongly associated with redistribution attitudes and actual redistribution through taxes and transfers across countries. Our findings illustrate how the interaction between fairness views and beliefs may shape redistribution across societies, highlighting the importance of jointly understanding preferences and beliefs in the political economy of redistribution.

f965d2251a:c5028e4bcde9f322.title: Wealth and Property Taxation in the United States*
f965d2251a:c5028e4bcde9f322.summary: Abstract We study the history and geography of wealth accumulation in the United States using newly collected historical property tax records from the early 1800s onward. These records come from the administration of the General Property Tax—a tax that aspired to cover all types of property. We construct wealth series at the state, county, and national levels. At the state level, we use annual assessed values of wealth from state-level reports drawn from multiple sources. Because assessed values may differ from market values, we also require assessment ratios, defined as the ratio of assessed to market wealth. We obtain state-level assessment ratios from decadal U.S. Census wealth data (drawn from various census reports, including those on “Wealth, Debt, and Taxation”), in which the census carried out detailed valuation work, complemented with information on changes in assessment practices from the state reports, to build higher-frequency series of assessment ratios. The result is long-run annual wealth series for states from 1850 (or earlier, depending on the state) to 1935. We obtain national wealth series by aggregating these state series. At the county level, we use assessed values (or market values where available) from the U.S. Census wealth data for each decade and apply either state-level or county-level assessment ratios, where available, to obtain market values of wealth for each decade from 1850 to 1930. We use these data to show, first, that the United States experienced extraordinary wealth accumulation after the Civil War and until the Great Depression. Second, spatial inequality in the United States has been large and highly persistent since the mid-1800s. We also examine the determinants of long-term wealth growth and find, among other results, that counties with a higher share of enslaved property before the Civil War or with higher wealth inequality experienced lower subsequent long-run wealth growth.

56c7f0b50e:9084ec65e34eef4d.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
56c7f0b50e:9084ec65e34eef4d.author: Xu, Yaling
56c7f0b50e:9084ec65e34eef4d.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

56c7f0b50e:43b515f4c0da2167.title: What is an AI worker? Evidence from Matched Vacancy-Hires
56c7f0b50e:43b515f4c0da2167.author: Hellsten, Mark
56c7f0b50e:43b515f4c0da2167.summary: Despite growing policy interest in AI workforce development, surprisingly little is known about what defines these workers, or indeed if they differ from their occupational peers. Using a novel matched vacancy-hire dataset linking Swedish job postings to the individuals hired to fill them, drawn from register data on the entire Swedish population, I study the characteristics of workers who develop and apply AI. Observable traits including high cognitive ability, a tertiary degree in STEM subjects, and a recent migrant background largely explain occupational sorting. Of these, only higher education, prior AI experience, and a science degree set them apart within occupation. I then use earnings as a window onto unobservable differences: AI workers earn approximately 5% more than their peers, entirely explained by firm-level wages. However, AI workers with a doctorate degree stand out sharply in both traits and earnings, indicating that AI workers split into segments that differ by the complexity of their skills and tasks. Taken together, these results point to two distinct policy levers: the supply of average AI workers, termed AI integrators, can be expanded via STEM education participation, while the elite AI developers are supplied by researchers moving to the private sector.

56c7f0b50e:2b9a4702799478ba.title: The Impacts of Unauthorized Immigration on U.S. Labor and Housing Markets: New Evidence from Administrative Microdata
56c7f0b50e:2b9a4702799478ba.author: Xiaoqing Zhou
56c7f0b50e:2b9a4702799478ba.summary: From early 2021 through early 2024, the U.S. experienced an unprecedented boom in unauthorized immigration, with substantial heterogeneity across local economies. Using administrative microdata, we construct new measures of national and local unauthorized immigration flows and exploit exogenous variation using multiple empirical designs. Unauthorized immigrant worker flows increased local employment approximately one-for-one, with mixed evidence of wage depression. They also raised house prices and rents without expanding housing supply. Finally, these flows reduced labor income per capita and government transfers. These findings help inform debates surrounding how unauthorized immigration impacts labor and housing markets and public finances in the U.S.

56c7f0b50e:f54a3feb3c0de2a2.title: Job Characteristics That Matter for Women : Evidence from a Large-Scale Experiment in Pakistan
56c7f0b50e:f54a3feb3c0de2a2.author: Tas, Emcet Oktay
56c7f0b50e:f54a3feb3c0de2a2.summary: In the presence of gender-specific barriers, certain workplace environments and amenities may be particularly important for women, yet difficult to observe during job search due to information frictions. A large-scale field experiment on Pakistan's online job board publicized these job characteristics—namely, supervisor gender, coworker gender composition, work flexibility, commuting support, and overnight travel requirements. Information on these characteristics was randomly disclosed in job advertisements and email alerts. Analysis at the job-alert level shows that female jobseekers respond to supervisor gender, remote work, and commuting support. At the job level, when these characteristics were disclosed, the number of female applicants increased as the jobs were more favorable to women.

56c7f0b50e:96c5d230d8e4fd96.title: Immigrant-Native Wage Gaps and Rent Sharing: A Segmented Assimilation Story?
56c7f0b50e:96c5d230d8e4fd96.author: Mélanie Volral
56c7f0b50e:96c5d230d8e4fd96.summary: Although an increasing body of literature has examined the relationship between firms’ profitability and wage inequality in the context of a diverse workforce, the role of rent sharing in explaining origin-based wage differentials has yet to be explored. Our paper aims to fill this gap using detailed Belgian matched employer-employee data from 1999 to 2016. After controlling for a wide range of covariates and addressing endogeneity issues, our estimates show that the wage-profit elasticity equals approximately 3% and does not differ statistically between native and immigrant workers, be they first or second generation. It therefore appears that firms share their profits equally with their employees, regardless of their origin. However, Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions suggest that rent sharing has a significant influence on immigrants’ wages through labour market segregation. Specifically, first-generation immigrants are found to earn lower wages than natives because of their higher concentration in firms with lower profit margins. The same is true for second-generation immigrants, but almost half as much. These findings, corroborated and refined by heterogeneity tests according to gender, educational attainment and level of collective bargaining, support the hypothesis of a segmented assimilation process for immigrants.

56c7f0b50e:00819b0aa70bab01.title: Parental job loss across child age and human capital formation
56c7f0b50e:00819b0aa70bab01.author: Alexander Willén

56c7f0b50e:29bc816d9d1ee5cb.title: Representation over Rents: Labor Market Beliefs and the Gender Wage Gap
56c7f0b50e:29bc816d9d1ee5cb.author: Ana Figueiredo
56c7f0b50e:29bc816d9d1ee5cb.summary: We study how labor market beliefs shape the gender wage gap in an equilibrium search model with endogenous wage setting and hiring, in which workers hold subjective expectations about wage offers, job arrival rates, and separation risk. Using data from the Survey of Consumer Expectations to estimate the model, we find that gender differences in beliefs account for 25% of the gender wage gap. Correcting these beliefs partly narrows the gap but is not welfare-improving, as it reduces lifetime earnings for both men and women. In contrast, equalizing labor market fundamentals substantially reduces the wage gap while increasing women's lifetime earnings.

56c7f0b50e:fb60906abf388e52.title: Labor-market drivers of intergenerational earnings persistence
56c7f0b50e:fb60906abf388e52.author: Stuhler, Jan
56c7f0b50e:fb60906abf388e52.summary: How does worker-firm sorting contribute to intergenerational persistence? Firm pay premia account for 36% of the intergenerational earnings elasticity in Sweden, rising to 50% with dynamic returns to firm-specific experience. Large pay gaps already open atlabor market entry, as children from privileged backgrounds find more favorable entry points; they then climb the firm pay ladder faster, switching firms more often and gaining more per switch. Skill sorting explains this widening but not the initial gaps, consistent with networks and employer learning. Privileged children’s firms are also more desirable overall, a gap that keeps widening after pay gaps stabilize.

56c7f0b50e:98b34f95b1356fc0.title: The Introduction of Universal Child Care in New Mexico: Initial Evidence on Mothers' Labor Supply
56c7f0b50e:98b34f95b1356fc0.author: Herbst, Chris
56c7f0b50e:98b34f95b1356fc0.summary: In November 2025, New Mexico became the first U.S. state to implement a universal, no-cost child care subsidy program. This paper estimates difference-in-differences and event-study models to evaluate the impact of universal child care on mothers' short-run labor supply adjustments. Using monthly Current Population Survey data, I find that the reform produced different responses across lower- and higher-skilled mothers. For lower-skilled mothers, the policy increased employment along both the extensive and intensive margins. Conversely, higher-skilled mothers, particularly those who are married, experienced reductions in paid work, with partially offsetting increases in school enrollment. Thus, while universal child care relaxes a binding constraint among disadvantaged families, it acts as an in-kind transfer for their advantaged counterparts.

56c7f0b50e:e600a1ab879971e7.title: Randomized to Opportunity: Measuring Place Effects for Refugee Children
56c7f0b50e:e600a1ab879971e7.author: Mircea Trandafir
56c7f0b50e:e600a1ab879971e7.summary: Area-level measures of economic opportunity are increasingly used to guide place-based policies. We study whether these measures predict long-run outcomes for a vulnerable population: over 12, 000 refugee children quasi-randomly assigned to municipalities under Denmark's 1986–1998 dispersal policy. We focus on predetermined measures of opportunity available when children arrive and validate them using a mover-exposure design among permanent residents. Moving from a low- to a high-opportunity area (a two-standard-deviation increase) raises adult income rank by 3 percentile points (7.5 percent) and employment by 4 percentage points. It also reduces criminal convictions by 14 percent and teen parenthood by 19 percent, with more modest effects on educational attainment. Economic opportunity predicts crime and teen parenthood more strongly than other area characteristics, including local crime rates. For adult income, area-level inequality is a particularly strong predictor. These findings suggest that social mobility in the areas where refugee children grow up meaningfully shapes their long-term wellbeing.

56c7f0b50e:ae7f4f25bcbe368d.title: Random Genetic Variation Links Personality to Earnings and Wealth
56c7f0b50e:ae7f4f25bcbe368d.author: Dilnoza Muslimova
56c7f0b50e:ae7f4f25bcbe368d.summary: Personality is associated with economic outcomes, but whether these relationships are causal remains unclear. We exploit within-family variation in genetic propensity toward the Big Five generated by random genetic transmission from parents to offspring. Combining polygenic indexes from the Lifelines cohort study with 19 years of administrative tax records in the Netherlands, we find that greater genetic propensity toward emotional stability increases earnings and household wealth, while genetic propensity toward conscientiousness increases household wealth. The other three traits show no consistent pattern across outcomes and specifications. The effect of genetic propensity toward emotional stability on earnings remains positive as we progressively account for genetic propensity toward educational attainment, cognitive performance, and depression. These findings strengthen the evidence that personality causally affects earnings and wealth.

56c7f0b50e:22d34de0e987d3af.title: Consumption, Savings, and Earnings Responses to Financial Windfalls
56c7f0b50e:22d34de0e987d3af.author: Barry Scholnick
56c7f0b50e:22d34de0e987d3af.summary: We estimate the causal effects of a financial windfall on consumption, savings, and wage earnings using linked administrative data on a large sample of Canadian lottery winners. Using separate linkages of lottery winners to income tax records and credit bureau data, we estimate how lottery winnings affect consumption measured through credit card spending, savings through financial asset accumulation and debt repayment, and wage earnings from tax records. We then examine how these responses vary across the income distribution. We find that high-income individuals allocated a larger share of lottery winnings to savings and leisure, while low-income individuals spent a larger share on consumption. We illustrate the policy relevance of these heterogeneous responses through three applications: designing fiscal stimulus programs, evaluating a Universal Basic Income (UBI), and determining optimal top tax rates on wage earnings and savings.

56c7f0b50e:f5e18bc1ab24b194.title: Workers, Firms, and Spatial Wage Inequality: Evidence from Hungarian Local Labor Markets
56c7f0b50e:f5e18bc1ab24b194.author: László Czaller
56c7f0b50e:f5e18bc1ab24b194.summary: This paper examines how workers and employers jointly shape spatial wage disparities across Hungarian local labor markets. We combine longitudinal linked employer–employee administrative data for 2012–2022 with functional local labor markets constructed from district-to-district commuting flows in the 2022 Hungarian Census. Our preferred delineation contains 29 commuting zones and raises the share of employed residents working within the same unit above 90 percent, compared with 72 percent for districts and 81 percent for counties. We estimate an additive worker–employer fixed-effect wage model and decompose wage variation at the individual level, between commuting zones, and within commuting zones. Differences in commuting-zone mean wages account for 2.8 percent of national log-wage variance and 1.1 percent when the Budapest commuting zone is excluded. Although the between-zone component is modest, its structure is systematic: zones with higher average worker effects also tend to have higher average employer wage premia, so the spatial alignment of worker and employer components accounts for an important part of spatial wage differences. Wage dispersion and the relative importance of worker heterogeneity, employer premia, and worker–employer sorting within local labor markets also vary substantially across the country. The results indicate that spatial wage disparities in Hungary reflect not only differences in workers’ earnings potential and the employer premia attached to their jobs, but also how these components are combined across local labor markets.

56c7f0b50e:8ea95b7db5cfe085.title: Labor Supply and Wages over the Life Cycle: Human Capital and Disability Benefits
56c7f0b50e:8ea95b7db5cfe085.author: Tom Waters
56c7f0b50e:8ea95b7db5cfe085.summary: Work experience has been found to be a key determinant of work and wages for educated women, but it seems to play a smaller role for the less educated. For them, welfare, tax credits and family composition matter more, and increasingly so does participation in disability programmes. Here we document how labor supply, wages, health, and disability claims have evolved in the UK over the last three decades, and examine how reforms to tax credits, disability benefits and other welfare programs have changed work incentives over this period. We then introduce these features into an empirical dynamic structural model of life-cycle labor supply, human capital and disability benefit application, in which human capital combines health capital, experience accumulated in work, and education. Estimating the model on a panel of working-age women in the UK, we examine the interactions between experience capital and health capital in driving life-cycle earnings across different education groups. Our results highlight the importance of interactions in the disability benefit, welfare and tax-credit systems for understanding the life cycle pattern of hours, employment, earnings, and disability claims, and for evaluating policy counterfactuals.

56c7f0b50e:9ca948709c7dc246.title: The Gendered Impacts of Perceived Skin Tone: Evidence from African American Siblings in 1870-1940
56c7f0b50e:9ca948709c7dc246.author: Luke C. D. Stein
56c7f0b50e:9ca948709c7dc246.summary: We study differences in economic outcomes by perceived skin tone among African Americans using full-count U.S. decennial census data from the late-19th and early-20th centuries. Comparing children coded as "Black" or "Mulatto" by census enumerators and linking these children across population censuses, we first document large gaps in educational attainment and income among African Americans with darker and lighter perceived skin tones. To disentangle the drivers of these gaps, we identify all 35, 992 families in which enumerators assigned same-gender siblings different Black/Mulatto classifications. Relative to sisters coded as Mulatto, sisters coded as Black had lower educational attainment, were less likely to marry, and had less-educated, likely lower-earning husbands. These patterns are consistent with more severe contemporaneous discrimination against African American women with darker perceived skin tones. In contrast, we find similar educational attainment, marital outcomes, and incomes among differently-classified brothers. Men perceived as African Americans of any skin tone faced similar contemporaneous discrimination, consistent with the "one-drop" racial classification rule that grouped together individuals with any known Black ancestry. Lower incomes for African American men perceived as having darker skin tone in the general population were driven by differences in opportunities and resources that varied across families, likely reflecting the impacts of historical or family-level discrimination.

56c7f0b50e:13a4d129461d8973.title: Targeted Acceleration in Middle School Math: Impacts on College Entry, Degree Completion, and STEM
56c7f0b50e:13a4d129461d8973.author: Laura Giuliano
56c7f0b50e:13a4d129461d8973.summary: We study an accelerated 3-year math curriculum offered in the middle schools of a large urban district that enables students to finish Algebra I and Geometry before high school. Entry to the program is based on 5th-grade math test scores, with a cutoff at the 80th percentile. Continuing eligibility requires at least a B grade in the previous year; successful completion of all three years is highly correlated with an index of non-cognitive skills. Following students for 6 years after high school graduation, we find that the impacts of admission vary widely by non-cognitive skill and gender. Marginally eligible boys with high non-cognitive skills have a 33 percentage point (ppt.) increase in the probability of completing calculus by 11th grade and a 12 ppt. increase in the probability of completing a major in STEM or business within 6 years; boys with lower noncognitive skills take more advanced math classes in high school but have no significant effects on their college outcomes. Like their male peers, marginally eligible girls with high non-cognitive skills are more likely to complete calculus by 11th grade (+17 ppt.). Their rate of graduating with a STEM or business major is unaffected, but they switch from social sciences to the core STEM majors (science, engineering and math). Girls in the two lower terciles of non-cognitive skill are also strongly affected by entry to the program, with higher participation in advanced math classes in high school, higher rates of entry to selective 4-year colleges, and higher rates of completing a STEM or business major (+12 ppt).

56c7f0b50e:481a2dede4116898.title: Which Workers Left the Labor Force Post-COVID Recession and Why?: Filing, Tax Credit Take-Up, and Labor Force Engagement by Occupation
56c7f0b50e:481a2dede4116898.author: Michael Stevens
56c7f0b50e:481a2dede4116898.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp initial rise in unemployment, followed by an unexpectedly tight labor market. Using a panel of tax data containing newly assembled information on worker occupation, we document persistent labor force exit, especially among low-income and low-skill workers. Low-skilled unmarried men are by far the most likely to exit, reinforcing recent concerns regarding the economic and social engagement of this group. Contrary to prevailing theories, we find little evidence that school closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments, or unemployment benefits explain these exits. Nor is the exit explained by additional upgrading of occupations or firm quality. Individuals who leave the labor force do not (on average) make up the missing income; however, self-employment income replaces roughly a quarter of the lost W-2 income. The facts suggest that the willingness to work for low pay decreased and preferences for leisure and job flexibility increased among a large set of workers who have found ways to get by with less income. These results have implications for tax policy, fiscal projections, and labor market dynamics in the post-pandemic economy.

56c7f0b50e:f32d0595fd9d0501.title: Understanding Migration Responses to Local Shocks
56c7f0b50e:f32d0595fd9d0501.author: Brian K. Kovak
56c7f0b50e:f32d0595fd9d0501.summary: A commonly used migration regression relates population changes to local labor demand shocks, often yielding small or statistically insignificant coefficients despite sizable effects on labor market outcomes. We argue that such findings need not imply that mobility is unresponsive to local economic conditions. Rather, conventional migration regressions can be biased, as they do not reflect how workers choose among competing locations. In a parsimonious equilibrium model, local population growth depends on differences between local shocks and those in relevant destinations; when these shocks are correlated, estimated responses are attenuated. Moreover, with industry-level shocks, standard shift-share measures misrepresent locations’ effective exposure, leading to further attenuation. Using simulation experiments based on Brazilian and German administrative data, we show attenuation can exceed 50% and that conventional regression estimates can be highly imprecise. We propose theory-grounded empirical approaches that correct the biases, deliver estimates with a clear structural interpretation, and improve the precision of estimated mobility responses.

56c7f0b50e:12449012f33a7700.title: The Intergenerational Cost of Parental Illness: Childrens' School Engagement in Chile
56c7f0b50e:12449012f33a7700.author: Libuy, Nicolás
56c7f0b50e:12449012f33a7700.summary: Severe health events are among the most common shocks households face, and in low- and middle-income countries their consequences are absorbed largely within the family. We study how a parents severe illness affects adolescents' education in Chile. Using linked administrative records for the universe of school-age children and quasi-random variation in the occurrence and timing of parents first cancer hospitalizations, we compare exposed students with untreated classmates in a stacked difference-in-differences design. The shock reduces school enrollment and attendance and raises chronic absenteeism, with effects that persist for up to four years and roughly double for high-severity cancers. Disruptions are substantially larger for girls, consistent with caregiving and household responsibilities falling disproportionately on them. The educational response varies little with households' pre-shock labor market position, and children's hospitalizations do not rise. These findings point to an intergenerational cost of parental illness and a role for social protection in mitigating it.

56c7f0b50e:cdac003a08cf4711.title: The Effects of a Shorter Workweek on Employment, Output, and Productivity
56c7f0b50e:cdac003a08cf4711.author: Nina Roussille
56c7f0b50e:cdac003a08cf4711.summary: Do shorter workweeks generate work-sharing and productivity gains, as intended by policymakers? We study France’s pay-preserving reduction in the workweek from 39 to 35 hours, bundled with employer payroll tax cuts. We first exploit the staggered implementation by firm size to identify the impact of the reform package. We then use differential exposure to the hours cut and tax cut to separate their effects. We combine matched employer-employee, balance-sheet, and survey data to study worker, firm, and local labor market effects. The reform package left employment unchanged. This zero masks large offsetting effects: absent the tax cuts, the shorter workweek would have reduced employment by 3.8%. The effects are skill-biased, raising employment among managers and professionals while reducing it among other employees. Finally, shorter hours raised total factor productivity by 2%, limiting the output decline to 1% despite a 6% fall in total hours. Surveys point to work intensification and organizational changes as potential drivers of productivity gains.

56c7f0b50e:d34f593b4605d3e5.title: Staying Connected: Experimental Effects of Coach-Delivered Text Messages in an Adult High School
56c7f0b50e:d34f593b4605d3e5.author: Patrick S. Turner
56c7f0b50e:d34f593b4605d3e5.summary: More than 23 million adults in the United States lack a high school diploma, and most who return to school drop out before graduating. We evaluate a randomized intervention of adult high school students in which coaches delivered text messages that encouraged persistence. We find that assignment to treatment increased graduation by 4.9 percentage points, and the effect of message receipt among compliers is 9.3 percentage points, a 41 percent increase relative to the control mean. The intervention operated on the intensive margin by increasing the number of courses completed, but did not affect student enrollment. The effects of the intervention are concentrated among students assigned to experienced coaches, who customized their messages more extensively. We contextualize the economic impact of the low-cost intervention by comparing labor market earnings of graduates to non-graduates, which implies an earnings benefit of $149 per treated student over four years.

56c7f0b50e:af0cab4f38380325.title: State Child Tax Credits and Parental Labor Supply: Evidence from Staggered Adoption
56c7f0b50e:af0cab4f38380325.author: Parolin, Zachary
56c7f0b50e:af0cab4f38380325.summary: States increasingly supplement the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) with credits that vary in generosity, refundability, and earnings requirements. We examine changes in parental employment, labor force participation, and work hours following state CTC adoption using the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC), 2004–2026. Our preferred stacked difference-in-differences design includes 12 adopting states with complete event-time support and compares them with never-treated states and states that adopted after our evaluation window. Averaging over the first three post-adoption survey years, the estimated effect is 0.05 percentage points (SE 1.03) for employment and −0.46 points (0.82) for labor force participation; estimates for work hours are also close to zero. Across secondary specifications and CPS Basic Monthly analyses, extensive-margin estimates were similarly small. Larger simulated benefits are associated with fewer hours among employed parents, but the relationship is also evident before adoption and may partly reflect how benefits depend on earnings. Overall, the estimates provide little indication that state CTC adoption has substantially reduced parental employment, although meaningful effects in either direction cannot be ruled out under moderate departures from parallel trends.

56c7f0b50e:9d3f7ebd90ac7707.title: Do weekend workers like their jobs?
56c7f0b50e:9d3f7ebd90ac7707.author: Mark Wooden
56c7f0b50e:9d3f7ebd90ac7707.summary: Weekend work is a pervasive feature of labor markets that comes with both potential benefits (e.g., higher pay, flexible schedules) and drawbacks (e.g., less social time). Nevertheless, robust evidence on weekend workers’ job satisfaction is lacking. Longitudinal data from 21 waves of the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey (n=211, 077; i=26, 273) are used to estimate the association between weekend work and several dimensions of job satisfaction. Estimates from fixed effects models reveal that weekend work is associated with significantly lower levels of satisfaction with working hours and flexibility, but this does not translate into lower levels of overall job satisfaction. Additional analyses were conducted to test whether results varied with employment status, occupation and parental status. In general, the main finding applied to all groups examined. There were, however, marked differences across sub-groups in satisfaction with other job domains. Overall, the results suggest that, for most workers, the benefits of working weekends offset its disadvantages.

56c7f0b50e:b35a02dd73bbfc25.title: Remote Work from the Office
56c7f0b50e:b35a02dd73bbfc25.author: Emma Harrington
56c7f0b50e:b35a02dd73bbfc25.summary: Roughly half of in-office days are spent entirely on Zoom calls or doing solo work according to a new survey of college-educated Americans. These workers commute in just to work remotely from the office. Existing measures of remote work that focus solely on working from home miss up to three quarters of its true prevalence. We use a collage of data to unpack the drivers of working remotely from the office. The biggest driver is geographic distance, which causes teammates to work in different offices or fully remotely. Other contributors include non-compliance with in-office policies, poor coordination on in-office days, and a tendency to take Zoom calls rather than booking meeting rooms even when everyone is in the office.

4bca44730b:34d7e3f243f58535.title: Speaking Engagements/Conferences
4bca44730b:34d7e3f243f58535.author: Francine
4bca44730b:34d7e3f243f58535.summary: I'm done traveling until 2020 when I'll attend the AAA-Audit Section meeting in Houston in January. See you there!

4bca44730b:39462350981770e8.title: My take on the latest at the PCAOB and KPMG
4bca44730b:39462350981770e8.author: Francine
4bca44730b:39462350981770e8.summary: In Episode 449 of the FCPA Compliance Report, I spoke with Tom Fox to discuss the current status of the KPMG defendants and what their conduct means for the audit profession going forward.

4bca44730b:e00b3f3b66af829c.title: Update: Botta v. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP, Case 3:18-cv-02615-RS
4bca44730b:e00b3f3b66af829c.author: Francine

0cf31f7a1a:943d59e495a01936.title: The Aftermath of the 2024 UK Riots: Reporting on Social Media, Misinformation, and Crime
0cf31f7a1a:943d59e495a01936.author: James Moir
0cf31f7a1a:943d59e495a01936.summary: On 30th July 2024, the UK saw its worst riots in over a decade following a knife attack in Southport that left three girls dead and ten injured. False claims about the attacker being a Muslim asylum seeker spread rapidly online, turning vigils into violence as far-right groups used X, TikTok and Telegram to coordinate attacks on mosques, asylum centres and local businesses. Many of the rioters received prison sentences for arson and racially aggravated offences. Information disorder played a central role in the 2024 riots, both triggering unrest and intensifying violence through the rapid dissemination of false narratives. Disinformation acted as the initial spark, later transforming into misinformation as unaware individuals reshared it. Social media sites such as Telegram involved the sharing of extremist material that merged transnational and domestic narratives. Global disinformation and local grievances became intertwined, merging foreign interference with home-grown mobilisation. As the riots took place there was evidence an online-offline feedback loop which resulted in prosecutions that relied heavily on digital evidence. This paper examines a corpus of newspaper reports on the issue of social media, disinformation, and crime in the ensuing two-year period since the riots. The news media sources were derived from a search using LexisNexis, a web-based archive of news titles in the UK. This is involved a selective search of news from the range of broadsheet and tabloid titles across the political spectrum. The key search terms were ?Stockport?, ?riots? ?social media?, ?misinformation?, ?disinformation? and ?police?. A discourse analytic approach was applied to the reports that reveal the different political stances taken on the issue of social media, misinformation, and crime. These are bound up with rhetorical constructions concerning the release of police information on the identities of alleged offenders, the control of social media, and social and…

0cf31f7a1a:7a4c906be75b9114.title: Demystifying Unconscionability: A Historical and Empirical Analysis
0cf31f7a1a:7a4c906be75b9114.author: McCall, Brian M.
0cf31f7a1a:7a4c906be75b9114.summary: The doctrine of unconscionability is encrusted with myths. First-year law students are taught that the doctrine was created in the twentieth century. Unconscionability is often presented as a novel one, born in the Uniform Commercial Code’s adoption of Section 2-302 in the mid-twentieth century. Even those scholars who are willing to look a bit further afield than the twentieth century for the origins of the unconscionability doctrine typically only reach the mid-eighteenth century. In addition to myths surrounding its origin, the doctrine has been presented as a dangerously vague and imprecise concept. Commentators and scholars have likewise characterized the doctrine as a license for courts to refuse, unpredictably and arbitrarily, to enforce some contracts. Some claim its application has the potential to destroy all of contract law. Beyond the fearmongering myths, another standard myth taught to first-year law students is that to succeed on a claim of unconscionability a party must offer at least some proof of both procedural and substantive unconscionability. This Article will thus attempt to dispel the following three myths about unconscionability: • It is a new, modern doctrine of law, • Its application is unpredictable and arbitrary, and • To prevail a party must prove both procedural and substantive unconscionability. The best way to dispel myths is through facts. This Article attempts to clear the clouds of confusion and fear surrounding the doctrine by turning to historical and empirical fact. Part I of this Article looks to the ancient past and finds that the idea that justice, and hence the law, should grant a remedy to at least some people who enter into inequitable bargains, is as old as philosophizing about justice itself (and certainly older than the mid-eighteenth century). Rather than a dangerous modern innovation, this principle of justice has ancient philosophical roots in Aristotle and ancient legal roots in Roman law. Part II of the Article…

0cf31f7a1a:442c40e658a78fd6.title: When Crime Enters City Hall: Organized Crime and Municipal Finance in Mexico
0cf31f7a1a:442c40e658a78fd6.author: Cesar Velazquez
0cf31f7a1a:442c40e658a78fd6.summary: Criminal organizations can affect local state capacity not only through violence but also through their interaction with local governments. This article examines whether criminal presence affects municipal public finances. Using 24 years of public finance data for the universe of Mexican municipalities and an event-study design, we exploit the timing of the first recorded presence of a criminal organization. We find that criminal presence is associated with lower unearmarked expenditures, driven particularly by a decline in absolute public investment and its share of total expenditure. Although the budget shares allocated to general services, personnel services, and transfers and subsidies increase, these changes do not necessarily reflect increases in absolute spending. We find no evidence of a change in own-source revenues, except in municipalities where only newly created criminal organizations are present, which exhibit higher own-source revenues. The contraction in expenditure is concentrated in municipalities with high criminal fragmentation and in those where historical criminal organizations are present. Overall, the findings indicate that organized crime is associated with a contraction in municipal expenditure and a change in budget composition.

0cf31f7a1a:867a5d651b803e1b.title: Dismissing Human Trafficking: Forced Arbitration of Survivors’ Civil Suits
0cf31f7a1a:867a5d651b803e1b.author: Werner, Daniel
0cf31f7a1a:867a5d651b803e1b.summary: For more than two decades, federal law has provided trafficked individuals the right to sue their traffickers in court and hundreds of survivors have filed suit. Their litigation has yielded millions in judgments and settlements, public accountability, development of the law, and a deeper understanding of human trafficking. Forced arbitration of human trafficking claims threatens these successes. Much has been written about the existence and enforcement of pre-dispute arbitration clauses, particularly in employment and consumer matters. This Article is the first to assess these pervasive contractual provisions in the context of human trafficking. It sets out the public and private functions of the federal private right of action for trafficking survivors. Informed by federal cases where alleged traffickers successfully compelled arbitration, the Article details how these important functions are undermined by forced arbitration and how the harms of human trafficking are exacerbated by it. Compelling arbitration of survivors’ civil claims erodes government efforts to combat human trafficking and to support survivors. This Article makes two recommendations to address this deepening and underappreciated problem. First, Congress should amend the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) to invalidate pre-dispute arbitration provisions in cases involving human trafficking. Second, the regulations governing temporary work visas for foreign nationals should prohibit pre-dispute arbitration provisions in their employment contracts. In the meantime, survivors can continue to challenge these provisions in court using contract defenses.

0cf31f7a1a:a19e9526bcbbffbf.title: First-Month Check-Ins as an Early Indicator in Pretrial Supervision
0cf31f7a1a:a19e9526bcbbffbf.author: Warren, Madeline
0cf31f7a1a:a19e9526bcbbffbf.summary: Pretrial supervision has a short window to keep a person on track to resolve their case without returning to jail, and most of what agencies use to set supervision intensity is fixed at booking. Published pretrial research has found static factors such as criminal history and prior failures to appear more predictive than dynamic ones (Bechtel, Lowenkamp, & Holsinger, 2011), but the findings reported here may challenge that conclusion. This paper asks whether something RePath records from the first day of supervision, the share of scheduled app check-ins a participant completes in the first 30 days, says anything about how the case ends. We examined Missouri pretrial cases across 65 agencies that closed successfully or unsuccessfully between October 1, 2025 and September 30, 2026 and were open at least 30 days (4, 833 closures). Among the 1, 504 cases with check-ins scheduled in the first month, participants whose cases closed successfully had completed 68.9% of them and those whose cases closed unsuccessfully 47.3%, a gap of 21.6 points (95% CI 17.2 to 26.0; Cohen's d = 0.67). Participants who completed fewer than half closed unsuccessfully 32.9% of the time, against 14.2% for the rest (risk ratio 2.31). The unsuccessful-closure rate was highest among participants who completed little or none of their first-month check-ins (39.5% at zero) and lowest among those who completed nearly all of them (7.9% at 90–99%; none of 26 at 100%), and first-month completion separated outcomes with an AUC of .69 (95% CI .66 to .72), within the range reported for two validated pretrial risk tools, the Public Safety Assessment (.55–.68) and the federal Pretrial Risk Assessment (.67–.73), though the populations, outcomes and timing differ. The gap held across case-length floors, within agencies, and with excluded closures recoded either way. We report the result with its boundaries: one state, one year, outcomes as provided by agencies, technical revocations and new arrests not…

0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.title: Can Civic Mobilization Reduce Sexual Violence? Evidence from March 4 Justice Demonstrations in Australia
0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.author: Astghik Mavisakalyan
0cf31f7a1a:fb60adac70e2fd09.summary: Civic mobilization is a common societal response to gender-based violence, but whether it actually changes sexual offending is largely unknown. We exploit geographic variation in exposure to the March 4 Justice (M4J) movement — a nationally coordinated series of protests against gender-based violence held across Australia on 15th March 2021 — as a natural experiment, using a difference-in-differences design. We find that areas hosting the protests experienced a 16 to 21 per cent reduction in recorded sexual assaults over the six to twelve months following the movement, with no significant effects across six other crime categories. This suggests a mechanism specific to sexual violence rather than general deterrence. These effects are larger in locations closer to protest activity and at sites with sizable crowds compared to smaller ones. Attitudinal data from the National Community Attitudes towards Violence against Women Survey reveal significant shifts in men’s attitudes: greater rejection of rape myths, increased survivor credibility, and reduced endorsement of patriarchal norms, with these shifts concentrated among younger and more educated men. The reductions in sexual assault are concentrated in male-represented areas, where the movement’s normative signal was more novel, and nationwide, we find suggestive evidence of a modest rise in female electoral support in 2022 relative to 2019. Together, these findings suggest that civic mobilization can reduce violence through the internalization of norms.

0cf31f7a1a:6d3606d9900690c5.title: Closure without Resolution in European Prison Oversight
0cf31f7a1a:6d3606d9900690c5.author: Ismail, Nasrul
0cf31f7a1a:6d3606d9900690c5.summary: Compliance with judgments of the European Court of Human Rights is conventionally recorded as a terminal status: a case is open or closed, a judgment executed or pending, an obligation met or unmet. These measures enable scholarly comparison, but they cannot show how a state engages with the supervision of a judgment or whether reform of prison conditions endures. As such, this article treats compliance as conduct and asks whether the closure of supervision reflects durable improvement in the conditions a judgment addressed. Drawing on the documentary record of Committee of Ministers supervision in three pilot-judgment jurisdictions (i.e., Italy, Romania, and Hungary), with two contextual comparators (i.e., Spain and England and Wales), it codes state disclosures for opacity and stance and reconstructs responsiveness descriptively from the dated supervisory sequence. Two independent coders reached strong agreement (Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.88 for stance and 0.90 for opacity, on small, well-specified eligible data sets). The cases did not form a single compliance scale but displayed distinct configurations. Specifically, Italy was transparent but shifted in its stated position before closure in 2016; Romania combined continuing engagement with capacity explanations; and Hungary combined formal but insubstantial engagement with selective disclosure. Set against current prison occupancy, the state that had completed supervision was the most overcrowded: Italy recorded 120.7 occupants per 100 places, exceeding Hungary's 114.5 and Romania's 111.2. Because the occupancy snapshot postdated Italy's closure, it could not reveal whether closure caused the later overcrowding, but it did manifest that closure did not secure lasting improvement in reforms. The article frames this durability gap as a problem of means-ends decoupling and offers a reproducible method for distinguishing compliance conduct from the substantive conditions oversight exists to change.

0cf31f7a1a:6570357cd13a1007.title: Optimal Line-Drawing for Legal Rules
0cf31f7a1a:6570357cd13a1007.author: David Weisbach
0cf31f7a1a:6570357cd13a1007.summary: Line drawing is a pervasive feature of legal systems. Across many domains, the applicable legal treatment turns on whether an activity falls above or below some threshold. We characterize the economic forces that determine the optimal placement of such thresholds, both generally and in specific legal settings involving monetary and non-monetary sanctions, prohibitions, and mandates. We apply our results to two important line-drawing questions in private law: the optimal due-care threshold for negligence liability and the optimal threshold for whether a shortfall in contract performance constitutes breach. In both applications, the optimal line takes the form of a population-level marginal cost-benefit rule, with the relevant costs and benefits weighted over the actors whose behavior the line induces to change.

0cf31f7a1a:e11f6205fdc6191f.title: The Regulatory Burden of Licensure Sales Laws: New Evidence on Race and the U.S. Tobacco Market
0cf31f7a1a:e11f6205fdc6191f.author: Joseph J. Sabia
0cf31f7a1a:e11f6205fdc6191f.summary: Licensure sales requirements are commonly justified as consumer protection regulations intended to improve seller compliance and reduce harm associated with risky products. However, licensure effects may differ across communities with heterogeneous enforcement intensity and seller responses. We study this question in the context of e-cigarette retail licensure laws (ERLLs), a policy intended to regulate access to e-cigarettes among youth. We find that state ERLLs with strong penalties for non-compliance reduce nicotine vaping among Black youths by 2.5-4.0 percentage points but have no effect on White youths. This racially disparate finding is driven by heterogeneous supply-side responses to increased regulatory burden. Vendors in Black neighborhoods are more likely to be targeted for inspections than those in White neighborhoods despite having lower pre-treatment rates of infractions. Moreover, vendors in Black neighborhoods are also less likely to sell e-cigarettes following ERLL adoption, consistent with a racially disparate regulatory burden. Together, our results suggest important distributional consequences of licensure requirements.

0cf31f7a1a:ce8cde7506173463.title: Who Replaces Spirit? Entry, Exit, and Low-End Fares
0cf31f7a1a:ce8cde7506173463.author: E. Mina Guler
0cf31f7a1a:ce8cde7506173463.summary: A federal court blocked JetBlue’s acquisition of Spirit Airlines in January 2024 to protect consumers who relied on Spirit’s low fares. Spirit failed anyway and ceased operations in May 2026. We ask whether the prohibition protected consumers. Using DB1B data for 2022–2025, we estimate the effect of Spirit’s exit across the 1, 427 routes it served. The 5th and 10th percentile fares rise by 8.6 and 5.8 log points; mean and median fares are unaffected. Where a carrier entered, the bottom is unaffected and mean fares fall. Theharm comes from exit without replacement, which entry policy does not reach.

0cf31f7a1a:ab73add37d884e06.title: A Path-Dependent Agent-Based Microsimulation of Crime and Violence Reduction Policy Portfolios in Bolivia: Survey Calibration, Adaptive Emulator Ensembles, Global Sensitivity, Tempered MCMC, and Multi-Objective Policy Analysis
0cf31f7a1a:ab73add37d884e06.author: Ricardo Alonzo Fern\'andez-Salguero
0cf31f7a1a:ab73add37d884e06.summary: This study develops a survey-calibrated, path-dependent agent-based microsimulation for evaluating crime and violence reduction policies in Bolivia. A synthetic population is constructed from the 2025 Household Survey and the fourth-quarter 2025 Continuous Employment Survey using official expansion weights and cross-survey donor matching. The model combines heterogeneous agents, place-based risk, criminal adaptation, institutional capacity, community organization, and multiple policy channels. Uncertainty is propagated through adaptive Gaussian-process and tree-ensemble emulators, global sensitivity analysis, tempered ensemble MCMC, and predictive meta-calibration. Simulated portfolios include focused policing, community control, Guardabosques-type incentives, social prevention, environmental interventions, justice reforms, investigation, rehabilitation, and financial-network disruption. Results are interpreted as structural policy scenarios rather than causal forecasts, with explicit attention to displacement, distributional effects, implementation capacity, and multi-objective trade-offs.

0cf31f7a1a:82aed7fba070816d.title: Aligning Platform and User Incentives in Social Media Age Restrictions
0cf31f7a1a:82aed7fba070816d.author: Christopher Roth
0cf31f7a1a:82aed7fba070816d.summary: Several countries are adopting social media bans for teenagers, yet early evidence suggests limited adherence to the age-based restrictions. Such bans ask platforms to remove profitable customers and teens to give up access to their online social networks. We study an alternative regulatory regime in which platforms remain liable for teens on the adult tier but may offer a safe tier that removes restricted features, such as algorithmic feeds, while preserving interactions with their relevant network. Provision of the safe tier and enforcement are complementary: teens can adhere without giving up access to their network, and platforms can retain displaced adult-tier users as lower-margin customers. This policy design makes the teen decision to avoid the adult tier less dependent on peer dynamics and increases teen welfare for a relevant range of regulatory penalties.

0cf31f7a1a:8b2a8c983e5cb139.title: How courts choose arbitrators
0cf31f7a1a:8b2a8c983e5cb139.author: Animesh Bordoloi
0cf31f7a1a:8b2a8c983e5cb139.summary: A court hearing a section 11 application decides whether an arbitrator should be appointed, and then who it should be. Indian arbitration law has developed considerable doctrine on the first question and very little on the second. The Act regulates several attributes of a person already under consideration and says nothing about how candidates are produced, whether alternatives are weighed, or what the court should record about the choice. This article examines the reported and retrievable section 11 orders of the Bombay and Madras High Courts from 2016 to 2024, a corpus of 372 orders naming 387 appointments among 201 individuals, with 36 semi-structured interviews. It reads orders as evidence of observable appointment practice, while distinguishing what the orders record from considerations (such as professional knowledge, informal inquiries, party suggestions) that may occur outside the published record. Retired judges took 63.3% of named appointments. The court named the individual in 84.7% of orders; 13.4% recorded both partiesâ€™ agreement to the person appointed. Only 4.8% of orders recorded any reason for choosing the person appointed, and 1.6% a reason specific to that person; none compared candidates. Bombay directed a section 12 dis- closure in 115 of 123 orders and Madras in four of 249. Of 387 named appointments, 186 went to someone the same court had already appointed. Where courts continue to appoint, publishing periodic aggregate data on section 11 appointments would make a public function observable over time without constraining any individual choice.

0cf31f7a1a:a5d90e328c340d09.title: Deliver Us from Crime? Gig Jobs, Labor-Market Opportunities, and Offending
0cf31f7a1a:a5d90e328c340d09.author: Picard, Ines
0cf31f7a1a:a5d90e328c340d09.summary: We study how access to low-barrier gig work affects labor markets and crime, exploiting the staggered rollout of food-delivery platforms across France. Platform entry increases delivery-worker registrations, reduces unemployment among men and inactivity among male migrants, and lowers crime, especially vandalism, petty theft, and drug offenses. Crime falls among young adults just above the legal minimum age of 18 for delivery work, but not among minors just below it. Using national criminal records, we also find that reoffending declines among offenders whose records permit platform work, but not among others. Lowering barriers to legal income can reduce low-skill offending.

0cf31f7a1a:6939ca146577e5fa.title: Immigration and Crime
0cf31f7a1a:6939ca146577e5fa.author: Mateus Maciel
0cf31f7a1a:6939ca146577e5fa.summary: The relationship between immigration and crime is one of the most salient issues in public discourse. Despite widespread public concern, most studies find no evidence that immigration increases crime rates in host countries. This article reviews recent empirical evidence on the relationship between immigration and crime. Rather than offering an exhaustive survey, it focuses on recent and seminal contributions, highlighting emerging trends and research frontiers. In particular, the article discusses how immigration policies can mediate the relationship between immigration and crime. It also discusses research on crimes against immigrants, a topic that has attracted increasing scholarly interest but remains largely neglected in public discourse. Finally, given the substantial gap between public perception and the empirical evidence, the article reviews research on immigration and crime perception.

0cf31f7a1a:c939c675e175e01f.title: When Does Randomized Oversight Align AI Agents That Can Conceal?
0cf31f7a1a:c939c675e175e01f.author: Richard T. Holden
0cf31f7a1a:c939c675e175e01f.summary: Oversight changes the evidence it relies on. We ask when randomized audits and scoring align AI agents that can conceal misconduct and alter records. Stronger auditing makes undeterred violations better hidden. Because the provider writes the agent’s objective, sanctions need not stop at forfeiture, and rare audits deter every type of agent if evidence survives concealment and audit draws cannot be learned in advance. When evidence can be erased, deterrence must come from lower gains from violation, such as credit for stopping, or from costlier or fewer ways to conceal. These conditions identify what failed when agents in OpenAI’s cybersecurity evaluations compromised parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure in July 2026.

0cf31f7a1a:f80315e437004bf2.title: Do Judges Move Markets? Ideological Shifts in the Supreme Court and Macroeconomic Expectations
0cf31f7a1a:f80315e437004bf2.author: Naixin Zhang
0cf31f7a1a:f80315e437004bf2.summary: This paper studies how judicial ideology shapes financial markets' expectations about the macroeconomy. We use unexpected deaths of U.S. Supreme Court Justices as quasi-experimental shifts in the Court's ideological balance. High-frequency asset price responses reveal how markets perceive the macroeconomic consequences of these ideological shifts. We find that a more conservative Court is associated with lower inflation expectations, lower real activity expectations, and lower bond yields. A shift towards a more liberal Court induces the opposite responses. The finding that inflation and activity expectations respond with the same sign suggests that markets revise their expectations about aggregate demand, rather than aggregate supply. Moreover, contrasting the yield responses with estimates from studies of fiscal policy news indicates that a more conservative (liberal) Court leads markets to expect tighter (looser) future fiscal policy. We validate our quasi-experimental setup with sectoral asset price dynamics, such as high-frequency responses of clean energy and health care stocks. Taken together, our findings are consistent with markets interpreting changes in the Supreme Court's ideological composition as news about future fiscal expansions or contractions.

daedf173a6:4914a026a9a1a3bc.title: New York Doctor Charged in $6.8M Medicare Fraud Scheme
daedf173a6:4914a026a9a1a3bc.summary: A federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida returned an indictment on Tuesday charging Dr. Edgard Salazar, 57, of Armonk, New York, with conspiring to bill Medicare for thousands of consultations that never occurred and millions of dollars of orthotic braces that Medicare patients did not want or need.

daedf173a6:4b8eb2f66980270c.title: Florida Man Sentenced for Stealing Millions of Dollars from Lenders Using Sham Cosmetic Surgery Clinics and Stolen Identities
daedf173a6:4b8eb2f66980270c.summary: Today, A Wellington, Florida, man was sentenced today to 84 months in prison for using sham cosmetic surgery clinics and the stolen identities of more than 100 people to defraud medical lenders of approximately $2.3 million, and for fraudulently seeking COVID-19 disaster relief loans.

daedf173a6:10f89290b902fa72.title: Arizona Federal Court Denies Request to Halt Hermosa Critical Minerals Project
daedf173a6:10f89290b902fa72.summary: The U.S. District Court for the District of Arizona last week denied a motion for a preliminary injunction to halt construction of the Hermosa Critical Minerals Project in southeastern Arizona. The project will establish a domestic source of manganese and substantially increase domestic production of zinc, which are essential to the steel used in military vehicles and naval vessels. In battery-grade form, manganese is also essential to the advanced lithium-ion batteries that power unmanned aerial vehicles, radios, and other defense equipment. The United States relies entirely on imports of manganese and almost entirely on imports of zinc, with China providing about 95% of global refining capacity for manganese used in advanced batteries.

daedf173a6:d3ee25ef683d061b.title: New Jersey Tax Preparer Pleads Guilty to Filing False Tax Returns for Clients
daedf173a6:d3ee25ef683d061b.summary: A New Jersey man pleaded guilty today to filing false tax returns for clients that caused an intended loss of $327,647 to the United States.

daedf173a6:cd4e201c129add25.title: Bergen County Orthopedic Surgeon Pleads Guilty to Employment Tax Crime
daedf173a6:cd4e201c129add25.summary: A New Jersey orthopedic surgeon pleaded guilty to failing to pay over trust fund taxes.

daedf173a6:c25618ad61f925bb.title: Court Orders Atlanta Area Tax Return Preparer to Permanently Shut Down Tax Preparation Business
daedf173a6:c25618ad61f925bb.summary: The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia issued a permanent injunction against tax return preparer Tanja D. Hollis, of Griffin, Georgia, and Hollis’s business, Tanja Tax Preparations, LLC. The injunction bars Hollis from acting as a return preparer, preparing tax returns or assisting others in the preparation of tax returns, engaging in conduct that substantially interferes with the proper administration and enforcement of the internal revenue laws and from promoting any false tax scheme.

daedf173a6:1a7c12a2a79cc859.title: Court Permanently Bars Florida Tax Return Preparer and Tax Preparation Business and Orders Disgorgement of More Than $550,000
daedf173a6:1a7c12a2a79cc859.summary: The U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida has permanently barred Juan Humberto Garcia and his tax preparation business, The Tax Master of BVL, Inc., from preparing federal tax returns for others and ordered them to pay $558,520. The court also barred Marcos Yariel Figueroa from preparing federal tax returns for others for two years.

daedf173a6:5f1675fca772491e.title: Social Adult Day Care Program Director Pleads Guilty to $127M Medicare and Medicaid Fraud Scheme
daedf173a6:5f1675fca772491e.summary: A Queens man pleaded guilty on Monday to defrauding Medicare and New York State Medicaid of approximately $127 million by billing for medically unnecessary prescription drugs and social adult day care (SADC) services that were not provided.

daedf173a6:c515253b780a96a4.title: Illinois Tax Preparer Sentenced for Stealing More than $11M from Taxpayers in COVID-19 Assistance Fraud Scheme
daedf173a6:c515253b780a96a4.summary: An Illinois woman was sentenced on Friday to 36 months, two years of supervised release, and ordered to pay $11,130,490 in restitution and a forfeiture money judgment of $1,965,712, for running a multi-million-dollar pandemic assistance and unemployment benefits scheme.

daedf173a6:699009d79c29c6c6.title: Three Iranian-Backed Operatives Indicted for Their Roles in Nearly 20 Terrorist Attacks and Attempted Attacks Across Europe and the United States
daedf173a6:699009d79c29c6c6.summary: An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

daedf173a6:988d440a53e79419.title: Multi-State Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Leads to 36 Indicted for Drug Trafficking and Money Laundering
daedf173a6:988d440a53e79419.summary: The Justice Department today announced that 36 individuals, nine of whom are illegal aliens, have been charged in a multi-state Homeland Security Task Force investigation involving drug trafficking and money laundering that spans international borders.

daedf173a6:2f56583471407dab.title: Idaho Man Sentenced to 18 Years in Prison for Attempting to Provide Material Support to ISIS in Plot to Attack Churches
daedf173a6:2f56583471407dab.summary: Alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, was sentenced today to 18 years in prison and lifetime supervised release by U.S. District Judge David C. Nye of the District of Idaho for attempting to provide material support and resources to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

daedf173a6:4feb245930f18f26.title: Dual Kazakhstani-Tajikistani Citizen Extradited from Egypt for Role in Alien Smuggling Conspiracy
daedf173a6:4feb245930f18f26.summary: Abdulhafiz Bahovatdiny, 36, a dual Kazakhstani-Tajikistani citizen made his initial appearance in court in Phoenix, Arizona, today after being extradited from Egypt to face charges for his role in a human smuggling conspiracy.

daedf173a6:ca7eed7d94a63b82.title: Justice Department Issues Fact Sheets About Lease Terminations for Servicemembers and their Dependents
daedf173a6:ca7eed7d94a63b82.summary: The Justice Department announced today that it has issued two fact sheets to help servicemembers, including those who are returning to civilian life as veterans, avoid unnecessary rent payments and costly fees. The first explains how servicemembers and their dependents can end a residential or business lease on receiving eligible military orders. And the second explains how they can end certain vehicle leases.

daedf173a6:aa2a8f3c30941e5d.title: AG Blanche and Missouri Officials Announce St. Louis as Winner of the Model Cities Initiative

daedf173a6:32b6eab98d75d64c.title: Justice Department Sues Lyft for Denying Rides to Passengers with Service Dogs, Wheelchairs
daedf173a6:32b6eab98d75d64c.summary: Today, the Justice Department (Department) filed a lawsuit against Lyft Inc., for discriminating against passengers with disabilities, including those who use service animals and mobility devices such as stowable wheelchairs. Lyft provides an important transportation option for millions of people throughout the United States. The lawsuit seeks $53 million for individuals with disabilities who Lyft has discriminated against, and who have submitted complaints to Lyft or the Department.

daedf173a6:f9d4721f7436223b.title: Justice Department Sues the City of Glendale, California for Violating Citizens’ Second Amendment Rights Through Unreasonable Fees and Processes for Legal Firearm Permitting
daedf173a6:f9d4721f7436223b.summary: Today, the United States Department of Justice sued the City of Glendale, California, for violating citizens’ fundamental rights under the Second Amendment by requiring unreasonable fees to obtain concealed carry permits.

daedf173a6:4162bfcc3956cc41.title: Justice Department Awards Jackson, Mississippi, more than $63M to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order Through Model Cities Initiative
daedf173a6:4162bfcc3956cc41.summary: Today, the Justice Department awarded Jackson, Mississippi, more than $63 million through its Model Cities Initiative (MCI), a flagship effort to reduce violent crime, restore law and order, and strengthen public safety in communities across the country.

daedf173a6:2b6b905c098af3f3.title: Justice Department Awards St. Louis more than $68M to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order Through Model Cities Initiative
daedf173a6:2b6b905c098af3f3.summary: Today, the Justice Department awarded St. Louis, Missouri, more than $68 million through its Model Cities Initiative (MCI), a flagship effort to reduce violent crime, restore law and order, and strengthen public safety in communities across the country.

daedf173a6:e01aafb08576c123.title: Prolific Human Smuggler Extradited from Brazil Pleads Guilty to Smuggling Aliens into the United States
daedf173a6:e01aafb08576c123.summary: Saiful Islam, 39, a Bangladeshi national, pleaded guilty today to charges related to his role in a conspiracy that smuggled numerous aliens through South America, Central America, and Mexico to the United States.

daedf173a6:e28b7867a2994d99.title: 14 Charged in Deadly Human Smuggling Scheme That Killed 7 Aliens Earlier This Year
daedf173a6:e28b7867a2994d99.summary: A federal grand jury in the Western District of Texas returned a superseding indictment charging a total of 14 individuals, including seven illegal aliens, three non-citizens, and four U.S. citizens, for their roles in a conspiracy to smuggle aliens into the United States for profit. This included a failed human smuggling event that resulted in the deaths of seven people, including one child, who died after being loaded into a poorly ventilated shipping container.

daedf173a6:0bdd8bbb1cad0ea5.title: California Laboratory and Its Owner Pay $1.25M to Settle Allegations of Kickbacks to Marketers
daedf173a6:0bdd8bbb1cad0ea5.summary: Clinical laboratory Lab Genomics LLC based in Fountain Valley, California, and its owner, Leena Dalal, have agreed to pay $1.25 million to the United States to resolve allegations that they violated the False Claims Act by paying illegal kickbacks to marketers.

daedf173a6:9ccbb86689dfdc5c.title: Justice Department Awards Jacksonville More Than $73M to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order Through Model Cities Initiative
daedf173a6:9ccbb86689dfdc5c.summary: Today, the Justice Department awarded Jacksonville, Florida, more than $73 Million through its Model Cities Initiative (MCI), a flagship effort to reduce violent crime, restore law and order, and strengthen public safety in communities across the country.
