daedf173a6:438f92a11f7caaff.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice issued the following statement today in connection with the closing of the Antitrust Division’s investigation into the proposed acquisition of Roku Inc. (Roku) by FOX Corporation (FOX) (together, the “Parties”).

daedf173a6:9501dfb9249615eb.title: Justice Department Awards East Baton Rouge Parish More Than $63.5M to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order Through Model Cities Initiative
daedf173a6:9501dfb9249615eb.summary: Yesterday, the Justice Department awarded East Baton Rouge Parish $63,532,285 million through its Model Cities Initiative (MCI), a flagship effort to reduce violent crime, restore law and order, and strengthen public safety in communities across the country.

daedf173a6:47d68df42b9c06fa.title: Homeland Security Task Force Investigation Leads to Mexican Federal Judge’s Arrest on U.S. Charges of Accepting $2 Million Bribe to Free Canadian Drug Trafficker Charged with Ryan Wedding
daedf173a6:47d68df42b9c06fa.summary: A Mexican judge has been arrested on a nine-count federal indictment charging him with accepting a $2 million bribe in exchange for granting bond to and ordering the release of a Canadian drug trafficker who was the second-in-command to a former Olympic snowboarder charged with leading a transnational cocaine trafficking operation and with murder and attempted murder, the Justice Department announced today.

daedf173a6:ab35df7a838804f5.title: The Department of Justice Files Complaint Against the Pennsylvania State University Challenging Its Policy that Provide In-State Tuition to Illegal Aliens
daedf173a6:ab35df7a838804f5.summary: Today, the U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against the Pennsylvania State University for violating federal law by prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands. The Department is challenging the Pennsylvania State University’s policy which grants in-state tuition to illegal aliens while denying reduced tuition to U.S. citizens. This policy unconstitutionally discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate, in direct conflict with federal law.

daedf173a6:54b902d1fb0b0fe1.title: Reward Offers Up to $50M for Information Leading to Arrests and/or Convictions of Foreign Terrorist Organization Tren de Aragua (TdA) Leaders Following Homeland Security Task Force Investigation
daedf173a6:54b902d1fb0b0fe1.summary: Note : Read the Superseding Indictment here. Foreign Terrorist Organization Tren de Aragua (TdA) leaders Yohan José Romero, also known as “Yohan Petrica,” 48; Giovanni Vicente Mosquera Serrano, also known as “El Viejo,” 37; and Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez, also known as “Juancho,” 44, were previously charged in a 2025 six-count second superseding indictment in the Southern District of Texas, for conspiring to provide and providing material support to TdA. A nine-count third superseding indictment was later returned in July 2026 and unsealed this week. In those indictments, Mosquera Serrano is also charged with conspiracy to manufacture and distribute cocaine and international cocaine distribution.

daedf173a6:492ad2858c54b7ae.title: Justice Department Says Federal Education Aid Cannot Be Tied to Unconstitutional Race-Based Criteria
daedf173a6:492ad2858c54b7ae.summary: Today, the Department of Justice’s Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion clarifying the limits on the Department of Education’s authority to consider race when administering the Magnet Schools Assistance Program (MSAP). MSAP is a federal grant program designed to promote voluntary school desegregation and expand educational opportunities for students through competitive grants to school districts. The opinion reaffirms the federal government’s longstanding support for magnet schools while ensuring that federal assistance is not conditioned on unconstitutional race‑based criteria.

daedf173a6:4eefba48c378c3d0.title: CEO and VA Employee Sentenced for Paying and Receiving Illegal Health Care Kickbacks and Bribes
daedf173a6:4eefba48c378c3d0.summary: Two Florida men were sentenced today for their roles in a conspiracy to pay and receive illegal health care kickbacks. Laurent Cassagnol was sentenced to 6 months in prison, and Heriberto Rivera was sentenced to 13 months in prison. In addition to the prison terms, Cassagnol was ordered to forfeit $175,172, and Rivera was ordered to forfeit $515,542, which represented the proceeds that the defendants obtained from the offense.

daedf173a6:703d9e3654392121.title: Former Kokomo Police Department Officer Sentenced to 40 Years in Prison for Sexually Assaulting Minor, Lying to Investigators, and Destruction of Records

daedf173a6:2d1e446ca814a36a.title: Texas Man Indicted for Sex Trafficking and Obstruction Offenses
daedf173a6:2d1e446ca814a36a.summary: A federal grand jury in the Northern District of Texas returned an eight-count superseding indictment charging Felix Omoruyi, 39, of DeSoto, Texas, with sex trafficking by force, fraud, or coercion, sex trafficking of a minor, and related charges.

daedf173a6:18521666d83e4a8f.title: Cleveland Gang Members Convicted of Racketeering, Murder, Kidnapping, Drug Trafficking, and Firearms Offenses
daedf173a6:18521666d83e4a8f.summary: Following a three-week trial, a federal jury in Cleveland convicted three members of the Fully Blooded Felons, a violent Cleveland street gang, of a number of crimes, including Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (RICO) Act murder, RICO conspiracy, RICO kidnapping, drug trafficking, and gun crimes.

daedf173a6:cb25ff7e632443ca.title: U.S. Trustee Program Prevails at Trial to Revoke $3.9M Discharge from Seattle Man Who Concealed Inheritance Rights and Business Interest
daedf173a6:cb25ff7e632443ca.summary: A Seattle man who concealed an inheritance and his interest in a business lost his bankruptcy discharge of more than $3.9 million after a trial victory by the Justice Department’s U.S. Trustee Program (USTP).

daedf173a6:2dd969bd3a1464a3.title: Department of Justice Launches Super Intelligence Task Force
daedf173a6:2dd969bd3a1464a3.summary: The U.S. Department of Justice is announcing the formation of its Super Intelligence (SI) Task Force (DOJ-SITF). President Trump has made clear that “America stands at the forefront of a new technological revolution in intelligence,” and the Department will be a leader in safeguarding against malicious SI actors.

daedf173a6:ba922de121eea7ea.title: Los Angeles Woman Charged for $18M COVID-19 Relief Fraud Scheme
daedf173a6:ba922de121eea7ea.summary: A federal grand jury in the Central District of California returned an indictment yesterday charging Marisela Nuno, 53, of Los Angeles, California, with an $18 million scheme to defraud the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) and the Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) program, federal stimulus programs authorized as part of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act.

daedf173a6:56f31da86da435de.title: Attorney General Blanche, Governor Landry, Senator Cassidy, and Louisiana Officials Announce East Baton Rouge Parish as Winner of the Model Cities Initiative

daedf173a6:2a53591c0a7847f1.title: Utah Minor Recovered by Law Enforcement After Oregon Man Allegedly Transported the Victim to Engage in Criminal Sexual Activity
daedf173a6:2a53591c0a7847f1.summary: An Oregon man is now in federal custody and charged in a criminal complaint with transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity after he allegedly met a Utah minor online in May 2025, drove to Utah to pick up the victim, and then transported the victim to his residence across state lines.

daedf173a6:a8338fb5ea5f29bb.title: DOJ To Monitor Elections in All 50 States for First Time
daedf173a6:a8338fb5ea5f29bb.summary: One of the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) most important missions is ensuring election integrity, supporting free and fair elections, and protecting the right to vote for U.S. citizens across the United States. The DOJ has sent election monitors in support of this mission since the enactment of the Voting Rights Act in 1965 across all Administrations.

daedf173a6:571a6f54def6e329.title: Oklahoma Man Charged in Connection with Sending Threatening Letters Containing Non-Toxic White Powder to Election and Government Officials Across the Country
daedf173a6:571a6f54def6e329.summary: Robin Patrick Martin, 67, of Oklahoma City, has been charged with conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications in connection with threatening letters mailed to state election officials, members of Congress, the FBI and others.

daedf173a6:e84db2cc3fed10cf.title: Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia
daedf173a6:e84db2cc3fed10cf.summary: Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

daedf173a6:42cdea27dcac3255.title: Defense and Aerospace Contractors ILC Dover and ILC Astrospace Agree to Pay $13M to Resolve Cybersecurity Fraud Allegations
daedf173a6:42cdea27dcac3255.summary: Defense and aerospace companies ILC Dover LP and ILC Astrospace LLC, of Frederica, Delaware, have agreed to pay $13 million to resolve allegations that they violated the False Claims Act by failing to comply with cybersecurity requirements in their contracts with the Department of the Army, the Missile Defense Agency, and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).

daedf173a6:f82aaeb41b6a7a38.title: Ohio Pet Breeder Agrees to Surrender Over 1,100 Chinchillas
daedf173a6:f82aaeb41b6a7a38.summary: The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio endorsed a consent decree entered between the United States and the owner of R & R Chinchilla Inc. to surrender over 300 remaining chinchillas at a breeding facility in Jenera, Ohio. The court order follows R & R Chinchilla’s voluntary surrender of roughly 800 additional chinchillas to animal welfare organizations pursuant to a modified temporary restraining order.

daedf173a6:6af5aa394bb55d76.title: American Man Extradited from Germany to Face Charges of Defrauding U.S. Consumers in Fake Psychic Mailing-Fraud Scheme
daedf173a6:6af5aa394bb55d76.summary: Mael Chemla, 61, a U.S., French, and Israeli national, previously residing in Aventura, Florida, was extradited to the United States from Germany and made his initial appearance in Miami federal court yesterday to face charges for his role in operating a mailing fraud scheme.

daedf173a6:21f1d33ada86bec9.title: Lockheed Martin Agrees to Pay $29.5M to Resolve Alleged Employment Discrimination Violations
daedf173a6:21f1d33ada86bec9.summary: Today, the U.S. Department of Justice and the U.S. Equal Employment Commission (EEOC) announced a two-part settlement against Lockheed Martin Corporation, headquartered in Bethesda, Maryland. Lockheed has agreed to pay a total of approximately $29.5 million to resolve allegations relating to employment discrimination and related false certifications of compliance with federal civil rights laws while serving as a federal contractor. This includes $22 million to be paid to the United States pursuant to an agreement with the Justice Department to resolve allegations that Lockheed violated the False Claims Act arising from failures to comply with anti-discrimination requirements in its federal contracts and by discriminating against employees and applicants on the basis of their race or sex. It also includes approximately $7.5 million to be paid to over 1,000 affected Lockheed employees pursuant to a negotiated settlement agreement with the EEOC resolving a 2025 Commissioner’s Charge filed by EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, which alleged Lockheed violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act by engaging in race discrimination against white employees, including in performance assessments and in bonus and other compensation decisions. This is the largest class of workers to publicly recover under an EEOC settlement on account of alleged Title VII violations arising from or relating to a DEI program or practices.

daedf173a6:8a775e25fc416bdb.title: Justice Department Announces Charges Involving 63 Individuals for Election-Related Crimes
daedf173a6:8a775e25fc416bdb.summary: Today, the Justice Department announced charges involving 63 individuals, including four illegal aliens, in connection with illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration, and related election crimes across the country. The cases include voting by aliens in federal elections, false claims of U.S. citizenship to register to vote or to vote, and the fraudulent submission of a voter registration application in another state.

daedf173a6:1aa5c8ee71463842.title: Former BizJet Sales Manager Pleads Guilty to Foreign Bribery
daedf173a6:1aa5c8ee71463842.summary: Jald Jensen, 73, of Panama City, and previously of Van Nuys, California, a former sales manager of BizJet International Sales and Support Inc. (BizJet), pleaded guilty today for his role in connection with a scheme to pay bribes to government officials in Latin America to secure business for BizJet.

daedf173a6:bc260bb4feb6f45c.title: Justice Department Announces Nearly $300 Million in Awards to Four Model Cities to Combat Violent Crime and Restore Law and Order
daedf173a6:bc260bb4feb6f45c.summary: Today, the Justice Department announced the selection of four jurisdictions to receive nearly $300 million in federal funding through its Model Cities Initiative (MCI), a flagship effort to reduce violent crime, restore law and order, and strengthen public safety in American communities.

ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.title: Partners on a Climb : Financial Sector Development and Tax Collections in Indonesia
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.author: Polat, Beyza
ef78496c13:ccfd929afb3cc211.summary: Shallow financial markets may act as an important structural constraint on a country’s ability to mobilize tax revenues. This paper explores this hypothesis in the context of Indonesia, a middle-income country with persistently low tax collections and low financial sector depth. At the macro level, relating cross-country financial development to new estimates of tax gaps, it finds that a 1 percent increase in private credit as a share of GDP could reduce the tax gap by approximately 0.2 percent. At the micro level, analysis of publicly listed Indonesian companies suggests that a one-decile increase in financial constraints is associated with a 0.18 percentage point drop in cash effective tax rates, indicating that financially constrained firms may be using tax planning as a liquidity tool. The results suggest that tax collections are positively associated with financial sector deepening.

ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.title: Low fertility rates: A fiscal policy perspective
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.author: Baur, Martin
ef78496c13:f94c98ad2bfc0d23.summary: Switzerland’s fertility rate fell below 1.3 children per woman in 2024 and has remained well below the replacement level for decades, reflecting a broader trend across advanced economies. This paper discusses the economic and fiscal implications of persistently low fertility, reviews its underlying causes and the extent to which family policy can influence fertility decisions, and presents policy options available for Switzerland. Low fertility slows growth of the domestic working-age population, accelerates population ageing, and reduces long-term economic growth potential. For public finances, it dampens tax revenues and social insurance contributions while increasing age-related expenditure, particularly on pensions and healthcare. The causes of low fertility are multifaceted, including the financial costs of having children, difficulties in reconciling work and family life, and broader changes in social norms and lifestyles. Evidence from OECD countries suggests that family policies can alleviate some constraints, but their effects on fertility are small and often temporary. Coherent and well-coordinated measures supporting families throughout the child-rearing years appear more promising than individual measures. As a sustained reversal of current fertility trends appears unlikely, economic and fiscal policy should focus on adapting to an ageing society by making better use of the domestic labour supply, facilitating labor-market-oriented immigration, and fostering productivity growth. Finally, reforms to strengthen the fiscal sustainability of pension and healthcare systems become even more important.

ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.title: The Fiscal Alibi: Hidden Spending Needs and Government Reputation
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:0be26042a1eac5e4.summary: A government may ask for a high tax because it faces a genuine expense. The same demand can also be made by a government that intends to keep the proceeds. We study this ambiguity in a two-period reputation model with privately observed spending needs and an endogenous tax base. The opportunist chooses between outright confiscation and levies that an honest government might impose. We characterize the three possible regimes through a single equilibrium equation. A mean-preserving spread of legitimate needs weakly raises the opportunist’s lifetime value, with a strict increase precisely when the spread changes the upper tail relevant for mimicry. We then give a necessary and sufficient curvature condition for this ordering to extend to a general reputational continuation prize. Verification reduces the value of concealment, but also changes how the opportunist extracts. In the benchmark economy, greater auditing weakly lowers current citizen welfare, even before audit costs, while improving the future allocation through better information. The welfare case for verification consequently depends on the balance between these two effects. Examples yield no auditing, an optimum within a regime, and an optimum at the boundary between regimes.

ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.title: Taxing Capital to Protect It
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.author: Ly, Hengrina
ef78496c13:1b25c4cb38967f26.summary: This paper studies the composition of taxation when the government cannot fully commit to respecting private returns after investment. A fiscal authority must finance a given expenditure from labor and capital income. Ordinary tax receipts are protected, but an opportunistic executive can seize part of the remaining capital payment. We show that a revenue-neutral increase in the capital tax raises the probability of compliance whenever the labor tax is below its local, fixedwage revenue peak, provided the equilibrium remains on a regular mixing branch. This result does not depend on the elasticity of substitution between capital and labor. The same reform can raise investment: the gain in expected retention must outweigh the decline in the opportunist’s continuation gain as compliance becomes less informative. We also characterize the Ramsey allocation conditional on full compliance. Limited commitment then imposes a ceiling on sustainable capital payments, rather than a general lower bound on the statutory capital-tax rate. Finally, we distinguish a change in the authority’s concern for the future from an increase in both actors’ patience. The former favors more informative policies when continuation welfare is convex; the latter has no unconditional direction in the reduced-form policy problem.

ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.title: Tax Expenditure Reporting as a Commitment Device for Revenue Mobilization
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.author: Gaël Tape
ef78496c13:06732b4140d7f719.summary: This note shows that publishing tax expenditure reports increases tax revenue mobilization over the medium term in emerging and developing countries. The results indicate that this effect emerges six to seven years after publication and is driven primarily by direct taxes. The effect is stronger when reports are published more frequently and on a regular basis. It is also more pronounced in low-income countries and in sub-Saharan Africa. Publishing tax expenditure reports acts as a commitment mechanism. By making tax exemptions visible, it raises the political cost of opaque exemptions and gradually strengthens the government's capacity to steer tax policy.

ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.title: AI subsidies as a tool for redistribution
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.author: Lucas Parmentier
ef78496c13:2a829ab142f8603a.summary: I study the optimal taxation of artificial intelligence (AI). My analysis highlights a wage-compression effect that provides a rationale for subsidizing AI, as AI adoption may reduce rather than increase wage inequality. When this effect outweighs AI's social costs, AI should be subsidized instead of taxed. I treat AI as a productive input distinct from robots, as the two technologies perform different ranges of tasks. Using numerical simulations, I demonstrate that the optimal policy for AI may differ sharply from that for robots. Under the benchmark calibration, AI is subsidized, whereas robots are taxed. Therefore, the case for taxing AI is weaker than is commonly assumed. When AI lowers the skill premium, fiscal policy may need to encourage, rather than slow, adoption.

ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.title: Perverse Tax Incentives and the Destruction of Creative Works
ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.author: Maher, Luke
ef78496c13:d25c012959c8c987.summary: In late 2023, Warner Bros. Discovery announced that it would be permanently shelving Coyote vs. Acme, a complete and hotly anticipated film about popular Looney Tunes characters. This announcement was widely understood—and admitted by Warner Bros. Discovery in its Securities and Exchange Commission filings—to be motivated, at least in part, by a desire to “write off” the film’s costs for tax purposes. This Article is the first to (1) provide a full account for the tax rules that govern what constitutes a “loss” for purposes of unreleased creative works, (2) evaluate whether those rules make sense from both a technical and policy perspective (concluding that they do not), and (3) compare the relative merit of other approaches to allowing tax losses for unreleased creative works. In so doing, this Article makes two necessary contributions to current tax scholarship: first, it links the robust property scholarship on waste to tax policy, setting forth a framework through which critical reappraisals of long-entrenched tax laws and policies can be conducted, identifying ossified policies that no longer comport with our policy goals and revenue-raising needs and developing ways to improve them. Second, it also offers guidance in the ways that the law can think about the ownership, abandonment, and taxation of intangible assets.

ef78496c13:3bb778580565e14b.title: Implicit Pension Taxes over the Life Cycle: Efficiency Costs and Tax Smoothing
ef78496c13:3bb778580565e14b.author: Lundberg, Jacob
ef78496c13:3bb778580565e14b.summary: This paper studies the efficiency cost of pay-as-you-go pension systems. The return on pension contributions – typically average income growth – is lower than the market return on capital. Because the gap between these returns compounds over the life cycle, early-career contributions have a higher implicit tax rate. I develop a sufficient-statistics framework in which the deadweight loss depends on the age profile of implicit tax rates. Deadweight loss is minimized when the implicit tax rate is constant, mirroring the logic of tax smoothing. I then propose an implementation within a notional defined contribution design: contributions are valorized at a higher, market-based rate of return, while a lower fraction of contributions is credited to notional accounts and the remainder treated as a pure tax. Finally, I apply my deadweight loss formula to OECD PAYGO pension systems. Under the assumed parameter values, the deadweight loss averages 19 percent. I find that only 0.2 percentage points is attributable to the uneven timing of implicit taxation.

ef78496c13:5fda887cad01a0f8.title: The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act
ef78496c13:5fda887cad01a0f8.author: Joshua Rauh
ef78496c13:5fda887cad01a0f8.summary: This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion. Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies. Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025). This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act's wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature. We estimate that California's billionaires contribute $3.3–5.8 billion annually in state income taxes. The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion. Across 100, 000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.

ef78496c13:a8cff203e584ffa1.title: Greed versus Fear: Optimal Time-Consistent Taxation with Default
ef78496c13:a8cff203e584ffa1.author: Vytautas Valaitis
ef78496c13:a8cff203e584ffa1.summary: This paper studies optimal time-consistent distortionary taxation with default. The government taxes labor income or issues non-contingent debt to finance an exogenous stochastic stream of fiscal shocks. Debt can be repudiated subject to default costs. Optimal policy is characterized by two opposing incentives that capture the double lack of commitment to old tax policies and to repaying debt, respectively: an incentive to postpone taxes by issuing more debt for the future (â€œGreedâ€ ), and an incentive to tax more currently to avoid punishing default premia (â€œFearâ€ ). A Generalized Euler Equation captures these forces and determines the optimal back-loading or front-loading of tax distortions. Even with small default risk, tax-smoothing and debt issuance are substantially limited when short-term debt is available. The same mechanisms operate in environments with long-term debt, but debt serves more as a fiscal absorber.

ef78496c13:dd6e53e0c11b6771.title: When Should Robots Be Subsidized?
ef78496c13:dd6e53e0c11b6771.author: Klaus Prettner
ef78496c13:dd6e53e0c11b6771.summary: This paper studies optimal robot taxation in a static model with routine and non-routine workers. Robots substitute for routine workers and complement non-routine workers. In addition, robots are produced in a monopolistic sector that charges a markup over marginal cost. In the absence of monopoly power, the optimal robot tax rate is zero. When robot producers have monopoly power, the optimal policy corrects the markup distortion by aligning the effective robot price with marginal cost, conditional on the labor supply induced by the income tax system. The wage premium rises with the expansion of the tasks that robots can perform and declines with higher robot production costs. The results clarify the conditions under which robot taxation serves as a corrective instrument.

ef78496c13:0450f280498fb7ba.title: State Child Tax Credits and Parental Labor Supply: Evidence from Staggered Adoption
ef78496c13:0450f280498fb7ba.author: Parolin, Zachary
ef78496c13:0450f280498fb7ba.summary: States increasingly supplement the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) with credits that vary in generosity, refundability, and earnings requirements. We examine changes in parental employment, labor force participation, and work hours following state CTC adoption using the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC), 2004–2026. Our preferred stacked difference-in-differences design includes 12 adopting states with complete event-time support and compares them with never-treated states and states that adopted after our evaluation window. Averaging over the first three post-adoption survey years, the estimated effect is 0.05 percentage points (SE 1.03) for employment and −0.46 points (0.82) for labor force participation; estimates for work hours are also close to zero. Across secondary specifications and CPS Basic Monthly analyses, extensive-margin estimates were similarly small. Larger simulated benefits are associated with fewer hours among employed parents, but the relationship is also evident before adoption and may partly reflect how benefits depend on earnings. Overall, the estimates provide little indication that state CTC adoption has substantially reduced parental employment, although meaningful effects in either direction cannot be ruled out under moderate departures from parallel trends.

ef78496c13:69562ce07e17f2f8.title: Taxing top wealth: migration responses and their aggregate economic implications
ef78496c13:69562ce07e17f2f8.author: Munoz, Mathilde
ef78496c13:69562ce07e17f2f8.summary: Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: a 1pp increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2%. A large fraction of the wealthy are business owners, and their businesses are negatively affected by owner out-migration. The aggregate effects are nevertheless modest: the migration responses to a 1pp increase in the top wealth tax rate reduce employment by 0.02%, investments by 0.07%, and value-added by 0.10%.

ef78496c13:5c102bc5df1c8bb3.title: Fiscal integration as a Pareto improvement
ef78496c13:5c102bc5df1c8bb3.author: Bonfanti, Giovanni
ef78496c13:5c102bc5df1c8bb3.summary: Fiscal integration in a currency union is generally understood as a transfer from fiscally strong to fiscally weak countries. I show that this changes when common debt is paired with a non-defaultable common tax, even if national debt remains defaultable. The risky country gains from intertemporal trade: it receives a grant financed by a perpetual obligation it discounts more heavily than lenders do. The cost to the safe member is second-order and the tax removes it by insuring imperfectly correlated cycles rather than transferring resources in expectation. The calibration delivers a narrow Pareto-improving region: the tax that eliminates the risky country’s perverse incentive to default is negligible, while the tax that compensates the safe country is an order of magnitude larger. Joint spending on a public good expands the region and reverses that ordering: the safe country gains even before the common budget balances. JEL Classification: F34, F36, F45, H63, H87

ef78496c13:20d85485adf414c5.title: Tax Productivity and Economic Development: A Quantitative Macroeconomic Analysis
ef78496c13:20d85485adf414c5.author: Yuntian Zhao
ef78496c13:20d85485adf414c5.summary: This paper examines the role of government capacity to collect taxes in driving economic development. We first draw on a new macro-historical database to document that tax collections relative to tax administration expenditures rise sharply with GDP per capita. We then interpret this finding in a neoclassical growth model with a tax administration sector in which labor inputs are required to raise tax revenues. Countries differ in their levels of tax productivity, capturing how effectively labor is used to raise taxes, as well as their levels of productivity in creating consumption and investment goods. Governments use tax revenues to provide public capital that complements private factors in production and to make transfers. Quantitatively, our model predicts that increases in tax productivity in low-income economies can raise GDP per capita substantially more than suggested by Hulten’s theorem.

b0a91b96f4:e32bca821dbdec7c.title: The AI Trade Deconstructed: AI Builders, AI Suppliers and AI Product firms!
b0a91b96f4:e32bca821dbdec7c.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:e32bca821dbdec7c.summary: When I posted my valuation of Anthropic a few days ago, I noted that turbulence lay ahead, both for the company and the market. I did not expect that turbulence to be this forceful and arrive this soon, but markets don't have an obligation to wait until it is convenient for investors, to adjust to new realities. With the election results on November 3 acting as a catalyst, investors initially responded positively with stocks up on Wednesday, but reversed course sharply on Thursday, with the NASDAQ down close to 6% and the S&P 500 declining 4%. This drop has again brought to the forefront questions about the AI trade and whether it has run its course. In this post, I will start by referring to my earlier note on AI as a business, and use the ideas in it to deconstruct the many players that are lumped together as AI companies, from those spending the money building the data centers (hyperscalers) to the firms benefiting from selling the builders the ingredients for these data centers (chip makers, electrical equipment, power and even real estate) to the companies that are spending considerable amounts , leasing these data centers for long periods (with the LLMs in the lead). I will argue that while all of these groups benefit, at least in general, from AI's success at creating large and profitable markets, we are at a point in the AI disruption, where their interests and payoffs will diverge, with implications for both the businesses and investors. I use last week's market carnage in technology and examine how the market treatment of these different groups may be a reflection of a more discerning market, less willing to mark up and mark down all AI companies, and more likely to treat them differently, as their business interests diverge. b0a91b96f4:cf161a55299bb135.summary: I knew that my post on Anthropic would draw strong reactions, when I made it public last week. I did mention in the course of the post that I have no interest in selling my estimate of value to the rest of the world, both because I don't own the high ground here and because it is meant to guide my decisions, not yours. That is why I made my model open to changes that you can make to my story and inputs, and while you have to trust my mechanics, I tried to carry your inputs into value. Much of the pushback I have received has been thoughtful and productive, some of it has been emotional (either from people who love Anthropic or from those who would not touch it with a ten-foot pole) and some of it, especially on the cost of capital, reflects a fundamental disconnect with market history, current market pricing and just basic business sense. I plan to play devil's advocate with my own valuation, looking at my story inputs, and ranking them in order of fragility, partly to stress-test my value estimate and partly to reinforce some corporate finance first principles, and then move on to your feedback and what I take away from it. Playing Devil's Advocate: A self-critique of my Anthropic valuation Since I posted my valuation only a week ago, rather than rehash how I approached the valuation and my end results, you can read the gory details in the post that accompanied it. I will start with a summary of the valuation, though, and then list the parts of my story that I believe are most directly driving my value estimate on both magnitude (how much it is affecting value) and fragility (how uncertain I feel about the part). b0a91b96f4:c4150c52a9a6c46f.title: The Anthropic Prospectus Arrives: My (but not the) IPO valuation!
b0a91b96f4:c4150c52a9a6c46f.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:c4150c52a9a6c46f.summary: I am a dabbler, by nature, moving on from topic to topic, but this year, I have spent more time than usual on AI, but that is because it seems to be part of almost every business or economy related story. I tried to value SpaceX ahead of and after the filing of the prospectus for its initial public offering before moving on to the question of whether it and OpenAI and Anthropic should be part of the S&P 500 index . I started my analysis of how AI would affect the rest of us , from doomsday to do-nothing scenarios, largely in response to Citrini and Citadel reports on the topic. in August 2026, I took my first big picture look at AI as a business, which I titled its bar mitzvah moment, with a look at its potential market, business economics and moats. That look was a prelude to the initial public offerings in the works (then) for Anthropic and OpenAI, and I provided a simple way to reverse engineer how much investors would need in revenues from these companies to justify their sky-high pricing. In early October, I looked at how the massive investments in AI are playing out in the aggregate earnings , cashflows and invested capital at US companies, and why it is contributing to holding the market intact, in the face of rising rates. Just last week, I argued that both Anthropic and OpenAI would be priced , rather than valued, for their initial public offerings, using what I called buzzy metrics (like annualized run rates) and promised that I would try to value the company, when it filed its prospectus. On October 26, Anthropic filed its prospectus , and at the risk of being called hopelessly wrong by both bulls and bears, I will try to value the company, using what I see as its most likely pathway, while also leaving the door open for you to disagree with me, and pick your own pathways to valuing the company. b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.author: Aswath Damodaran (noreply@blogger.com)
b0a91b96f4:7ec112c975bad06e.summary: I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies. While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs) rather than total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows. b0a91b96f4:913bec6c309fd068.summary: In a post at the end of August 2026, I talked about interest rates in 2026 and marveled at the capacity of equities to keep rising in the face of rising rates. I argued that the resilience of stocks during the year could be traced to higher-than-expected earnings being reported by companies in 2026, and a concurrent increase in expected earnings in 2027 and 2028. Now that September 2026 is one for the record books, it is time to take stock and dig a little deeper, especially since the month brought about one of the largest increase in treasury yield rates in recent memory, and stock prices still held their own. In particular, I want to examine the earnings at US companies, in the aggregate and by sector, trying to trace out where the earnings increase is coming from, and how that increased earnings is playing out on corporate balance sheets and cash flows. 1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.title: Anti-Monopoly as Industrial Policy: The Chicago School Versus Adam Smith
1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.author: Richard R. John
1aa97d921e:bd2718ce7fe44e03.summary: Jolted by the Great Depression of the 1930s, Thurman Arnold devised an anti-monopoly industrial policy for the United States Justice Department that breathed fresh life into a then-moribund Sherman Anti-Trust Act. Arnold’s jurisprudence built on Adam Smith’s discovery that market-making could promote national security and forestall civil unrest. Smith’s insights had informed the industrial policy of Alexander Hamilton, who laid the groundwork in the 1790s for the country’s economic development. Edward H. Levi brought Arnold’s pragmatic anti-monopolism to the University of Chicago. Here, ironically, Arnoldian jurisprudence would be transmogrified into the doctrinaire company-over-country market fundamentalism of the Chicago School of Economics. Today, writes Richard R. John, as we envision for the 21st century a new pro-market, pro-freedom, pro-national security industrial policy, it is worth recalling how U. S. economic development took the form that it did, why the Chicago School repudiated the enduring wisdom of Adam Smith, and what this portends for the world of today. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.title: How George Stigler and the Chicago School Opened the Marketplace of Ideas to Business
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.author: Edward Nik-Khah
1aa97d921e:1bc106d2fe57d9bb.summary: Henry Simons, the “Crown Prince” of the Chicago School and a professor in the economics department and the law school prior to World War II, sought to develop a laissez faire economics program devoted to eliminating monopoly and pursuing egalitarian goals. George Stigler and the Chicago School abandoned Simons’s anti-monopoly and egalitarian program. The best market became one driven by the search for profits, and the best-functioning marketplace of ideas arose where winning ideas reflected the greater funding backing them, writes Edward Nik-Khah. 1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.title: The Chicago School Abandoned the Positive Freedom of Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.author: Maha Rafi Atal
1aa97d921e:93e02838a27ed28b.summary: Adam Smith’s theory of political economy did not begin with the isolated individual but rather the individual who operates to earn the respect of others. Wealth and freedom grew from these relationships and engaging with others to create a free society, or what 20th century philosopher Isaiah Berlin’s would call positive freedom. In the 1970s and ‘80s, the Chicago School abandoned this aspect of freedom in preference of the isolated individual, which in turn produced a weaker concept of freedom, morality, and society that has stifled the cultivation of all three in the United States, writes Maha Rafi Atal. 1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.title: Adam Smith’s Moral Philosophy Complicates Interpretations by the Chicago School and Its Critics
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.author: Sandra Peart and David Levy
1aa97d921e:8cf8fcb20f958484.summary: The connections between Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations and Theory of Moral Sentiments reveal a much more complicated understanding of how markets work than developed in the common interpretation by the Chicago School of economics or that of its critics. Smith’s political economy based on commerce, sympathy, and competition produced social good but only when complemented and checked by other forces. When not checked, Smith worried about “factions” that produce bad outcomes, write Sandra J. Peart and David M. Levy. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.title: Why Economics Forsook Democracy
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.author: Robert Van Horn
1aa97d921e:21d2bb63cb082313.summary: The post-World War II Chicago School of Aaron Director and Milton Friedman reimagined a new (neo) liberalism that treated economic liberties and the free market as the greatest defense of political rights. The United States continues to suffer from neoliberalism’s prescriptions, and addressing the concerns of today’s populist movements will mean rediscovering ideas of freedom that the Chicago School denigrated, writes Robert Van Horn. 1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.author: David Mitch
1aa97d921e:d2d33a26a587fd61.summary: The Chicago School is often associated with laissez-faire economics that reads into Adam Smith’s philosophy of political economy justifications for self-interest and prudential motivations. However, a careful history of the University of Chicago’s early Economics Department and School of Commerce and Administration reveals a more complicated understanding of how economics and business were to interact with one another and society. The early University of Chicago pursued a program that emphasized that laissez-faire economics and a concern for the public interest were not antagonists but perfectly compatible, writes David Mitch. 1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.title: America Became Rich Because of Liberalism
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.author: Peter J. Boettke
1aa97d921e:f1e2511bf4ba4c0f.summary: Adam Smith and the Founding Fathers envisioned a society in which economic and political freedom, grouped together in the ideology of liberalism, would produce a wealthy, free, and peaceful society. Centuries later, this vision has come to fruition, and F. A. Hayek and Milton Friedman helped elaborate and advance that vision in their economic and philosophical works. The lesson for today’s populist moment is not to abandon these principles, but to continue to pursue them, as it is their imperfect realization, not their imperfect conceptualization, that burdens today’s society, writes Peter Boettke. 1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.title: American Antitrust Has Yet To Figure Out Conglomerates
1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.author: Paul Friederiszick
1aa97d921e:c0503e070848a375.summary: The Neo-Brandeisians and Chicago School have employed different statistics to show respectively that markets are both concentrated and not concentrated, leaving Americans in the dark about who really holds corporate power. The evidence only looks contradictory due to the failure of American antitrust scholarship and regulation to understand how conglomerates collect market power across many neighboring markets, through what Paul Friederiszick calls “adjacent market takeovers.” This strategy can make firms more efficient, but it can also raise prices and weaken competition even as each individual market still looks competitive, he writes, drawing on his new paper, “The Conglomerate Power Puzzle.” Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:ad66736fb16d41a6.author: Eli Orbach
1aa97d921e:ad66736fb16d41a6.summary: The transaction fees that businesses incur using credit and debit cards cost Americans billions of dollars each year. Despite the availability of alternative, cheaper account-to-account options that cut out the middleman, Americans have been slow to move away from card payment systems due to market mechanisms that hide the true costs of card transactions to consumers, writes Eli Orbach. 1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.author: Roger D. Blair and Javier D. Donna
1aa97d921e:6ae56baa9c09d5f6.summary: Two recent court rulings on casino-hotels using a shared software to fix prices reveal the importance of information exchanges as a super plus factor: an indicator of illegal conspiracy to limit trade. Roger D. Blair and Javier D. Donna discuss how these court cases and other recent lawsuits elucidate the role of the information exchange and the two vectors that determine its strength as a plus factor: data sensitivity and a give-to-get understanding among firms that if they shared their data, competitors would do the same. 1aa97d921e:ef855389029b02b3.title: The Foreignness of Africa’s Startup Ecosystem
1aa97d921e:ef855389029b02b3.author: Emanuele Colonnelli, Marcio Cruz, Mariana Pereira-Lopez, Tommaso Porzio and Chun Zhao
1aa97d921e:ef855389029b02b3.summary: Startups in Africa rely heavily on an equity market dominated by foreign investors and founders who studied or worked outside the continent. In new research, Emanuele Colonnelli, Marcio Cruz, Mariana Pereira-Lopez, Tommaso Porzio and Chun Zhao show that this dynamic exists because local equity is expensive, the pool of local entrepreneurs seeking out funding is small, and local entrepreneurs have limited access to foreign investors. Read it at ProMarket >>

1aa97d921e:a2b535c9fa459ffc.title: States Can Facilitate an AI Slowdown Without the Federal Government
1aa97d921e:a2b535c9fa459ffc.author: Noah Hoffman and Fiona Scott Morton
1aa97d921e:a2b535c9fa459ffc.summary: The artificial intelligence industry recently called for an antitrust exemption to coordinate self-regulation as the risks their models pose to the internet and society grow. Industry-wide self-regulation might well violate antitrust law and would certainly give Big Tech too much power with too little supervision. In the absence of federal action, states can and should provide the required antitrust immunity to enforce safety rules so long as they oversee the conduct, write Noah Hoffman and Fiona Scott Morton.
