59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.title: Supporting into-work benefit reform in Spain
59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.author: OECD
59ec699e9f:f28acccd2e3e34a5.summary: In Spain, the Complemento de Apoyo al Empleo (CAE) allows individuals to receive unemployment benefits whilst in employment. This paper sets out the findings and recommendations of a project aimed at improving the CAE, drawing on international good practice, as well as analyses carried out using the OECD TaxBen model and administrative data. Strengthening the role of CAE as wage insurance – by linking its amount either to UI entitlements or directly to the previous wage – would provide stronger work incentives when wage loss at re-employment is greater; and would limit low-wage traps for full-time workers. However, such reforms would tend to offer lower net income and weaker work incentives for workers transitioning between two low-paid jobs, compared with the current CAE. Strengthening the role of CAE as wage insurance would also increase CAE coverage among re-employed individuals and, consequently, fiscal costs, albeit to a moderate extent. Higher CAE coverage would particularly benefit certain vulnerable groups whose coverage is currently relatively low, such as the low skilled, the youth, and workers in southern regions.

59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.title: Return-to-Work Policies for Disability Insurance Recipients: The Role of Financial Incentives
59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.author: Tojerow, Ilan
59ec699e9f:dda2f04a09163d0b.summary: This paper studies how financial incentives shape labor supply decisions among disability insurance (DI) recipients who already combine benefits with part-time work. We exploit a distinctive feature of the Belgian Adapted Work Program, in which DI benefits are progressively withdrawn as earnings increase and the marginal withdrawal rate rises sharply at predefined thresholds. Because participants cannot freely adjust their working hours, this setting allows us to estimate how higher implicit taxation affects transitions out of partial work. Using administrative data and a Regression Kink Design, we find that higher implicit tax rates induce exits in two opposite directions: toward full-time employment and back to full DI. A oneeuro increase in the implicit marginal tax per working day raises the probability of returning to full DI by 3.0 percentage points and of resuming full-time employment by 1.5 percentage points, corresponding to elasticities of 0.84 and 0.85. A simple labor supply framework rationalizes these divergent responses. Our findings show that the financial design of partial-benefit schemes can determine whether partial work serves as a bridge toward full employment or instead leads recipients back to full benefit dependency.

59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.title: Earnings Dynamics under Firm Heterogeneity
59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.author: Timo Virtanen
59ec699e9f:4dc37001414a6d77.summary: We develop a permanent–transitory earnings process in which permanent shocks depend on a latent firm type and workers’ exposure to firm types is persistent. Persistence can substantially slow the finite-horizon attenuation of earnings skewness and excess kurtosis over the life cycle relative to an iid mixture benchmark. We estimate the model from matched employer-employee data, first grouping firms based on the distribution of residual earnings changes and then using worker transitions across groups to estimate persistence. Finnish data reveal heterogeneity in permanent-shock variances and persistent exposure to firm groups. Although skewness and excess kurtosis are not targeted in estimation, over ages 35–50 the extended model accounts for 49 percent of average empirical skewness and 39 percent of average excess kurtosis, compared with 4 percent and 3 percent under the iid benchmark. Quantitative exercises show that persistence increases the life-cycle cost of earnings risk and affects saving behavior.

59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.title: Informal Work as a Fallback: Vision Impairment, Employment, and Policy in Brazil
59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.author: Marcio V. Correa
59ec699e9f:663cd29996be8b3a.summary: Informal work may allow workers with functional limitations to remain employed when formal jobs become too costly to hold, rather than reflecting exclusion from good jobs. In Brazilâ€™s 2019 Pesquisa Nacional de Saude, severe but partial vision impairment is associated with a formal employment rate 20.9 percentage points lower than among individuals with no difficulty, but with no difference in informal employment. The asymmetry survives adjustment for observables and other functional limitations, and it is not shared by mobility, upper-limb, or mental limitations. These patterns alone cannot reveal where affected workers would go if informal work were unavailable, or how policy would reallocate them. To answer these questions, we build a general-equilibrium incomplete-markets model in which individuals choose among formal work, informal work, and non-employment. Informal work is less productive, while formal work carries a rigidity cost that rises with functional limitation. We calibrate the model to occupational shares across four vision states. In the model, eliminating informal work lowers employment by 17.6 percentage points among individuals with a vision limitation. In illustrative counterfactuals, policies that reduce informality send workers to different destinations: stricter enforcement into non-employment, workplace accommodation into formal jobs, and broader disability-benefit eligibility into supported non-employment. Changes in informality are therefore an unreliable guide to the effects of disability and formalization policy.

59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.title: Do Firms Know What Workers Want?
59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.author: Max Müller
59ec699e9f:8adc421389f4ec9c.summary: Labor supply depends on wages and amenities, and standard models implicitly assume that firms hold accurate beliefs about workers’ amenity valuations. In a survey with firms and workers in Germany linked to administrative data, we measure workers’ valuations of five different amenities and firms’ beliefs about workers’ valuations. We find that firms systematically underestimate workers’ valuations of all five amenities. These misperceptions are driven by interpersonal projection: managers project their own preferences—they value amenities less—onto workers. Through the lens of a simple model of imperfect competition, we show that firm misperceptions result in (i) labor shortages and (ii) excess labor costs for biased firms. Empirical tests confirm these predictions: a simple calibration suggests that non-providing firms could reduce their labor costs by 5% by providing amenities.

59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.title: Rent Sharing under Innovation Tax Breaks
59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.author: Ana Popovici
59ec699e9f:379dd822086a39e8.summary: We study whether firms share gains from innovation tax incentives with incumbent workers and whether such rent sharing is associated with increased worker retention. The Dutch innovation box reduces tax rates on profits from in-house innovation. Linking first-time beneficiaries to matched employer-employee data, we combine nearest-neighbour matching with staggered difference-in-differences. Part of the additional after-tax surplus is passed on to incumbent workers: wages rise by 3.27% on average, with increases of 2.05% for workers least involved in R&D and 4.14% for tertiary-educated STEM workers. Descriptively, treated non-R&D incumbents are 3.47 percentage points less likely to switch employers following treatment.

59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.title: The Long-Term Mental Health Consequences of Emotional and Interpersonal Work Demands
59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.author: Vincent Vandenberghe
59ec699e9f:ad3435bd07c6f4c0.summary: This paper examines how career-long emotional/interpersonal work demands are associated with mental health among adults aged 50 and older. Using retrospective work histories from SHARE combined with ISCO-4-level occupational characteristics from O*NET, we construct employment trajectories capturing cumulative exposure to emotionally/interpersonally demanding work and examine its association with later-life depressive symptoms, measured by the EURO-D scale. Our findings show that careerlong emotional/interpersonal demands are associated with a higher risk of depression after age 50, although their relative importance is modest. Career instability, such as employment gaps, redundancies, and part-time work, emerges as a stronger predictor. Pre-labour-market factors, including childhood health and educational attainment, also play a substantial role, highlighting the lasting importance of early-life circumstances for later-life mental health.

59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.title: The Great Household Divergence - Economic Inequality and the Roots of Social Fracture for the 99%
59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.author: Andrews, N. O.
59ec699e9f:48da82d21695aba1.summary: For decades, the debate over American inequality has centered on a single question: how unequal has the United States become? Increasingly, the more important question is different: does it matter that some Americans are pulling dramatically away from everyone else, even as real income rises for most people? This paper argues that the United States has undergone a Great Household Divergence: four decades of extraordinary prosperity coinciding with widening disparities in household market position â€” disparities that shape employment, status, dignity, health, and neighborhood opportunity. Economic distance has become social distance, accompanied by rising polarization and democratic strain. Mobility eroded for large segments of the population, leaving some American communities with world-class opportunity while others resemble the developing world. This paper weaves together literatures on inequality, mobility, polarization and social policy. It argues that the prevailing policy model has focused too heavily on correcting market outcomes after the fact, and points upstream toward pre-distribution policies that shape wages, collective bargaining, state-level employment institutions and macroeconomic conditions aimed at tighter labor markets. The central implication is that social cohesion in the U.S. cannot be restored through post-tax redistribution alone. Addressing inequality is more than the simple arithmetic of redistribution; it also requires attention to social cohesion, the earning power of Americans and human dignity.

59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.title: Which types of education raise firm productivity? Evidence for managers and workers in the UK
59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.author: Hall, Tessa
59ec699e9f:0ed7bbffe915604a.summary: This paper estimates the firm productivity returns to degree field, institution quality, and degree level, and compares them with wage returns. I link a LinkedIn panel from Revelio Labs to Orbis financial accounts for over 20, 000 UK firms over 2015?2024. Within firms, a bachelor's degree raises a worker's productivity by around 20%; a top-20 institution adds a further 10% and a postgraduate qualification 6%. The returns differ by organisational role. A bachelor's degree raises productivity for managers and non-managers alike. Specialist credentials - a STEM field, an elite institution - raise productivity for non-managers but not for managers, whose premium loads instead on postgraduate qualifications, above all MBAs. Managers also contribute around 26% more than otherwise identical non-managers, a premium that education does not explain. Averaged over the workforce, wage premia are close to productivity premia for each type of degree. However, the average conceals two wedges of opposite sign: STEM-trained non-managers are paid below their relative productivity, and degree-holding managers above it. Finally, for a subset of firms matched to the World Management Survey, workforce education accounts for around a quarter the well-documented correlation between management practices and productivity.

59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.title: What is an AI worker? Evidence from Matched Vacancy-Hires
59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.author: Hellsten, Mark
59ec699e9f:f5b8235ba0add730.summary: Despite growing policy interest in AI workforce development, surprisingly little is known about what defines these workers, or indeed if they differ from their occupational peers. Using a novel matched vacancy-hire dataset linking Swedish job postings to the individuals hired to fill them, drawn from register data on the entire Swedish population, I study the characteristics of workers who develop and apply AI. Observable traits including high cognitive ability, a tertiary degree in STEM subjects, and a recent migrant background largely explain occupational sorting. Of these, only higher education, prior AI experience, and a science degree set them apart within occupation. I then use earnings as a window onto unobservable differences: AI workers earn approximately 5% more than their peers, entirely explained by firm-level wages. However, AI workers with a doctorate degree stand out sharply in both traits and earnings, indicating that AI workers split into segments that differ by the complexity of their skills and tasks. Taken together, these results point to two distinct policy levers: the supply of average AI workers, termed AI integrators, can be expanded via STEM education participation, while the elite AI developers are supplied by researchers moving to the private sector.

59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.author: Xu, Yaling
59ec699e9f:960e30d00dd2351d.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.title: The Impacts of Unauthorized Immigration on U.S. Labor and Housing Markets: New Evidence from Administrative Microdata
59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.author: Xiaoqing Zhou
59ec699e9f:14a4ac00a73d4089.summary: From early 2021 through early 2024, the U.S. experienced an unprecedented boom in unauthorized immigration, with substantial heterogeneity across local economies. Using administrative microdata, we construct new measures of national and local unauthorized immigration flows and exploit exogenous variation using multiple empirical designs. Unauthorized immigrant worker flows increased local employment approximately one-for-one, with mixed evidence of wage depression. They also raised house prices and rents without expanding housing supply. Finally, these flows reduced labor income per capita and government transfers. These findings help inform debates surrounding how unauthorized immigration impacts labor and housing markets and public finances in the U.S.

59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.title: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.author: Camilo Morales-Jimenez
59ec699e9f:184c4bb43ea570f1.summary: The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.title: Do Pension Reforms Affect Migrants Differently? Evidence from Germany and Spain
59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.author: Hao Wei
59ec699e9f:e66d905962381a13.summary: This paper examines whether migrants and native-born workers respond differently to pension reforms that encourage longer working lives. Using longitudinal data from SHARE Waves 4â€“9 for Germany and Spain, we construct individual reform exposure based on country-specific reform timing, birth-cohort eligibility, and proximity to retirement age, and estimate models with individual and survey-wave fixed effects. Reform exposure is associated with a lower probability of retirement, with suggestive evidence of an additional decline among migrants. This migrant differential is particularly pronounced in Spain, while the corresponding estimate is small and statistically insignificant in Germany, although formal cross-country tests do not establish a statistically significant difference between the two countries. Complementary analyses indicate that adjustment is concentrated around retirement ages rather than reflecting a broad increase in employment, while evidence for effects on mental health and generalized trust is limited. Overall, the findings suggest that migrants may respond differently to pension reform, but that these differences are concentrated at specific retirement margins and depend on the institutional context

59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.title: Exploitation Cycles: Eco-Evolutionary Dynamics in Labor Markets with Predatory Employers
59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.author: Rusch, Hannes
59ec699e9f:02084d85fa7d6593.summary: Exploitative employers damage the very labor force on which they depend. Accordingly, this paper models exploitation and labor-force quality as a coupled dynamical system: exploiters spread when high-quality labor makes extraction profitable, but their success degrades the labor environment that sustains those profits. We show that this coupling generates persistent cycles rather than convergence toastable level of exploitation. Our policy extension shows that responsive enforcement can dampen these cycles, induce convergence, and improve welfare. We contribute by elucidating exploitation dynamics and demonstrating how eco-evolutionary methods can be applied to study labor markets on which employers compete with exploiters.

59ec699e9f:8c4a0ee6918676fc.title: Reconstructing the Pre-Industrial Occupational Structure of Swedish Parishes - Data and Methods, 1749–1855
59ec699e9f:8c4a0ee6918676fc.author: Sandgren, Fredrik
59ec699e9f:8c4a0ee6918676fc.summary: This paper reconstructs the occupational structure of 1720 Swedish pseudo-parishes between 1749 and 1855 using the data contained in Tabellverket, a unique collection of population and occupational records covering the country from the mid-eighteenth to the mid-nineteenth century. The original Tabellverket records are characterized by an unsystematic coverage in time and space and across occupational categories, changes in parish and pastorate boundaries, and missing observations that have so far inhibited its use at the parish level. We develop a procedure for transforming these records into a balanced panel data. The resulting dataset provides for the first time parish-level estimates of employment for 11 categories for the entire period 1749-1855 and 43 more detailed categories for the period 1805-1855 for both genders for 27 benchmarks, establishing a new empirical basis for studying long-run structural change in pre-industrial Sweden.

59ec699e9f:0307413d56381e8a.title: Slave raiding in the twentieth century
59ec699e9f:0307413d56381e8a.author: Rusch, Hannes
59ec699e9f:0307413d56381e8a.summary: Slave-making and trading lastingly shaped global demographics. However, no quantitative studies of enslavement as a day-to-day business exist. We address this gap using a unique dataset coded from the surviving records kept by notorious slave raider Hamman Yaji (c. 1863–1929). Spanning fifteen years and over 300 events, the data reveal whom Yaji targeted, how he timed his raids, and how destructive they were. Panel regression analyses show how Yaji’s decisions were shaped by political, military, ecological, and economic constraints on profit maximization. Situated in colonial eastern Nigeria, our results provide unprecedented insight into the microeconomics of slave raiding

59ec699e9f:18910aa023bf6b61.title: Immigrant-Native Wage Gaps and Rent Sharing: A Segmented Assimilation Story?
59ec699e9f:18910aa023bf6b61.author: Mélanie Volral
59ec699e9f:18910aa023bf6b61.summary: Although an increasing body of literature has examined the relationship between firms’ profitability and wage inequality in the context of a diverse workforce, the role of rent sharing in explaining origin-based wage differentials has yet to be explored. Our paper aims to fill this gap using detailed Belgian matched employer-employee data from 1999 to 2016. After controlling for a wide range of covariates and addressing endogeneity issues, our estimates show that the wage-profit elasticity equals approximately 3% and does not differ statistically between native and immigrant workers, be they first or second generation. It therefore appears that firms share their profits equally with their employees, regardless of their origin. However, Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions suggest that rent sharing has a significant influence on immigrants’ wages through labour market segregation. Specifically, first-generation immigrants are found to earn lower wages than natives because of their higher concentration in firms with lower profit margins. The same is true for second-generation immigrants, but almost half as much. These findings, corroborated and refined by heterogeneity tests according to gender, educational attainment and level of collective bargaining, support the hypothesis of a segmented assimilation process for immigrants.

59ec699e9f:db042d02c0399e10.title: Sorting into entrepreneurial teams
59ec699e9f:db042d02c0399e10.author: Marta Morazzoni
59ec699e9f:db042d02c0399e10.summary: This paper studies how entrepreneurs sort into founding teams and how team composition shapes the firm distribution. We develop a theory of career choice and team formation in which skill complementarities make team entrepreneurship attractive for agents with unbalanced skill profiles, while talent similarity makes teaming preferable to other career options. Using matched employer-employee and balance-sheet data from Portugal, we show that teams combining similar talent with diverse specializations create larger, more productive, and longer-lived firms; yet founders with dissimilar skills are less likely to start firms together. We calibrate the model to reproduce these patterns and use it to quantify the cost of imperfect founder matching. Counterfactuals show that reducing founders’ biased exposure reallocates activity from low-productivity solo firms toward more productive teams. An optimal-assignment benchmark reveals that even unbiased random search leaves substantial gains unrealized because high-surplus matches fail to form.

59ec699e9f:121d1506ddc9d1e7.title: Female Jobs and Fertility: Long-term Experimental Evidence from Ethiopian Factories
59ec699e9f:121d1506ddc9d1e7.author: Getahun, Tigabu
59ec699e9f:121d1506ddc9d1e7.summary: We conducted an experiment with multiple factories in Ethiopia to test the widespread hypothesis that formal employment among women reduces fertility. Tracking respondents over eight years, we find that women who were randomly offered a job had more children than the control group. The effect on fertility emerged once the effect on wage employment faded away, around three years after baseline. There are clear effects on household income and savings, but not on bargaining power or marriage. These patterns are consistent with a Beckerian model in which the income effect dominates the substitution effect and households are credit constrained.

59ec699e9f:af16af4a109df3c0.title: Lacunes en matière de compétences des travailleurs selon la perception des employeurs
59ec699e9f:af16af4a109df3c0.author: Genevieve Dufour
59ec699e9f:af16af4a109df3c0.summary: This report uses data from Statistics Canada’s Survey of Employers on Workers’ Skills (SEWS) to provide an overview of the skills sought, available, and developed within Canadian businesses. It focuses in particular on basic mathematics skills, numeracy, critical thinking, and problem-solving, comparing Quebec with Ontario and the rest of Canada. Our results show that basic mathematics skills are rarely perceived as a skills gap by businesses, both in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada. Quebec businesses, however, place relatively greater emphasis on technical, managerial, and computer skills, and less emphasis on critical thinking, problem-solving, and communication, both when recruiting and when developing employees’ skills. The results also show that Quebec businesses differ in how they manage skills. They assess their skills needs less frequently, make less use of informal skills-development practices such as mentoring and feedback, and report greater recruitment difficulties, regardless of the level of education required. Across all three regions, more than half of businesses attribute these difficulties to a lack of interested applicants, suggesting that job attractiveness is as much an issue as an actual shortage of skills. Finally, when faced with skills gaps, businesses tend to favour internal work reorganization rather than investing in human capital development. Ce rapport utilise les données de l’Enquête auprès des employeurs sur les compétences du personnel (EECP) de Statistique Canada pour brosser un portrait des compétences recherchées, disponibles et développées dans les entreprises canadiennes. Il porte une attention particulière aux compétences mathématiques de base, aux capacités de calcul, à la pensée critique et à la résolution de problèmes, en comparant le Québec à l’Ontario et au reste du Canada. Nos résultats montrent que les compétences mathématiques de base sont rarement perçues comme une lacune par les entreprises, au Québec comme ailleurs…

59ec699e9f:d2246d8d800ae0a2.title: Return-to-Work Policies for Disability Insurance Recipients: The Role of Financial Incentives
59ec699e9f:d2246d8d800ae0a2.author: Ilan Tojerow
59ec699e9f:d2246d8d800ae0a2.summary: This paper studies how financial incentives shape labor supply decisions among disability insurance (DI) recipients who already combine benefits with part-time work. We exploit a distinctive feature of the Belgian Adapted Work Program, in which DI benefits are progressively withdrawn as earnings increase and the marginal withdrawal rate rises sharply at predefined thresholds. Because participants cannot freely adjust their working hours, this setting allows us to estimate how higher implicit taxation affects transitions out of partial work. Using administrative data and a Regression Kink Design, we find that higher implicit tax rates induce exits in two opposite directions: toward full-time employment and back to full DI. A oneeuro increase in the implicit marginal tax per working day raises the probability of returning to full DI by 3.0 percentage points and of resuming full-time employment by 1.5 percentage points, corresponding to elasticities of 0.84 and 0.85. A simple labor supply framework rationalizes these divergent responses. Our findings show that the financial design of partial-benefit schemes can determine whether partial work serves as a bridge toward full employment or instead leads recipients back to full benefit dependency.

59ec699e9f:ca215887f7b38530.title: Beyond Employment: Minimum Wage Effects on Hours Worked
59ec699e9f:ca215887f7b38530.author: Hikaru Ota
59ec699e9f:ca215887f7b38530.summary: This study estimates the effect of minimum wage increases on low-wage employment and working hours using an event study analysis based on 138 state-level minimum wage changes in the United States. The results show that employment declines in wage bins below the new minimum wage are largely offset by increases in employment at and above it, yielding a near-zero net employment effect. Applying the same wage bin framework to total usual weekly working hours, the analysis finds no significant reduction in total working hours. However, hours worked per worker decrease significantly in the wage bin at the new minimum wage. This pattern may reflect firms adjusting along the intensive margin, but it may also arise from changes in the composition of workers within that wage bin; the analysis cannot distinguish between these explanations. Nevertheless, the findings demonstrate that stable employment levels can mask underlying changes in hours worked.

59ec699e9f:4566d866866f19f5.title: What Aggregation Hides: Disaggregated Wage Returns to Tertiary Education in New Zealand, 2016-2024
59ec699e9f:4566d866866f19f5.author: Cristóbal Castro Barrientos

59ec699e9f:c6e8101a1e5a5e7c.title: Minimum Wages and Cost-Push Inflation: Economy-Wide Evidence from Germany
59ec699e9f:c6e8101a1e5a5e7c.author: Maximilian Priem
59ec699e9f:c6e8101a1e5a5e7c.summary: We provide the first estimates of minimum wage effects on the aggregate price level using data on the near-full German consumer basket across four national reforms, 2015-2024. Drawing on a structural model of pricing under imperfect competition, we utilise minimum wage cost shocks rather than the commonly used firm-level ‘bite’ that we show to be biased under strategic complementarity. Labour cost pass-through is 83-94 percent, at the higher end of estimates for other cost shocks. The implied macro-price elasticity is 0.024. The largest increase in October 2022 to €12 raised the aggregate price level by 0.39 percent.

59ec699e9f:1259b9097c565374.title: Labor-market drivers of intergenerational earnings persistence
59ec699e9f:1259b9097c565374.author: Stuhler, Jan
59ec699e9f:1259b9097c565374.summary: How does worker-firm sorting contribute to intergenerational persistence? Firm pay premia account for 36% of the intergenerational earnings elasticity in Sweden, rising to 50% with dynamic returns to firm-specific experience. Large pay gaps already open atlabor market entry, as children from privileged backgrounds find more favorable entry points; they then climb the firm pay ladder faster, switching firms more often and gaining more per switch. Skill sorting explains this widening but not the initial gaps, consistent with networks and employer learning. Privileged children’s firms are also more desirable overall, a gap that keeps widening after pay gaps stabilize.

59ec699e9f:2be2a6c1df388255.title: Entry Motivations Shape Preferences for Social Protection Among Platform Workers
59ec699e9f:2be2a6c1df388255.author: Thil, Laurène
59ec699e9f:2be2a6c1df388255.summary: We study platform workers' preferences for social protection â€” in the form of sick pay and paid annual leave â€” distinguishing between workers who entered platform work out of economic necessity (the "pushed") and those attracted by its flexibility and advantages (the "pulled"). Using a discrete-choice experiment administered to nearly 800 taxi, delivery, and cleaning platform workers in Germany, Italy, and Poland, we find an average willingness to pay at 3.7% of earnings for sick pay coverage and 4.6% for paid annual leave. Preferences, however, differ sharply by motivation: pushed workers are willing to forgo on average 5.3% of earnings for sick pay, and 5.6% for paid annual leave, while pulled workers' valuations are substantially lower (3.1% and 4.2%, respectively). This difference is most pronounced among workers without access to these benefits, suggesting that the absence of protections is particularly consequential for those who entered platform work under greater economic constraint. The findings indicate that the welfare impact of extending social protections to platform workers â€” as proposed by the EU Platform Work Directive â€” might depend on the share of necessity-driven workers in the platform workforce.

59ec699e9f:0d2acd1a2ef7962d.title: Consumption, Savings, and Earnings Responses to Financial Windfalls
59ec699e9f:0d2acd1a2ef7962d.author: Barry Scholnick
59ec699e9f:0d2acd1a2ef7962d.summary: We estimate the causal effects of a financial windfall on consumption, savings, and wage earnings using linked administrative data on a large sample of Canadian lottery winners. Using separate linkages of lottery winners to income tax records and credit bureau data, we estimate how lottery winnings affect consumption measured through credit card spending, savings through financial asset accumulation and debt repayment, and wage earnings from tax records. We then examine how these responses vary across the income distribution. We find that high-income individuals allocated a larger share of lottery winnings to savings and leisure, while low-income individuals spent a larger share on consumption. We illustrate the policy relevance of these heterogeneous responses through three applications: designing fiscal stimulus programs, evaluating a Universal Basic Income (UBI), and determining optimal top tax rates on wage earnings and savings.

59ec699e9f:96eceb11d490f61c.title: Adolescent Skills, Mental Health, and Early-Adult Educational and Labour-Market Outcomes
59ec699e9f:96eceb11d490f61c.author: Lindsey Macmillan
59ec699e9f:96eceb11d490f61c.summary: We examine how different dimensions of adolescent development---cognitive skills, socio-emotional functioning, and mental health---are associated with educational attainment and labour-market engagement at age 23. Using the Millennium Cohort Study, we show that these dimensions are linked to distinct outcomes in early adulthood. Attention difficulties are most strongly associated with lower educational attainment, while emotional, conduct, and peer difficulties are more closely related to weaker labour-market engagement and a higher likelihood of being not in education, employment, or training (NEET). Persistent behavioural and mental-health difficulties are particularly predictive of NEET status. We further document substantial socioeconomic inequalities in educational attainment and labour-market engagement and assess the extent to which adolescent skills and mental health account for these disparities. Our findings show that different dimensions of adolescent development are associated with distinct pathways through education and into the labour market, while also contributing to persistent socioeconomic inequalities in early-adult outcomes.

59ec699e9f:374c56dc655d6f15.title: Instrumental-Variable Estimation of Fixed-Effects Fractional-Outcome Panel Data Models, with an Application to a Major Disability Support Policy Reform
59ec699e9f:374c56dc655d6f15.author: Staub, Kevin
59ec699e9f:374c56dc655d6f15.summary: We develop a fixed-effects estimation framework for fractional-outcome panel models with a logit conditional mean. Pairwise quasi-differencing eliminates individual effects from the moment conditions, yielding a generalized method of moments estimator that is consistent under the stated moment restrictions even when the number of time period is finite and fixed. The framework allows unrestricted dependence between individual effects and covariates, accommodates endogenous regressors through instrumental variables, and extends to multivariate shares that sum to one. Boundary observations require no adjustment, and average semi-elasticities can be estimated without recovering the individual effects. We apply the framework to Australia's National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), using HILDA (Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia) survey data for 2011-2023 and instruments based on the scheme's staggered geographic rollout. We examine how NDIS receipt affects the allocation of time across paid work, housework, disability care, and remaining activities for recipients and other household members. The estimates indicate that recipients reduce work and disability care, while other household members increase disability care.

59ec699e9f:a77799a51ab463ef.title: The Introduction of Universal Child Care in New Mexico: Initial Evidence on Mothers' Labor Supply
59ec699e9f:a77799a51ab463ef.author: Herbst, Chris
59ec699e9f:a77799a51ab463ef.summary: In November 2025, New Mexico became the first U.S. state to implement a universal, no-cost child care subsidy program. This paper estimates difference-in-differences and event-study models to evaluate the impact of universal child care on mothers' short-run labor supply adjustments. Using monthly Current Population Survey data, I find that the reform produced different responses across lower- and higher-skilled mothers. For lower-skilled mothers, the policy increased employment along both the extensive and intensive margins. Conversely, higher-skilled mothers, particularly those who are married, experienced reductions in paid work, with partially offsetting increases in school enrollment. Thus, while universal child care relaxes a binding constraint among disadvantaged families, it acts as an in-kind transfer for their advantaged counterparts.

59ec699e9f:b09a42580ba445b8.title: Capital-Skill Complementarity Beyond Firm Boundaries
59ec699e9f:b09a42580ba445b8.author: Stijn Vanormelingen
59ec699e9f:b09a42580ba445b8.summary: New machinery has long been argued to raise the relative demand for skilled labor, yet firm-level evidence finds no such shift at investing firms. We resolve this puzzle by looking beyond firm boundaries. Linking Belgian data on capital investments, buyer–supplier transactions, and worker skills, we show that the skill bias of new machinery arises entirely at external suppliers. Following machinery investment spikes, purchases from suppliers raise firms’ total demand for high-STEM workers by 45%, three times the rise for other skill groups, while in-house hiring raises it by less than 5%, evenly across skill groups. This external demand comes first from machine integrators and later from complementary services such as software, and is stronger for smaller firms, lumpier investments, and rapidly advancing capital, consistent with fixed and adjustment costs of hiring high-STEM workers in-house. In a general-equilibrium model estimated on our event studies, the rise in machinery per worker from 2003 to 2021 raises relative demand for high-STEM workers by 8.8 log points and their wage premium by 3.1. Measured on payrolls alone, both would fall.

59ec699e9f:d4c2ef32d1497188.title: Labor Supply and Wages over the Life Cycle: Human Capital and Disability Benefits
59ec699e9f:d4c2ef32d1497188.author: Tom Waters
59ec699e9f:d4c2ef32d1497188.summary: Work experience has been found to be a key determinant of work and wages for educated women, but it seems to play a smaller role for the less educated. For them, welfare, tax credits and family composition matter more, and increasingly so does participation in disability programmes. Here we document how labor supply, wages, health, and disability claims have evolved in the UK over the last three decades, and examine how reforms to tax credits, disability benefits and other welfare programs have changed work incentives over this period. We then introduce these features into an empirical dynamic structural model of life-cycle labor supply, human capital and disability benefit application, in which human capital combines health capital, experience accumulated in work, and education. Estimating the model on a panel of working-age women in the UK, we examine the interactions between experience capital and health capital in driving life-cycle earnings across different education groups. Our results highlight the importance of interactions in the disability benefit, welfare and tax-credit systems for understanding the life cycle pattern of hours, employment, earnings, and disability claims, and for evaluating policy counterfactuals.

59ec699e9f:dec6e54e4738e321.title: Physicians' Occupational Licensing and the Quantity-Quality Trade-off
59ec699e9f:dec6e54e4738e321.author: Cristóbal Otero
59ec699e9f:dec6e54e4738e321.summary: Occupational licensing is a widespread quality regulation that potentially increases the quality of labor but reduces its quantity. We provide a theoretical framework to empirically quantify this trade-off in public hospitals, where both clinical quality and physician shortages are critical concerns. Using quasi-exogenous variation driven by a recent and unprecedented migration of physicians to Chile, together with growth in domestic medical schools, we show that more physicians improve patient outcomes, while lower-quality physicians—as measured by licensing exam performance—worsen them. Incorporating these findings into our theoretical framework, we evaluate the implications of locally changing the stringency of the licensing policy.

59ec699e9f:e18367ee31a0e58b.title: How Heavily Are PhD Students Offloading Their Scientific Writing to AI? Evidence from US STEM PhD Dissertations
59ec699e9f:e18367ee31a0e58b.author: Hansen Zhang
59ec699e9f:e18367ee31a0e58b.summary: Large language models are diffusing rapidly into science, raising concerns that delegating research writing to AI may undermine the development of expertise that scientific training is supposed to build. We measure AI-generated writing in the dissertations of a near-census of US STEM PhD graduates from 2019 to 2026 and link graduates to their subsequent employment. AI writing is absent before 2023, present in 29% of dissertations filed in 2026, and rapidly growing. Use is more common among students from non-English-speaking countries and at lower-ranked programs. Among graduates in the same program and cohort, those whose dissertations contain AI writing are less likely to enter academic research careers and more likely to enter non-tenure-track roles or industry, with this pattern strongest among US-origin students. At the same time as AI may increase research productivity, it thus appears to also be displacing a potentially important portion of the work through which scientific expertise is developed.

59ec699e9f:c5b030775cec6849.title: Consumption, Savings, and Earnings Responses to Financial Windfalls
59ec699e9f:c5b030775cec6849.author: Barry Scholnick
59ec699e9f:c5b030775cec6849.summary: We estimate the causal effects of a financial windfall on consumption, savings, and wage earnings using linked administrative data on a large sample of Canadian lottery winners. Using separate linkages of lottery winners to income tax records and credit bureau data, we estimate how lottery winnings affect consumption measured through credit card spending, savings through financial asset accumulation and debt repayment, and wage earnings from tax records. We then examine how these responses vary across the income distribution. We find that high-income individuals allocated a larger share of lottery winnings to savings and leisure, while low-income individuals spent a larger share on consumption. We illustrate the policy relevance of these heterogeneous responses through three applications: designing fiscal stimulus programs, evaluating a Universal Basic Income (UBI), and determining optimal top tax rates on wage earnings and savings.

59ec699e9f:5e726b4adc7b0fe8.title: Workers, Firms, and Spatial Wage Inequality: Evidence from Hungarian Local Labor Markets
59ec699e9f:5e726b4adc7b0fe8.author: László Czaller
59ec699e9f:5e726b4adc7b0fe8.summary: This paper examines how workers and employers jointly shape spatial wage disparities across Hungarian local labor markets. We combine longitudinal linked employer–employee administrative data for 2012–2022 with functional local labor markets constructed from district-to-district commuting flows in the 2022 Hungarian Census. Our preferred delineation contains 29 commuting zones and raises the share of employed residents working within the same unit above 90 percent, compared with 72 percent for districts and 81 percent for counties. We estimate an additive worker–employer fixed-effect wage model and decompose wage variation at the individual level, between commuting zones, and within commuting zones. Differences in commuting-zone mean wages account for 2.8 percent of national log-wage variance and 1.1 percent when the Budapest commuting zone is excluded. Although the between-zone component is modest, its structure is systematic: zones with higher average worker effects also tend to have higher average employer wage premia, so the spatial alignment of worker and employer components accounts for an important part of spatial wage differences. Wage dispersion and the relative importance of worker heterogeneity, employer premia, and worker–employer sorting within local labor markets also vary substantially across the country. The results indicate that spatial wage disparities in Hungary reflect not only differences in workers’ earnings potential and the employer premia attached to their jobs, but also how these components are combined across local labor markets.

59ec699e9f:a447ce1c46303d0e.title: Which Workers Left the Labor Force Post-COVID Recession and Why?: Filing, Tax Credit Take-Up, and Labor Force Engagement by Occupation
59ec699e9f:a447ce1c46303d0e.author: Michael Stevens
59ec699e9f:a447ce1c46303d0e.summary: The COVID-19 pandemic caused a sharp initial rise in unemployment, followed by an unexpectedly tight labor market. Using a panel of tax data containing newly assembled information on worker occupation, we document persistent labor force exit, especially among low-income and low-skill workers. Low-skilled unmarried men are by far the most likely to exit, reinforcing recent concerns regarding the economic and social engagement of this group. Contrary to prevailing theories, we find little evidence that school closures, virus exposure, stimulus payments, or unemployment benefits explain these exits. Nor is the exit explained by additional upgrading of occupations or firm quality. Individuals who leave the labor force do not (on average) make up the missing income; however, self-employment income replaces roughly a quarter of the lost W-2 income. The facts suggest that the willingness to work for low pay decreased and preferences for leisure and job flexibility increased among a large set of workers who have found ways to get by with less income. These results have implications for tax policy, fiscal projections, and labor market dynamics in the post-pandemic economy.

59ec699e9f:0a01c3a05b0d2cb2.title: Gang Crackdowns
59ec699e9f:0a01c3a05b0d2cb2.author: María Micaela Sviatschi
59ec699e9f:0a01c3a05b0d2cb2.summary: What are the consequences of restoring state authority in territories governed by criminal organizations? Combining household surveys and administrative records with detailed maps of former gang-controlled areas, we study how El Salvador’s 2022 State of Exception, which ended two decades of gang territorial control, reshaped Salvadoran society. We find that the removal of gang control integrated previously segmented labor markets, improving mobility, employment outcomes, household income, and financial inclusion. Areas with greater pre-2022 gang exposure also experienced larger increases in business formation and property investment. However, the legacy of criminal governance persists through residence-based discrimination: employers remain less willing to hire otherwise identical applicants from former gang-controlled neighborhoods. Finally, although overall support for the crackdowns remains high, individuals who witnessed police abuse report substantially greater distrust of the police and the national government, suggesting that abuses of state authority may undermine the political sustainability of tough-on-crime policies.

59ec699e9f:876437d22495089d.title: Avoiding Regulation: Evidence from Nursing Homes
59ec699e9f:876437d22495089d.author: Riley League
59ec699e9f:876437d22495089d.summary: We study strategic responses by firms to threshold-based regulations. We document extensive bunching in response to additional staffing requirements for California nursing homes with at least 100 beds. To estimate the regulation’s effect on staffing, we develop a novel treatment effects estimator for threshold-based regulations under precise manipulation, by decomposing firms into response types based on counterfactual and realized staffing and size, separating causal effects from selection. We estimate that higher staffing above the threshold is nearly entirely due to selection, with low-staffing facilities manipulating their size to avoid the regulation. These size distortions limit access, particularly for disadvantaged patients.

59ec699e9f:36f08e7f123cb64b.title: Schooling and Political Activism in the Early Civil Rights Era
59ec699e9f:36f08e7f123cb64b.author: Bhashkar Mazumder
59ec699e9f:36f08e7f123cb64b.summary: Does education lead to political activity? We find that a large, early 20th century school construction program, the Rosenwald schools, led to more NAACP branches in the rural South starting in the early 1940s, i.e. prior to the classic U.S. Civil Rights Movement. Branch growth was stronger where Jim Crow occupational segregation prevented Black men from realizing some of the economic gains of their education. Our findings lend support to theories emphasizing that economic context can act as a critical mediator in determining whether human capital causes political engagement.

59ec699e9f:f6618a5a531cd251.title: Asymmetric Information in Wage Contracts: Experimental Evidence and Welfare Implications
59ec699e9f:f6618a5a531cd251.author: Daniel Herbst
59ec699e9f:f6618a5a531cd251.summary: Compared to self-employment or performance-based pay, fixed wages reduce earnings uncertainty but are prone to market distortions through moral hazard and adverse selection. Using a model of wage contracts under asymmetric information, I show that these distortions map to marginal treatment response functions in a marginal treatment effects (MTE) framework. I apply this framework to a field experiment in which data-entry workers choose between a randomized fixed wage and a piece rate. I find evidence of both moral hazard and adverse selection: Fixed wages reduce worker productivity by an estimated 8.74 percent relative to the mean. Meanwhile, a 10 percent increase in the wage offer attracts a marginal worker whose productivity is higher by 1.90 percent of the mean. Using semi-parametric MTE estimation, I calculate the welfare loss associated with asymmetric information and the marginal values of public funds (MVPFs) for policies aimed at recovering this loss. I find that a tax on piece rates can mitigate adverse selection into fixed wages, generating tax revenue at social costs as low as $0.88 per dollar.

59ec699e9f:d6a700b3dd4eeed9.title: High and Rising Institutional Concentration of Award-Winning Economists
59ec699e9f:d6a700b3dd4eeed9.author: Hanzhang Zhou
59ec699e9f:d6a700b3dd4eeed9.summary: We analyze the academic affiliations of nearly 6, 000 award-winning researchers in 18 major fields in the natural sciences, engineering, and social sciences from the 1820s to the 2020s, focusing on the 1960s onward. The analysis reveals a trend of declining concentration in the institutional affiliations of award-winning researchers, shifting from a few science-strong universities in high-income countries to a more diverse set of institutions across the world. The decline in concentration is observed in all fields except one: economics. The institutional affiliations of prizewinning economists have become more concentrated over time, making economics the most concentrated field. We associate the higher concentration of prizewinning work in economics with the field’s stronger sorting by institutional prestige, its lower reliance on specialized equipment and instruments, and its assessment of findings based on a synthesis of evidence rather than on decisive experiments or proofs. We discuss the benefits and costs of this high and rising institutional concentration of prizewinning economists.

59ec699e9f:9d27b423c2fc7efb.title: The Effects of a Shorter Workweek on Employment, Output, and Productivity
59ec699e9f:9d27b423c2fc7efb.author: Nina Roussille
59ec699e9f:9d27b423c2fc7efb.summary: Do shorter workweeks generate work-sharing and productivity gains, as intended by policymakers? We study France’s pay-preserving reduction in the workweek from 39 to 35 hours, bundled with employer payroll tax cuts. We first exploit the staggered implementation by firm size to identify the impact of the reform package. We then use differential exposure to the hours cut and tax cut to separate their effects. We combine matched employer-employee, balance-sheet, and survey data to study worker, firm, and local labor market effects. The reform package left employment unchanged. This zero masks large offsetting effects: absent the tax cuts, the shorter workweek would have reduced employment by 3.8%. The effects are skill-biased, raising employment among managers and professionals while reducing it among other employees. Finally, shorter hours raised total factor productivity by 2%, limiting the output decline to 1% despite a 6% fall in total hours. Surveys point to work intensification and organizational changes as potential drivers of productivity gains.

59ec699e9f:3a087ac3579aa2d5.title: Capital-Skill Complementarity Beyond Firm Boundaries
59ec699e9f:3a087ac3579aa2d5.author: Stijn Vanormelingen
59ec699e9f:3a087ac3579aa2d5.summary: New machinery has long been argued to raise the relative demand for skilled labor, yet firm-level evidence finds no such shift at investing firms. We resolve this puzzle by looking beyond firm boundaries. Linking Belgian data on capital investments, buyerâ€“supplier transactions, and worker skills, we show that the skill bias of new machinery arises entirely at external suppliers. Following machinery investment spikes, purchases from suppliers raise firmsâ€™ total demand for high-STEM workers by 45%, three times the rise for other skill groups, while in-house hiring raises it by less than 5%, evenly across skill groups. This external demand comes first from machine integrators and later from complementary services such as software, and is stronger for smaller firms, lumpier investments, and rapidly advancing capital, consistent with fixed and adjustment costs of hiring high-STEM workers in-house. In a general-equilibrium model estimated on our event studies, the rise in machinery per worker from 2003 to 2021 raises relative demand for high-STEM workers by 8.8 log points and their wage premium by 3.1. Measured on payrolls alone, both would fall.

59ec699e9f:c7db468f7ea4510e.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
59ec699e9f:c7db468f7ea4510e.author: Christopher T. Stanton
59ec699e9f:c7db468f7ea4510e.summary: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

59ec699e9f:f64ae324df50676f.title: When Should Robots Be Subsidized?
59ec699e9f:f64ae324df50676f.author: Klaus Prettner
59ec699e9f:f64ae324df50676f.summary: This paper studies optimal robot taxation in a static model with routine and non-routine workers. Robots substitute for routine workers and complement non-routine workers. In addition, robots are produced in a monopolistic sector that charges a markup over marginal cost. In the absence of monopoly power, the optimal robot tax rate is zero. When robot producers have monopoly power, the optimal policy corrects the markup distortion by aligning the effective robot price with marginal cost, conditional on the labor supply induced by the income tax system. The wage premium rises with the expansion of the tasks that robots can perform and declines with higher robot production costs. The results clarify the conditions under which robot taxation serves as a corrective instrument.

59ec699e9f:4926134e7038ecd7.title: Do weekend workers like their jobs?
59ec699e9f:4926134e7038ecd7.author: Mark Wooden
59ec699e9f:4926134e7038ecd7.summary: Weekend work is a pervasive feature of labor markets that comes with both potential benefits (e.g., higher pay, flexible schedules) and drawbacks (e.g., less social time). Nevertheless, robust evidence on weekend workers’ job satisfaction is lacking. Longitudinal data from 21 waves of the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey (n=211, 077; i=26, 273) are used to estimate the association between weekend work and several dimensions of job satisfaction. Estimates from fixed effects models reveal that weekend work is associated with significantly lower levels of satisfaction with working hours and flexibility, but this does not translate into lower levels of overall job satisfaction. Additional analyses were conducted to test whether results varied with employment status, occupation and parental status. In general, the main finding applied to all groups examined. There were, however, marked differences across sub-groups in satisfaction with other job domains. Overall, the results suggest that, for most workers, the benefits of working weekends offset its disadvantages.

59ec699e9f:63bb9b30e3b5783c.title: State Child Tax Credits and Parental Labor Supply: Evidence from Staggered Adoption
59ec699e9f:63bb9b30e3b5783c.author: Parolin, Zachary
59ec699e9f:63bb9b30e3b5783c.summary: States increasingly supplement the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC) with credits that vary in generosity, refundability, and earnings requirements. We examine changes in parental employment, labor force participation, and work hours following state CTC adoption using the Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS-ASEC), 2004–2026. Our preferred stacked difference-in-differences design includes 12 adopting states with complete event-time support and compares them with never-treated states and states that adopted after our evaluation window. Averaging over the first three post-adoption survey years, the estimated effect is 0.05 percentage points (SE 1.03) for employment and −0.46 points (0.82) for labor force participation; estimates for work hours are also close to zero. Across secondary specifications and CPS Basic Monthly analyses, extensive-margin estimates were similarly small. Larger simulated benefits are associated with fewer hours among employed parents, but the relationship is also evident before adoption and may partly reflect how benefits depend on earnings. Overall, the estimates provide little indication that state CTC adoption has substantially reduced parental employment, although meaningful effects in either direction cannot be ruled out under moderate departures from parallel trends.

59ec699e9f:aaca82fd71727bfa.title: Staying Connected: Experimental Effects of Coach-Delivered Text Messages in an Adult High School
59ec699e9f:aaca82fd71727bfa.author: Patrick S. Turner
59ec699e9f:aaca82fd71727bfa.summary: More than 23 million adults in the United States lack a high school diploma, and most who return to school drop out before graduating. We evaluate a randomized intervention of adult high school students in which coaches delivered text messages that encouraged persistence. We find that assignment to treatment increased graduation by 4.9 percentage points, and the effect of message receipt among compliers is 9.3 percentage points, a 41 percent increase relative to the control mean. The intervention operated on the intensive margin by increasing the number of courses completed, but did not affect student enrollment. The effects of the intervention are concentrated among students assigned to experienced coaches, who customized their messages more extensively. We contextualize the economic impact of the low-cost intervention by comparing labor market earnings of graduates to non-graduates, which implies an earnings benefit of $149 per treated student over four years.

59ec699e9f:66a32ceabaadbcc6.title: Beyond Mincer: Revisiting the Returns to Education in Thailand
59ec699e9f:66a32ceabaadbcc6.author: Lusi Liao
59ec699e9f:66a32ceabaadbcc6.summary: This paper investigates the private and social return to higher education in Thailand. First, we analyze the individual return to higher education by using Socio-Economic Survey (SES) panel data and employing three treatment effects including propensity score matching (PSM), endogenous switching (ES) regression and endogenous binary treatment using probit two stage least square (Probit-2SLS) model. Then, we estimate the social return to higher education using Labor Force Survey (LFS). We identify the social return by estimating the effect of share of higher educated workers living in each province on individual wage and provincial wage gap using instrumental variable (IV) and pseudo panel approach at provincial level accounting for cohort effects. The results show that obtaining higher education increases wage by around 0.98 to 1.78 log points, and the increase in the provincial share of higher education raises individualâ€™s wage and reduce the wage inequality among different provinces. The findings suggest that investment in higher education will improve the income distribution as it contributes more to workers with less education and in lower wage occupations.

59ec699e9f:15149e4e209225d2.title: Mind the M’s: A review of the implications of menstruation, maternity, and menopause for work performance and attendance
59ec699e9f:15149e4e209225d2.author: Elsy Verhofstadt
59ec699e9f:15149e4e209225d2.summary: Menstruation, maternity, and menopause, collectively referred to as the three M’s, affect many employees as a growing number of women participate in the labour force. However, their implications for these women’s working lives have received limited and fragmented attention in the literature. This study therefore provides the first systematic literature review integrating evidence on the impact of the three M’s on work performance and attendance. Following the SPIDER framework and PRISMA guidelines, this study systematically reviews 57 articles. Across all three M’s, findings consistently show reduced work performance, increased presenteeism, and higher absenteeism, explained by interacting biological, psychological, and contextual factors. This study also identifies important limitations in the existing literature, including the dominance of crosssectional designs, the reliance on subjective measures, and the lack of attention to workplace solutions that address the three M’s collectively.

59ec699e9f:6424e43eed858923.title: AI Innovation and Labor Market Polarization: Evidence from European Regions
59ec699e9f:6424e43eed858923.author: Francesco Venturini
59ec699e9f:6424e43eed858923.summary: We study whether AI innovation changes labor-market polarization by weakening the relative position of high-skilled workers. We develop a CES production framework showing how AI affects the wage-cost ratio between high- and low skilled workers through wage and employment margins. We test the model's predictions using European regional labor-market data and find that AI reduces the relative wage-cost ratio by nearly 7 percent on average, with effects broadly split between wage and employment adjustments. These results are primarily driven by regions in countries highly specialized in AI technologies. Overall, our evidence suggests that AI may counteract the polarization effects associated with over two centuries of technological change.

59ec699e9f:8eefd12f4bee26d3.title: Burning the Bridge. Imported Intelligence, Reversibility Loss, and External Liquidity
59ec699e9f:8eefd12f4bee26d3.author: Levy Yeyati, Eduardo
59ec699e9f:8eefd12f4bee26d3.summary: Foreign-provided agentification can be understood as black-box offshoring: a domestic task is delegated to a technological system supplied from abroad rather than to a foreign workforce. As adoption spreads, firms may stop performing the task locally and gradually thin the shared pool of workers, training routes, routines, and complementary suppliers needed to bring it back. No individual buyer owns that pool or has much reason to preserve it for the sector. Under concentrated foreign provision, the weaker domestic fallback can raise future imported-agent payments. This is a dynamic terms-of-trade externality whose source is endogenous: today’s imports make tomorrow’s outside option worse. The broader macroeconomic implication is that agentification can raise productivity while tightening the external constraint. It replaces part of a domestic production bill with recurring foreign-currency payments, and capability erosion can make that bill more persistent or more expensive over time. This liquidity channel is not unique to AI, and it can reverse sign when agentification generates enough tradable earnings. Ex ante competition can redistribute lifecycle rents through introductory concessions, but early inflows and later foreign-currency outflows need not be socially equivalent when external liquidity is valued differently across states or dates. The policy implication is to preserve valuable reversibility, contestability, contractual protection, and external-liquidity buffers rather than to impose a general tax on AI.

59ec699e9f:23eaf324bb68415f.title: Collective bargaining in Italy over the past 25 years: evidence from Banca d'Italia's database on the most representative CBAs
59ec699e9f:23eaf324bb68415f.author: Gaetano Basso
59ec699e9f:23eaf324bb68415f.summary: This paper describes the institutional framework for national collective bargaining and examines the trends in negotiated wages between 2000 and 2025, using Banca d'Italia's database on the 50 most representative collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) in the non-farm private sector. The bargaining framework allows for substantial flexibility in sector-level negotiations, both in the timing of renewals and in determining wage increases and any adjustments for deviations between expected and actual inflation. Over the past 25 years, negotiated wages increased by 61.2 per cent overall in nominal terms, on average across sectors, but declined by 1.3 per cent in real terms, mainly owing to the high inflation recorded in 2021-23. The loss in the purchasing power of negotiated wages was more pronounced in private services, where delays in CBA renewals were longer. The analysis of the relationship between negotiated and actual wages suggests that second-level bargaining partly compensated workers during these delays.

59ec699e9f:98648981e98fb677.title: Mind the Gap: Gender Inequality in Europeâ€™s Twin Transition
59ec699e9f:98648981e98fb677.author: Tomasi, Chiara
59ec699e9f:98648981e98fb677.summary: This paper examines gender disparities in the European labour market during the twin digital and green transitions. Using the European Skills and Jobs Survey matched with the ESCO occupational classification, it identifies digital and green occupations based on their skill content and analyses both access to these jobs and wage outcomes within them. Women are significantly less likely to work in digital and green occupations and, conditional on employment, face larger wage gaps than comparable men. They are also less likely to hold managerial positions and benefit less from STEM educational backgrounds, despite the positive returns associated with these qualifications. Finally, stronger regional STEM-oriented university environments are associated with smaller gender gaps in access to digital occupations and wages, suggesting that the twin transition may reinforce existing gender inequalities unless accompanied by targeted policies.

59ec699e9f:04e1b2d8369293ec.title: Immigrant Earnings and Labour-Market Positioning in a Transforming Digital Labour Market: Evidence from Canada, 1971â€“2021
59ec699e9f:04e1b2d8369293ec.author: Sweetman, Arthur
59ec699e9f:04e1b2d8369293ec.summary: Using Canadian Census microdata, 1971â€“2021, we compare immigrant and native-born earnings across ten arrival cohorts by gender and age at arrival. For two recent cohorts, an earnings-based positioning measure combines industry mean annual earnings with full-time or part-time status; multinomial-logit average marginal effects are estimated. The study also maps 2021 industry employment shares to external digital-intensity and telework-feasibility classifications. We find entry earnings gaps and incomplete cohort convergence persist, especially among women and recent cohorts. Across the two positioning cohorts, immigrants are less likely than comparable native-born workers to hold full-time jobs in higher-earnings industries; gaps vary by source region and do not uniformly narrow. Education is associated with better positioning but does not eliminate gaps. Immigrant employment is more concentrated in many digitally intensive categories but less concentrated in several higher-earnings, high-telework-feasibility industries; digital intensity is not systematically related to immigrant employment shares.

59ec699e9f:d1594b1c11985fe9.title: Occupational Upgrading and Within-Occupation Wage Gaps: Immigrant Earnings Integration in Canada, 2006â€“2021
59ec699e9f:d1594b1c11985fe9.author: Sweetman, Arthur
59ec699e9f:d1594b1c11985fe9.summary: This paper studies immigrant earnings integration in Canada using Labour Force Survey data from 2006 to 2021 and an empirical framework that separately models actual wages, counterfactual wages predicted from age- and gender-specific native wage profiles within detailed occupations, and the within-occupation wage gap between actual and predicted wages. This separation allows us to distinguish wage growth driven by occupational upgrading from within-occupation wage convergence. We find that years since migration are associated with substantial wage growth, primarily through movement into higher-paying occupations rather than rapid wage catch-up within occupations. While within-occupation wage gaps do narrow modestly over time, convergence along this margin remains slow and incomplete. These patterns are robust across gender and immigrantsâ€™ region of origin. The results indicate that persistent wage gaps are primarily associated with limited access to high-paying occupations rather than differential pay within jobs alone. This highlights occupational placement and the transferability of human capital as central margins along which immigrant earnings integration unfolds in Canada.

59ec699e9f:f7fac338a1386f4a.title: Employer Concentration and Minimum-Wage Employment Effects: Evidence from China's Transition
59ec699e9f:f7fac338a1386f4a.author: Duan, Wenjing
59ec699e9f:f7fac338a1386f4a.summary: How do local labour markets shape the employment effects of minimum wages? We evaluate this question using comprehensive manufacturing firm data and over 28, 000 hand-collected county-level minimum wages during China's market transition (1998-2007). We find that, consistently with monopsony models, the employment response to higher minimum-wage exposure becomes less negative as local employer concentration increases, with positive point estimates arising in highly concentrated markets in some specifications, particularly among domestic private firms. Higher minimum-wage exposure may also be associated with lower reported training expenditure and greater firm exit. Our findings indicate that the employment effects of minimum wages can depend critically on local market structures, highlighting the importance of geographical and institutional heterogeneity when assessing labour regulation in transitioning economies.

59ec699e9f:2eec4978910d3596.title: Training Your Replacement: Worker Incentives and the Pace of Automation
59ec699e9f:2eec4978910d3596.author: Peter Landry
59ec699e9f:2eec4978910d3596.summary: Firms ask workers to train AI systems that will replace them. We model this with a worker who can shirk, cooperate with training, or obstruct training while maintaining productivity. Because training ends the job but only cooperation completes training, dismissal becomes a weaker penalty for shirking. The firm must raise the worker’s rent, and the worker gains from their replacement. AI can create jobs paying more than they produce and eliminate jobs it never automates. Firms paying only wages may slow training. A credible completion bonus equal to the worker’s rent without AI removes both the gain and the slowdown.
