4a32a2255e:bb760a062e7cf749.title: The Costs of Access: Freeway Disamenities Across U.S. Cities
4a32a2255e:bb760a062e7cf749.author: Jeffrey Lin
4a32a2255e:bb760a062e7cf749.summary: We construct city-level measures of freeway disamenities and examine their association with metropolitan growth. We combine neighborhood-level estimates from Brinkman and Lin (2024) with calibrated spatial models for U.S. metropolitan areas. Each city measure is based on a counterfactual that removes estimated disamenities while holding modeled travel times fixed. Cities with larger estimated disamenities grew more slowly, conditioned on total freeway mileage and initial population. Total freeway mileage is positively associated with growth in the same specification. Estimated disamenities are larger in cities with greater 1950 populations, more centralized freeway networks, and coastal geography. These patterns are consistent with local quality-of-life costs attenuating regional access related growth benefits.

4a32a2255e:0f2aa77e10d8dd28.title: Agglomeration, the Price-Index Effect, and Migration in Post-NAFTA Mexico
4a32a2255e:0f2aa77e10d8dd28.author: Keisuke Kondo
4a32a2255e:0f2aa77e10d8dd28.summary: This study examines how multiple agglomeration and dispersion forces shaped Mexico’s regional economic geography during the early post-NAFTA period. When economic activity becomes geographically concentrated, consumers gain better access to differentiated varieties and face lower effective transport costs, reducing the local consumption price index and making a region more attractive as a migration destination. Building on this price-index mechanism from New Economic Geography, we focus on four spatial forces: proximity to the U.S. market, the manufacturing price-index effect, the service price-index effect, and density-related urban costs. Using bilateral interstate migration between 1995 and 2000, we proceed in two stages. First, we estimate the structural parameters of the model and recover state-level price indices for manufactured goods and services. Second, we examine how destination–origin differences in nominal wages, price indices, and urban costs are associated with migration across sectors, while controlling for the additional locational advantage of U.S. border states. The manufacturing price index is strongly and negatively associated with migration of manufacturing workers, whereas its cross-sector effects are more limited. By contrast, the service price index is negatively and significantly associated with migration across all sectors, indicating a broad domestic agglomeration force. Employment density is generally negatively associated with migration, consistent with urban costs acting as a centrifugal force, while real-wage differentials are positively associated with migration across most industries. Taken together, the findings suggest that post-NAFTA Mexico was shaped by the interaction of border-oriented manufacturing agglomeration, domestic service-sector agglomeration, and urban-cost-driven dispersion.

4a32a2255e:cc6bd3f1bb61011e.title: University as catalyst of public R&D expenditures? An empirical assessment on EU NUTS 3 regions
4a32a2255e:cc6bd3f1bb61011e.author: Saverio Barabuffi
4a32a2255e:cc6bd3f1bb61011e.summary: This study examines whether universities shape the regional innovation effects of public R&D expenditure and whether this role varies across regional development trajectories. We analyse a panel of 1166 EU NUTS 3 regions over the period 2007-2020, combining data on European public R&D funding, patenting performance, university presence and regional development traps. Toa ddress the endogeneity of public R&D expenditure, we employ a control function aproach. The results show that public r&D expendirue positively affects patenting performance in both university and non-university, but the difference between them is not statistically significant. University presence therefore does not sistematically amplify the returns to public R&D. However, its moderating role becomes more pronounced in regions exposed to development trap risk and in regions experiencing persistent stagnation, while evidence is weaker for trap intensity. These fundings suggest that universities act as contingent rather than unviersal catalyst of public R&D. Their contribution appears particularly relevant in vulnerable and persistently stagnant regional trajectories, but less able to offset sever structural constraints. The study contributes to debates on the geography of public R&D and regional development traps by showing that the effectiveness of research funding depends not only on institutional presence, bu also on the development rajectory in which that institutional capacity is embedded.

4a32a2255e:51084300a740f2be.title: Living in a Ghost Town: The Geography of Depopulation and Aging
4a32a2255e:51084300a740f2be.author: Yuta Suzuki
4a32a2255e:51084300a740f2be.summary: How do depopulation and population aging evolve differently across regions within a country, and what are their implications for aggregate economic activity and regional inequality? Using spatially disaggregated data from Japan over the past several decades, we show that rural areas have experienced significantly faster depopulation and aging than urban areas, driven by low fertility and sustained out-migration of young cohorts. Regions undergoing these trends face declining local amenities and rising per-capita public service costs. To study the future evolution and economic consequences of these dynamics, we develop and calibrate a dynamic life-cycle spatial general equilibrium model. The model predicts widening geographic disparities in depopulation, aging, and economic activity in the coming centuries. While subsidies to declining regions can lower regional inequality, they come at the cost of lower aggregate efficiency and higher public service expenditures.

4a32a2255e:9c162c7ce408fe2b.title: Climate Cooperation and Spatial Industrial Relocation: Stability, Emissions, and Regional Policy Incentives
4a32a2255e:9c162c7ce408fe2b.author: Angela Martiradonna
4a32a2255e:9c162c7ce408fe2b.summary: Climate policy changes production costs and can reshape the geography of production. We study this spatial channel in a focused model where mobile industrial activity responds to local attractiveness, agglomeration strengthens attractiveness, and carbon policy lowers the profitability of emissions-intensive locations. The model yields an explicit carbon-policy threshold separating spatial instability from stability. When emissions intensity rises with local industrial density, spatial concentration raises aggregate emissions even with unchanged total industrial activity. Embedding these dynamics in a two-jurisdiction policy game creates a wedge between regional and collective incentives: each government values the industrial activity located within its own territory, while aggregate welfare internalizes the effect of policy on economy-wide concentration. With transferable utility, cooperation can select a policy on the stable side of the threshold while the non-cooperative policy lies on the unstable side. A numerical exercise illustrates this regime change. European regional evidence, based on industrial emissions and gross value added at NUTS2 level, documents a positive emissions-activity association and identifies the empirical quantities needed to measure relocation and concentration effects. The analysis links climate cooperation to the spatial organization of production and establishes a benchmark for policy-induced industrial relocation.

4a32a2255e:9722bf720ad9d723.title: Workers, Firms, and Spatial Wage Inequality: Evidence from Hungarian Local Labor Markets
4a32a2255e:9722bf720ad9d723.author: László Czaller
4a32a2255e:9722bf720ad9d723.summary: This paper examines how workers and employers jointly shape spatial wage disparities across Hungarian local labor markets. We combine longitudinal linked employer–employee administrative data for 2012–2022 with functional local labor markets constructed from district-to-district commuting flows in the 2022 Hungarian Census. Our preferred delineation contains 29 commuting zones and raises the share of employed residents working within the same unit above 90 percent, compared with 72 percent for districts and 81 percent for counties. We estimate an additive worker–employer fixed-effect wage model and decompose wage variation at the individual level, between commuting zones, and within commuting zones. Differences in commuting-zone mean wages account for 2.8 percent of national log-wage variance and 1.1 percent when the Budapest commuting zone is excluded. Although the between-zone component is modest, its structure is systematic: zones with higher average worker effects also tend to have higher average employer wage premia, so the spatial alignment of worker and employer components accounts for an important part of spatial wage differences. Wage dispersion and the relative importance of worker heterogeneity, employer premia, and worker–employer sorting within local labor markets also vary substantially across the country. The results indicate that spatial wage disparities in Hungary reflect not only differences in workers’ earnings potential and the employer premia attached to their jobs, but also how these components are combined across local labor markets.

33e1d7779a:fc7646e65e0474d8.title: 3,000 flights cancelled as FAA ground stop chaos stretches into 2nd day
33e1d7779a:fc7646e65e0474d8.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:fc7646e65e0474d8.summary: The chaos from the FAA's nationwide ground stop lingered into early Saturday morning, with thousands of flights cancelled as airlines played catch-up. Why it matters: Millions of travelers will find themselves inconvenienced over what the government says was simply old technology that couldn't keep up with modern upgrades. Driving the news: As of 5:15 a.m. ET Saturday, nearly 3,300 flights into, out of, or within the United States were already cancelled for the day, per FlightAware . Nearly 1,000 flights already had delays. Between the lines: The most heavily impacted airports were Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson, New York's JFK and Boston Logan. Among the major airlines, FlightAware's data showed Delta more affected than United or American. Zoom in : The ground stop wreaked havoc on college football in particular, with many schools unable to travel to their game locations. ESPN reported a number of high-profile match-ups were postponed to either late Saturday or Sunday as a result. What to watch: Whether Congress responds to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's request for $50 billion in emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system. This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

33e1d7779a:729635c933e3da18.title: FAA ends hours-long nationwide ground stop
33e1d7779a:729635c933e3da18.author: Alex Fitzpatrick
33e1d7779a:729635c933e3da18.summary: The FAA lifted its nationwide ground stop Friday night after hours of chaos and thousands of delays and cancellations. Why it matters: The effects of the rare and extreme move will likely ripple through the weekend, with travelers stranded and airlines' planes and crews out of position. Driving the news: In a Friday evening press conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop was issued after outdated air traffic control communications equipment suffered from "overloaded data, and they went down." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin added that officials are looking into incompatibilities between that older equipment and newer technology currently being installed. Mullin added that there's no evidence that the problems were tied to a cyberattack. Yes, but: Duffy and Mullin didn't specify the exact initial cause of the problems. "We're still working on the details of what went wrong today," Duffy said. Duffy spent much of the press conference pushing Congress for more funding for air traffic control upgrades. "I can't build things if I don't have money," he told reporters at the White House briefing room. He later added that similar problems could occur again without more funding. Catch up quick: The FAA initially issued the stop due to "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety." "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the agency said in an earlier statement after the ground stop was issued. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates." Air Route Traffic Control Centers, often simply called "centers," mostly handle high-altitude en route airspace between airports. Between the lines: The FAA has been rolling out a new AI tool designed to help manage airspace congestion, but it's unclear if that system has any connection to Friday's communication issues. The developer of that tool denied any…

33e1d7779a:5f4639ad9c8ec029.title: Mississippi River cruise crash has no fatalities, critical injuries
33e1d7779a:5f4639ad9c8ec029.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:5f4639ad9c8ec029.summary: Thirty-two people are in local hospitals and all passengers and crew are accounted for after an Atlantic Asphalt tanker collided with a Mississippi River cruise ship near the Port of New Orleans , officials said Friday. The big picture: With approximately 180 people on the ship, the rescue of all aboard is "truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said at a press conference. Catch up quick: The American Heritage, a vessel operated by American Cruise Lines, had docked for passengers to disembark at the port Friday afternoon about two hours before it was hit, according to a press release from the Port of New Orleans. A city spokesman confirmed to Axios that the riverboat had rolled onto its side in the water, which social media videos appear to corroborate. Zoom out: The Atlantic Asphalt tanker is registered in the Marshall Islands, and had arrived at the Port of New Orleans on Nov. 11. Per data from myshiptracking.com, the tanker began its current journey in Paulsboro, New Jersey, in late October. Zoom in: The tanker was immobilized on the river Friday at about 2pm CT, with two tugs positioned on either side. Another dozen vessels were in the water nearby as a helicopter roamed overhead and sirens rang out over the water. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry posted on X that he was aware of the incident and en route to New Orleans. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:26fb447e524f9a80.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
33e1d7779a:26fb447e524f9a80.author: Adriel Bettelheim
33e1d7779a:26fb447e524f9a80.summary: The Trump administration announced a six-month delay Friday in enforcing the Medicaid work requirements that were scheduled to take effect in January. Why it matters: The announcement pauses a set of rules that state officials have warned they're not ready to handle — and that could cause millions of people to lose their health coverage. Driving the news: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said there will be an "optional hold harmless period" through June 30 that will give states "a transition period to further modernize systems, improve processes, and streamline the applicant and beneficiary experience. Hospitals have been so worried about the impact of the work requirements that they've created their own outreach campaign to prepare people on Medicaid, per the New York Times . The concern is not that people will be kicked out of the program for not working, but that they'll be kicked out because they don't understand the reporting rules and won't be able to prove they've met the requirements. This is breaking news. Check back for updates.

33e1d7779a:9321f6ec53e0ba4a.title: The senators who could join Van Hollen's insurgency against Schumer
33e1d7779a:9321f6ec53e0ba4a.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:9321f6ec53e0ba4a.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory , with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave. Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership." "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people." The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen. "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer. Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington. By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted. Senators backing Van Hollen State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon. Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership. Who wants new leadership? Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate. Before Van Hollen…

33e1d7779a:60c9f17eae11bd2c.title: Senate Dems break 32-year drought on leadership challenges
33e1d7779a:60c9f17eae11bd2c.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:60c9f17eae11bd2c.summary: As House Democrats barrel toward a speakership coronation , Senate Dems are getting their first contested race for leader in over 30 years. Why it matters: Democrats have spent years tearing themselves apart over the party's direction — without forcing their leaders to win a head-to-head vote. Senate Democrats will get that fight this year for the first time since Tom Daschle vs. Chris Dodd in 1994 — courtesy of Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) challenging Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.). But no one's challenging Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) for speaker. The last contested Democratic House leader race was in 2016, when Tim Ryan failed to beat Nancy Pelosi for minority leader. Between the lines: House Democrats are being bombarded with calls and emails urging them to oppose Jeffries, but the two most frequently floated alternatives — Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) — don't appear to want the job. Raskin told Axios that chairing the Judiciary Committee is his "dream job" and that he's "absolutely ... not a candidate for speaker in any way." "I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," Raskin added. Pressley has privately told colleagues she isn't interested, multiple House Democrats told Axios. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." The big picture: Since the last contested Democratic leadership election, Republicans have endured the rise of MAGA, former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell's fall from power and a revolving door of House GOP leaders. In 2018, Kevin McCarthy drubbed Jim Jordan 159–43 to become House minority leader. In 2022, McConnell had to beat Rick Scott after the Florida Republican challenged him for Senate GOP leader. In 2023, McCarthy…

33e1d7779a:3f2f79064cdd8c37.title: How the Microsoft outage impacted courts and governments
33e1d7779a:3f2f79064cdd8c37.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:3f2f79064cdd8c37.summary: Courts and governments worldwide felt the impact of this week's Microsoft outage, which sidelined work and stymied communication. Why it matters: When Microsoft's popular workplace software went offline Thursday, it meant an extended lunch break for some offices — but for the courts and governments, it raised questions about the vulnerabilities of the technology underpinning justice and governance. Case in point: The state of Maine's judicial branch warned in a Thursday alert that requests for protection orders filed by email — urgent requests to keep parties safe from harm — may not have been received. Multiple court documents reviewed by Axios show lawyers requesting deadline extensions or alerting judges to the outage impacting their work. That includes DOJ lawyers: Government attorneys asked for an extension in the case brought by Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) over President Trump 's Kennedy Center takeover , saying the outage prevented them from "completing the necessary coordination." In a separate filing, Beatty's team acknowledged they were impacted as well. Zoom out: The impacts were also felt in courtrooms and offices internationally. The AP reported that a U.K. criminal trial was delayed as a result, with a Manchester judge saying, per BBC's reporting , "We are learning of the dangers of relying on computers and data systems." U.K.-based police forces also urged the public Friday to call first responders for aid, rather than using online forms. The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it, too, was affected by the outage. What they're saying: "We obviously need backup methods to keep the wheels of justice turning," says Gissou Nia, the founder and director of the Atlantic Council's Strategic Litigation Project. She pointed to a prior incident that previewed international reliance on U.S. tech: Though not exposed by an outage, the Trump administration's sanctions on the International Criminal Court prompted the Netherlands-based court to move off of…

33e1d7779a:866319e998c2cd4d.title: Nobody wants to run against Hakeem Jeffries for speaker
33e1d7779a:866319e998c2cd4d.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:866319e998c2cd4d.summary: The movement to prevent House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) from becoming speaker is struggling to get off the ground due to a fatal flaw: Nobody else wants the job. Why it matters: Despite the phone calls and online petitions, the demands from progressive holdouts, Jeffries' ascent has become a self-fulfilling prophecy. The House Democrats most often floated as potential challengers don't appear to be interested: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) told Axios on Thursday his "dream job" is to chair the House Judiciary Committee. "I am not a candidate for speaker in any way. ... I am supporting Hakeem and voting for Hakeem," said Raskin. Rep. Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) has privately told colleagues she doesn't want the role despite an online movement seeking to draft her, according to multiple House Democrats who have spoken directly with her. "Congresswoman Pressley is in active conversations with Leader Jeffries about how to leverage this majority, meet the moment, and deliver for the people," spokesperson Ricardo Sanchez said in a statement to Axios. "She is aware of and appreciates the groundswell of support from people in her district and across the country lifting up her leadership." "He's the only one running," Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.) told Axios on Thursday when asked if she plans to vote for Jeffries as speaker. Said Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.): "I am really encouraging our leadership to make it easy for me to vote for the one person that's running. But as of right now, there's ... no one else that has put their name forward." "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only person running," said Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). Jeffries said in a NY1 interview : "Someone could always emerge in the next week or so, but right now there are no declared challengers, no indication that anyone may put themselves forward." The intrigue: For once it's the Senate, not the House, providing all the drama on Capitol Hill. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.)…

33e1d7779a:5c55308a1c024c9d.title: The global economy's Achilles' heels
33e1d7779a:5c55308a1c024c9d.author: Neil Irwin
33e1d7779a:5c55308a1c024c9d.summary: A defining story of this decade has been a series of global economic shocks: pandemic, war and geopolitical shifts. New research quantifies a rising set of vulnerabilities for the global trade system . The big picture: Many crucial global goods are built on supply chains that have one or more Achilles' heels, a report from the consulting firm McKinsey finds — a critical input, concentrated suppliers and geopolitical strain. That manifests partly in physical chokepoints. The Strait of Hormuz is the one most in the news, but the McKinsey researchers identify a couple dozen others globally, through which 80% of maritime trade passes (although with varying levels of difficulty for shippers to route around). In effect, as the global economy has become more integrated over the last few decades, these vulnerabilities have become more pronounced — which in turn helps explain why the 2020s have brought an ongoing series of disruptive supply shocks. By the numbers: They find that the share of global imports that face at least two of three major vulnerabilities has risen to 23% in 2024 from 15% in 2000. The list of items with overlapping vulnerabilities includes basic materials like iron ore and more advanced items like lithium-ion batteries, smartphones and memory chips. What they're saying: "It's not necessarily that trade has gotten less reliable," Tiago Devesa, a co-author of the report, tells Axios. "I think it's more that we have the realization that we actually want to understand what are the potential points of failure, so we can anticipate them." "I think you could make a case that throughout all of these shocks, trade has continued to increase, and trade was actually a very important balancing mechanism," he adds. "It's been increasing precisely in part because we've integrated the fabric of the global economy much more, and in particular, we've led a specialization effort that led to more concentration around the world," says Devesa, a senior fellow at the…

33e1d7779a:579523ff4775b3ae.title: Inside the aftermath of the Logan Circle shooting
33e1d7779a:579523ff4775b3ae.author: Mimi Montgomery
33e1d7779a:579523ff4775b3ae.summary: It took just minutes for a gunman to shoot six people and upend one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Thursday morning's violence left one person dead in a Logan Circle gym and five others injured nearby. The gunman later shot himself, police said. The massive police response shut down streets, sent nearly a dozen schools into lockdown and forced residents to shelter in place. By evening, the streets around VIDA Fitness, where the shooting began, were quiet. Several nearby businesses remained closed, with police tape blocking off storefronts and officers standing watch. Councilmember Brooke Pinto held a vigil . People left flowers and notes outside of the VIDA . "Logan Circle is still a place for love," read one. "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many," read another. But life also carried on: A delivery van unloaded Christmas trees at Whole Foods, and 14th Street bars put out signs advertising happy hour. Flowers and handwritten notes line the outside of VIDA Fitness. Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios One note reads: "VIDA, you are and will continue to be a safe haven for many." Photo: Mimi Montgomery/Axios What we know: At an afternoon press conference, interim MPD chief Jeffery W. Carroll identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who lived in the apartment building connected to VIDA Fitness. The man killed was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building's manager and a Northwest D.C. resident, Carroll said. Police believe the shooting was linked to an ongoing dispute between Lambert and his condominium association over maintenance issues, including mold. The timeline: Police responded to a shooting inside VIDA Fitness, at 15th and P streets NW, just before 8am. Additional reports of shootings nearby followed. Carroll said the shootings themselves likely unfolded in less than five minutes, though investigators are still reconstructing the timeline. Police announced a sixth shooting victim — a woman with nonfatal injuries…

33e1d7779a:b5bdf3ffe612eb78.title: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
33e1d7779a:b5bdf3ffe612eb78.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:b5bdf3ffe612eb78.summary: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad is in Washington Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran , according to three sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters : The visit by Roman Gofman, one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran. Driving the news: Gofman is meeting with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the sources said. He is also expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff, one of the sources said. Mossad, the CIA and the White House declined to comment. State of play: Trump has so far rejected pressure from Netanyahu to return to combat. The two discussed the Iran war during a Nov. 5 call, per a U.S. official. Instead, the president has sided with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE to continue the naval blockade and economic pressure campaign against Iran, while seeing if a deal is possible. "I could end it immediately. At the request of the nations that I'm looking to protect, we are doing it a little bit longer way, a little bit more civilly," Trump said on Thursday. "Saudi Arabia has asked me to please just let it be the way it is now for a while, because [Iran is] disintegrating. Qatar, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, all of them would much prefer the waiting period." The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel. His opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, has received a mandate to form a new government. It is unclear whether he'll be able to do so. In the meantime, leaders of the Israeli opposition are concerned Netanyahu will try to launch an attack on Iran — or provoke Iran to attack Israel — in order to undermine Eisenkot's efforts, sources say. Netanyahu would be removed from power if Eisenkot succeeds. On Thursday, Netanyahu met with Eisenkot for two hours and briefed him on the situation with Iran. A source close to Eisenkot said he doesn't think…

33e1d7779a:e883101ad14e4a47.title: Bessent puts Megaspeed heat on Lutnick: "Commerce has the pen"
33e1d7779a:e883101ad14e4a47.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:e883101ad14e4a47.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a Friday interview that while his department and others agreed on placing Megaspeed on a special list of companies that pose national security concerns, the Commerce Department "has the pen." Why it matters: Bessent didn't deny reports of tension between him and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who has come under scrutiny for his inaction over Megaspeed. The Singapore tech company has been accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China, and former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted he had an affair with an executive from the company. The U.S. has identified the woman, Alice Huang , as a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Driving the news: " Treasury, War, USTR, and State — they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent said on CNBC Friday morning. "You ... have to ask them about their internal processes," he added. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:423b01f0850daed3.title: Oil supplies bounce back, but prices are still high
33e1d7779a:423b01f0850daed3.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:423b01f0850daed3.summary: Oil markets are heading into an unusual period as the Iran conflict remains in dangerous limbo: The supply crunch is easing, but prices could stay stubbornly high. Why it matters: While gasoline prices have dropped lately, don't expect pre-war levels anytime soon even as Middle East exports fitfully recover. Getting oil out of the region is expensive, which filters down to consumers. The threat of new attacks can keep oil costs higher, too, thanks to the risk premium embedded in prices. The big picture: Traders are watching the state of potential diplomacy — and the possibility of a prolonged stalemate. Oil prices jumped yesterday after President Trump said on his Truth Social that "we don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." Driving the news: Crude oil export levels bounce around, but have recently returned to pre-war levels at times, barrel-tracking firms and analysts say. Yet shipping threats will "persist in 2027," and attacks spiked last month ( see the chart above ), per political risk intelligence firm Verisk Maplecroft. A new agreement on navigating the Strait of Hormuz would just be a piece of the puzzle — if it ever happens. "The threat of a renewed wave of shipping attacks will remain high as long as the underlying confrontation over Iran's nuclear and missile programmes remains unresolved," the firm's analysis states. Catch up quick: Tracking how much supply is returning is a moving target, and higher production from countries outside the Middle East — including the U.S. — matters too. The oil market is "showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the International Energy Agency said this morning . Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf region rose to 82% of pre-war levels last month, though recovery of refined product shipments is weaker, its monthly analysis states. With supply rising and oil demand lowered by the conflict, IEA…

33e1d7779a:4ec49f82bf192236.title: Doctors want liability shield from AI mistakes
33e1d7779a:4ec49f82bf192236.author: Adriel Bettelheim
33e1d7779a:4ec49f82bf192236.summary: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence in hospitals and clinics is leading the nation's biggest physicians group to lobby for new legal protections if AI harms patients. Why it matters: The use of increasingly sophisticated AI tools and recommendations is blurring the lines around negligence in health care, raising questions about whether doctors should be held responsible for decisions that rely on software. There's added urgency as autonomous AI takes on more and more important medical tasks with less direct oversight. The question is who's responsible when something goes wrong. Driving the news: The American Medical Association this week called for federal and state legislation to protect physicians from liability when AI products injure patients, despite physicians using the tools as intended. The group also is pressing for new laws mandating that AI companies carry adequate liability insurance and disclose product limitations and performance data. Hospitals, health systems, insurers and health tech vendors should be responsible if the required use of specific AI products results in harmful errors, the AMA policy states. Between the lines: The group's push comes as AI clinical tools are flooding the health system, unlocking new efficiencies but giving algorithms increasing power to make decisions like whether to order a diagnostic test or prescribe an expensive drug. Legal and medical experts point to the possibility of triage errors, in which AI systems that process clinical histories, vital signs and imaging can misjudge the severity of a case without the attending doctor's knowledge. The AMA also raises the possibility of an AI system making a plausible recommendation for treatment, but with incomplete laboratory results or an outdated diagnoses. In such cases, a physician may be unable to verify the inputs. In cases where a patient is harmed, responsibility should fall on AI manufacturers and vendors — and possibly on health systems that require…

33e1d7779a:88d6ec4aa5983961.title: Democrats in power confront the social media trap
33e1d7779a:88d6ec4aa5983961.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:88d6ec4aa5983961.summary: Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries are both cautious, calm, compromise-minded leaders fantasizing about a serious, sensible Democratic-run Congress. But social media is a temptress no party leader has tamed. The seduction of attention, likes and followers invariably proves too strong for the savviest, most self-promotional politicians to resist. Why it matters: That's the lesson of the Internet Era of American Politics — the algorithms always win. A few provocative members of Congress and online activists dominate the national conversation because they master the biggest social media platforms. That creates the impression that their views reflect a party, or a nation, when in reality they don't. And it shapes the party's image and agenda. Rep. Josh Gottheimer (D-N.J.), vice chair of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus , told us: "Governing isn't about getting the most followers on X — it's about delivering actual results ... It's easy to scream and yell, and say no — it's much harder to figure out a way forward." By the numbers: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed had 1.6 million Instagram followers as of Sept. 13. Today: 7.6 million and rising. One clip of him pulled an estimated 50 million-plus views across X, Instagram and TikTok. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, sits at 466,000 Instagram followers . A man who hasn't been sworn in has roughly 15x the leader's audience. El-Sayed telegraphed this in July: "If you're Chuck Schumer, I'm pretty damn dangerous!" True. Jeffries has nearly 1 million followers on Instagram. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has 9.8 million on her personal account alone. Yes, President Trump remade the GOP. But social media sucked in countless others to try to copy him, pushing rhetoric or ideas few politicians would've touched in the past. You see this in the rise of celebrity politicians who do little legislating but lots of instigating. You see this in the explosion of not just Instagram, X and YouTube followers by…

33e1d7779a:9a73df5bc71e8464.title: The AI boom will survive without Jensen Huang, but there's a $500 billion funding hole to fill
33e1d7779a:9a73df5bc71e8464.author: Bradley Olson
33e1d7779a:9a73df5bc71e8464.summary: The AI boom without Jensen Huang will test a hard truth: Even if the tech world has grown somewhat less reliant on Nvidia's chips, it remains highly dependent on its checkbook. Why it matters : With rival chips maturing and recent software breakthroughs, the tech ecosystem has achieved what would've seemed impossible a year ago: a viable path around Nvidia. But replacing a CEO willing to bankroll startups, backstop billions in cloud debt and aggressively fund rivals to the AI giants will be much harder. The big picture : The next chapter without Huang will be more cautious, but the industry is capable of absorbing the change, for two key reasons: 1. New chips - Semiconductor competition has become harder to contain. At OpenAI and other startups, a longstanding joke was that the best way to get a discount on Nvidia chips was to openly talk to Google or others about alternatives. Huang would often swoop in enthusiastically, eager to lock in a customer. The progress of custom chips from Google, Amazon, Microsoft and OpenAI , as well as new deals with Broadcom and Nvidia rival AMD, gives those conversations more substance. Customers have options, and far more leverage than ever. AI itself has also made those offerings easier to use. Anthropic says its Mythos model helped run certain workloads on AMD chips in about three days , compared with six to 12 months in the past. 2. Washington - In DC, China hawks are ascendant. Huang's departure strengthens calls from administration forces, some lawmakers, and companies such as Anthropic that have pushed for tighter controls on chip sales. Legislation is rapidly advancing to cut off loopholes and strengthen export restrictions for advanced chip sales to China, and the Commerce Department is reportedly preparing additional ways to limit such access. Cutting off those routes could help protect America's lead and offer a major pre-IPO boost to Anthropic and OpenAI. Reality check : Alternative chips and leaps forward in software…

33e1d7779a:d5ff0d0bfca71974.title: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
33e1d7779a:d5ff0d0bfca71974.author: Justin Green
33e1d7779a:d5ff0d0bfca71974.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he'll challenge Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Why it matters: Van Hollen's bid gives grassroots activists nearly three weeks to pressure Senate Democrats before they cast secret ballots in the Dec. 1 leadership election. The attempt to oust Schumer (D-N.Y.) underscores that deep divisions are plaguing the Democratic Party despite their overwhelming midterm success . Van Hollen (D-Md.) has served in the Senate since 2017 and has been in Congress since 2003. Schumer has been the Senate Democratic leader since 2017 and has served in the Senate since 1999. Driving the news: "In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement on Thursday. "They called for a change from Donald Trump's disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people." "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader." Zoom in: Opposition to Schumer has been building: "[T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who demanded a plan for change from her party leadership. Progressives have accused Schumer of not fighting hard enough against President Trump and the MAGA agenda. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is a vocal backer of Van Hollen for majority leader. Van Hollen, who is also considering a 2028 presidential run, said he's been listening to calls for him to challenge Schumer and considering his options.

33e1d7779a:e0e13ddf37c6c66c.title: House Democratic leaders face fallout over poorly timed floor vote fumbles
33e1d7779a:e0e13ddf37c6c66c.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:e0e13ddf37c6c66c.summary: A week that was supposed to see House Democrats transition seamlessly from a landslide midterm victory to a leadership coronation has instead been pocked by surprise Republican victories on the House floor. Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week. "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why." "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one." What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present. The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event. That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition. The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills. What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition. "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the…

33e1d7779a:84bd7d9343515d6c.title: Senate Dems can look forward to unlikely MAGA allies
33e1d7779a:84bd7d9343515d6c.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:84bd7d9343515d6c.summary: Senate Democrats could find some of their most surprising allies next Congress from the right wing of the Republican Party . Why it matters: Senate Democrats are on track to need only four GOP votes to break filibusters next Congress. They could find those votes from a bloc of GOP senators with a shared appetite for taking on corporate power. Enter Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), Jim Banks (R-Ind.), Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.). Each has already worked with Democrats, and their votes could put legislation over the top. Who we're watching: Hawley has co-led multiple pieces of legislation with progressive star Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) this Congress. Hawley is often viewed as a loner in the GOP, pairing populist economics with hardcore culture war issues from abortion to transgender care to religious freedom. He's been scathing in his postelection critiques. "This Congress did not come and work for the people. This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers, and it worked for big tech companies," he told reporters on Tuesday. He's scoping out areas for potential bipartisan deals: "You want to raise the minimum wage? I'm for that. You want to work to get gas prices down? I'm for that. I am open to anything to bring down the cost of health care," he said. Zoom in: Watch the health care space, specifically undoing cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drug price controls. President Trump has specifically asked Congress to codify his most favored nations drug pricing deals, which could give Republicans an opening to work with Democrats. Hawley and moderate Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) were among the loudest GOP voices opposing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act credits last year. Zoom out: Social Security and tech safety issues could also be huge areas of unexpected bipartisan work. Over the summer, Warren and Moreno released a sweeping plan to "save Social Security." Warren and Banks have…

33e1d7779a:d458fdcc5ba7a2f5.title: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
33e1d7779a:d458fdcc5ba7a2f5.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:d458fdcc5ba7a2f5.summary: Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang , who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse. The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom. Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure. The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure. Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor , leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm. In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company. Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots. Colette Kress Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters . Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, praised Kress for her deep understanding of the company's business and customers. Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives. She's also the only person, aside from Huang, who had much visibility across the company, according to Axios' Ina Fried. Huang had several dozen direct reports, many of…

33e1d7779a:4e9f7436aceaf3fb.title: Scott Colom's win in Mississippi puts political change to the test
33e1d7779a:4e9f7436aceaf3fb.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:4e9f7436aceaf3fb.summary: Mississippi, a state with the largest share of Black residents in the country, has elected its first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years. Why it matters: For generations, Black Mississippians left the state to escape Jim Crow and pursue economic and political opportunities elsewhere. Now, Mississippi faces a new question: Was Scott Colom's victory a once-in-a-generation breakthrough, or the beginning of an era of Black political power? Driving the news: Colom's defeat of incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith broke a barrier that had stood since Reconstruction. Mississippi was the first state to send Black senators to Congress, before violence and disenfranchisement stripped Black residents of their political power. In Colom's race, Democrats gained ground in 75 of the state's 82 counties, Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, told Axios. "It wasn't just a fluke of super high turnout in one particular region," he said. "Scott Colom's victory can signal that maybe Mississippi is ready to govern differently." The big picture: During the Great Migration , roughly 6 million Black Americans left the South to escape discrimination and seek better opportunities. Many Black Mississippians built political power in Northern cities such as Chicago, said Keneshia Grant, a Great Migration expert at Howard University. For many, the question became, "should we go and try for a better life in these other places ... or should we stay and fight where we are?" Grant said. "It was about economic opportunity, but I also think it was about terrorism too," Cassandra Overton Welchlin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable, told Axios, pointing to the lynchings that drove families away. Welchlin left Mississippi for graduate school and considered staying away. "I did not want to come back to Mississippi because it is hard here," she told Axios. Mentors encouraged her to return. She did,…

33e1d7779a:91b0f5bf63324dc4.title: Jensen Huang's implosion at Nvidia leaves trail of collateral damage
33e1d7779a:91b0f5bf63324dc4.author: Nathan Bomey
33e1d7779a:91b0f5bf63324dc4.summary: Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself . Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise. The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap. "His visionary leadership is going to be missed — it's not going to be replaced," Joel Shulman, CEO of ERShares, which has owned Nvidia shares since 2005, tells Axios. Zoom in: With the uncertainty over Huang's tenure at Nvidia now resolved, the attention will quickly pivot to a slew of unanswered questions, including: What will the investigations uncover? Just because he's gone doesn't mean this is over. If the FBI probe or the independent investigation ordered by the board show that Huang gave favorable treatment to Megaspeed — the company led by the suspected spy Alice Huang — he and Nvidia could face serious consequences. Huang is also expected to testify behind closed doors next week before a Congressional committee. Critics say the Nvidia board wasn't fulfilling its duty to provide proper oversight of Huang — particularly if it had any reason to be aware of his reported affairs before they become public. Peter Jaworski, business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said the situation raises questions about what the board knew and when they knew it. Nvidia reps haven't responded to Axios requests for comment on the board's handling of the matter. Who takes the permanent role as CEO? CFO Colette Kress was named to the interim role, but the board is conducting a global search that will consider outside and internal candidates for a permanant successor. She "has built enormous credibility internally and externally…

33e1d7779a:7c0e45bd90c588d8.title: 1 killed, 4 injured in Logan Circle shooting; suspect dead
33e1d7779a:7c0e45bd90c588d8.author: Mimi Montgomery
33e1d7779a:7c0e45bd90c588d8.summary: A gunman killed one person and injured four others in Logan Circle on Thursday morning before fatally shooting himself, police say, prompting a massive law enforcement response in one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods. The latest: The suspected gunman died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound while barricaded in his apartment, said D.C. interim police chief Jeffery Carroll . Residents were told to shelter in place until around 11:35am, but police are still urging people to avoid the area while the investigation continues. The big picture: A gunman fatally shot one person inside VIDA Fitness, a popular neighborhood gym at 15th and P streets NW, police said at a Thursday morning press conference. Four others were injured, including one seriously, police say. Police said some victims were injured at a construction site across the street, but their exact locations remain under investigation. Zoom in: MPD announced around 11:10am that the barricade concluded and the scene was safe. Earlier, police said officers reported hearing a gunshot during negotiations with the suspect, and had not heard communication since. Mayor Bowser said the lone gunman had been "contained." People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Zoom out: The massive law enforcement response blocked off nearby streets and the neighborhood Whole Foods. Nearly a dozen DC Public Schools in the vicinity, from Columbia Heights to Adams Morgan, went into lockdown . DCPS tells Axios the schools have resumed normal operations after police gave the all-clear around 11:15am. Police helicopters circled overhead throughout the morning, rattling windows in surrounding neighborhoods. U.S. Park Police and other federal authorities could be seen speeding down 18th Street and other major thoroughfares in response. A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle…

33e1d7779a:b6f66424a8c447d0.title: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
33e1d7779a:b6f66424a8c447d0.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:b6f66424a8c447d0.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it. Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign. But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight. That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy. What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday . Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month. Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated. The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%. Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June. The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually…

33e1d7779a:8e758e03e330f32b.title: Trump sticks by Commerce Secretary Lutnick despite Nvidia inaction
33e1d7779a:8e758e03e330f32b.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:8e758e03e330f32b.summary: The White House is standing by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick despite a view within the administration that Lutnick delayed action to address concerns over chip smuggling to China. Why it matters: Congress smells blood in the water following bombshell reports that U.S. national security may have been jeopardized by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Lawmakers want to know what the Trump administration did or did not do in response to that intelligence — and Lutnick, the official in charge of the department at the center of export control policy, is squarely in their field of view. President Trump, however, is not distancing himself from the secretary. "Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump's America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments," a White House official tells Axios. "President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history." Catch up quick: Lutnick was sent intelligence about Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and repeatedly did not take export control action — despite pressure from the broader administration and the president himself, Axios first reported. Lutnick's role is prompting scrutiny on the Hill from members on both sides of the aisle. "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military," Senate Banking Committee Chair Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement. "The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told Politico. "Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country," Kennedy added. "I mean, there will be a congressional investigation. But I don't think…

33e1d7779a:266e9a0c5a630e97.title: Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system throttled again
33e1d7779a:266e9a0c5a630e97.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:266e9a0c5a630e97.summary: The Ukrainian government has asked the Pentagon and SpaceX to explain new restrictions it says are disrupting the satellite system its military uses to intercept Russian drones. Why it matters: This is the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine reported that Starshield, made by Elon Musk's SpaceX, was impeded. The Ukrainian military uses Starshield — the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system — to control and operate its reconnaissance and to intercept drones. Driving the news: Ukrainian President Zelensky said Thursday he was briefed by the minister of defense and the commander of the Ukrainian military that "units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations" along the entire front line and in the parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia. "The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he wrote on X. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side." Zoom in: A Ukrainian official said the restrictions have been happening for three days. "On the first day there were 10% limitations, on the second day 50%, and today 100% of the missions fail because of restrictions," the official said. Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the U.S., Denys Sienik, said the Starshield system shuts down when drones fly at more than 100 miles per hour. "We don't have clarification from SpaceX or Pentagon at the moment," he said. State of play: Zelensky said the new restrictions began shortly before President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday. Kushner and Witkoff are expected to meet Zelensky later on Thursday in Dublin. Catch up quick: Ukraine relies on two SpaceX satellite services. Starlink, the commercial service, supports battlefield communications and logistics. Starshield is designed for government and military customers. Ukraine accesses it…

33e1d7779a:402e12256ec26483.title: Trump pitches Apple's Tim Cook as new Nvidia CEO
33e1d7779a:402e12256ec26483.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:402e12256ec26483.summary: President Trump is backing Apple executive chairman Tim Cook to replace tech giant Jensen Huang after Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, though it's unclear whether he meant it as a joke. The big picture: Trump didn't weigh in on the controversy surrounding Huang's departure following alleged affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and an Nvidia executive, instead calling Huang "a Legend" in his Truth Social post . Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:71378d0ad1b2d2b2.title: Jensen Huang, an architect of the AI boom, resigns as Nvidia CEO
33e1d7779a:71378d0ad1b2d2b2.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:71378d0ad1b2d2b2.summary: Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had two affairs, including one with a purported Chinese spy. Why it matters: It's impossible to overstate how critical Huang is to Nvidia, to the AI buildout, to the stock market and economy. His departure could, per Wall Street sources, be the catalyst that endangers a ballooning AI bubble. It's also unlikely to ease congressional scrutiny of the company or Huang himself. Driving the news: Nvidia's board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, while launching a search for a permanent replacement. Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, will continue serving as CFO while overseeing the company. Harvey C. Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair. The board said it expects Nvidia's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Zoom out: Huang's resignation follows revelations about two extramarital relationships. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him. Nvidia's board had previously launched an independent investigation into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia did not provide a reason for Huang's resignation in Thursday's announcement, which comes after reports that the board had an emergency meeting over whether to oust the CEO. By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell more than 10% after news of Huang's resignation. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. 🚨 Stunning stat: At these levels, Nvidia will have lost about $1.4 trillion in market capitalization in two weeks, since the initial Times report about linking Jensen Huang and Alice Huang. The big picture: This will likely go down as one of the biggest executive scandals in history. Nvidia is also one of the largest holdings in major index…

33e1d7779a:9e07f0745d862417.title: Jensen Huang's ouster triggers an AI earthquake
33e1d7779a:9e07f0745d862417.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:9e07f0745d862417.summary: Jensen Huang's potential ouster from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023. Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy , with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars. At the center of that vast financial flywheel is Huang, who spent 33 years making himself synonymous with Nvidia — and Nvidia synonymous with the AI revolution. "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time," economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on X , warning of contagion across the AI industry. Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable. Even after his affair with a suspected Chinese spy came to light, President Trump and Nvidia's board stood behind him, Silicon Valley's elite rallied to his defense and betting markets suggested he would survive. It took revelations of a second affair — this time with an executive who reported directly to Huang — to shatter that consensus and bring his storied reign to the brink of a stunning end. Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate, though there was still no decision as of early Thursday morning. The White House was read in. The market reaction has been brutal. Nvidia had already shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the initial scandal erupted, and shares plunged further in after-hours and pre-market trading overnight. One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang. Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the…

33e1d7779a:a4a1fa09b4d70839.title: Trump orders Vance to focus on "corruption" in Democrat-run areas, not Iran
33e1d7779a:a4a1fa09b4d70839.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:a4a1fa09b4d70839.summary: President Trump directed Vice President JD Vance on Thursday to turn his "complete and total attention" toward alleged corruption in Democrat-run cities and states, contending that "[w]e don't need a deal with Iran." The big picture: After Vance concluded that the Iran war drove Republicans' stunning midterm walloping, Trump is reorienting his No. 2's focus — and directing him to go after Democrats the president labeled as "CORRUPT AND EVIL." Oil prices surged, and stocks sank after Trump's post reinjected a note of uncertainty into a market that was acting like the Iran war was all but over. Driving the news: "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Also on Truth Social Thursday, he threatened new tariffs on Mexico and criticized GOP senators for failing to pass the Save America ACT — adding that failure to do so was "devastating" for Republicans during the midterms. He said that he had asked Vance to "focus his complete and total attention" on so-called "Corruption and Crime" in Democrat-run cities and states, naming Minnesota, California and Illinois. Vance has chaired Trump's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud since the president created it via executive order earlier this year. Throughout the first half of his administration and federal crackdown on U.S. cities, Trump has repeatedly framed blue areas as hotbeds of crime and corruption, even when the stats haven't necessarily backed up those arguments. Catch up quick: Vance was recently heavily involved in a push to reach a new ceasefire with Iran and resume nuclear negotiations, Axios' Barak Ravid reported. Vance was a skeptical voice in Trump's inner circle about the war, Ravid reported, and led U.S. negotiating delegations after it began. Vance's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Between the lines: Vance offered a surprisingly candid assessment of the midterm shellacking, writing in an X post last week…

33e1d7779a:5d11cbb5a4203627.title: Bracing for Nvidia's impact
33e1d7779a:5d11cbb5a4203627.author: Matt Phillips
33e1d7779a:5d11cbb5a4203627.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's apparent from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the AI ecosystem that he did much to create. Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia. Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy. Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported Wednesday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang. Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session. Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years. The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers. Chip makers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down roughly 30% from their recent high through Wednesday's close, vaporizing nearly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth. There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a big new report on the investment cycle. "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness." Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost over…

33e1d7779a:de1edcc66cc7502e.title: From Emmett Till to Robert Johnson, the Delta powered Scott Colom's historic Senate bid
33e1d7779a:de1edcc66cc7502e.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:de1edcc66cc7502e.summary: Scott Colom 's path to a historic U.S. Senate upset ran through the Mississippi Delta — where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form. Why it matters: Nearly 150 years after Reconstruction, Mississippi sent a Black American to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1881. The votes pushing Colom toward that milestone came from communities where Black residents spent generations fighting for the ballot. Driving the news: The Associated Press projected the race for Colom on Wednesday, handing Democrats a historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. By the numbers: An Axios analysis of AP county returns found Colom ahead in 16 of the 18 counties in the Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area . Colom collected roughly 100,000 votes to Hyde-Smith's 62,000 — a 38,000-vote advantage. In 2020, Democrat Mike Espy carried 15 of those counties by about 25,000 votes, according to Mississippi's certified county returns . Colom's share of the two-party vote climbed from about 56% to 62%. Statewide, Colom led Hyde-Smith by about 4,700 votes out of more than 962,000 counted when the AP called the race Wednesday — a margin of roughly half a percentage point. What they're saying: "Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out," NAACP president Derrick Johnson said in a statement. Johnson said Mississippi voters showed up despite efforts to remove voters from the rolls . Zoom in: Colom's electoral map traces some of the most painful and defining chapters of Black American history. Coahoma County: Home to Clarksdale and the famed crossroads associated with the legend that bluesman Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil. Colom led with about 4,700 votes to 1,300. Leflore and Tallahatchie counties: Emmett Till was abducted near Money in Leflore County in 1955. His body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River in Tallahatchie County, where an all-white…

33e1d7779a:3c160034bb573adb.title: Democrats debate taking a page from Trump's economic playbook
33e1d7779a:3c160034bb573adb.author: Amy Harder
33e1d7779a:3c160034bb573adb.summary: President Trump is turning the federal government into an investor in dozens of private companies, and some Democrats are considering following his lead as their party emerges emboldened from the midterm elections. Why it matters: Democrats are gaining new power to scrutinize Trump's corporate investments, even as his approach gains traction within their own party. They're looking at investments and aid for clean energy and other priorities, like support for energy infrastructure. State of play: The Trump administration's investments in energy, critical minerals and other industries are already drawing calls for congressional investigations . "The Trump administration has widened the aperture for industrial policy," Jennifer Granholm, who served as President Biden's Energy Secretary, said at a gathering of energy and climate experts Axios attended in Berkeley, Calif., last month. "You're not going to have state ownership of enterprises," Granholm told Axios in an interview afterward. "But maybe you do take a little bit of an ownership slice" for national security or global competitiveness reasons, she said. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has also expressed openness to federal ownership stakes, while raising concerns about the Trump administration's lack of transparency and accountability, he told Semafor . Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) has argued that the U.S. needs to consider a more aggressive industrial policy to compete with countries like China, while warning against direct government ownership. "We are long overdue for having a conversation about, 'should the United States even have an industrial policy?'" Casten said at a recent University of Chicago event . "For a long time, we viewed industrial policy as something that socialists do." Casten said he would support the U.S. ensuring domestic manufacturing of certain parts of supply chains, like electronic control systems that operate energy infrastructure, and even pursuing "smart tariff policy" to have…

33e1d7779a:c5fce0e7186a6f03.title: Democrats unite against Big Health Care
33e1d7779a:c5fce0e7186a6f03.author: Caitlin Owens
33e1d7779a:c5fce0e7186a6f03.summary: Newly elected Democrats from ruby red states are leading a charge to take on corporate health care and some business practices that they say drive up health care costs. Why it matters: Democrats may not be anywhere close to agreement on Medicare for All, but they're relatively united around confronting Big Health Care after campaigning hard on the populist theme. Driving the news: While expanding Medicare, reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and reviving enhanced Obamacare subsidies are getting most of the attention, there's a subtle shift in rhetoric and policy positions toward blaming big health companies for the affordability crisis. It reflects the reality that a substantial expansion of the federal government's role in health care isn't in the cards while President Trump is in office, but populist themes could unite the rank-and-file and even draw in some Republicans. Even candidates who didn't constantly rail about drugmakers or insurers have adopted policy ideas that, until recently, were confined to left-leaning think tanks. Case in point: Incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico ran on breaking up big health care companies and "stop[ping] hospitals and insurance companies from overcharging patients." (He also supports allowing Americans under 65 to join Medicare.) South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews ran on limiting insurer profits per enrollee, expanding the number of drugs subject to Medicare drug price negotiations and banning private equity-owned hospitals. Incoming Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton supports expanding Medicare drug price negotiations and extending the negotiated prices to private health plans, as well as addressing Medicare Advantage overpayments from the federal government. Other targets include medical debt, pharmacy benefit manager practices and caps on out-of-pocket drug costs. Many of these ideas already have buy-in from more-senior progressives. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has sponsored the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which is co-sponsored by…

33e1d7779a:821d9fd67181e1d7.title: Scoop: AOC shakes up team again as 2028 decision looms
33e1d7779a:821d9fd67181e1d7.author: Alex Thompson
33e1d7779a:821d9fd67181e1d7.summary: New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life. Why it matters: The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's seat, which is up the same year. Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision. At the same time, sources said, she's brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who oversaw Bernie Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns. Middle Seat has been key to Ocasio-Cortez's operation. Over the past two years, she has paid the firm more than $6 million — about a quarter of her operation's disbursements during that period. AOC is close with Sanders, and if she decides to run for president, progressives say, she would be able to quickly staff up with his former advisers. But Ocasio-Cortez's latest move doesn't necessarily signal that she's leaning toward a presidential run or a Senate bid.
