Tagaris' firm has helped power the small-dollar fundraising operation for California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's widely expected to run for the White House. It also has worked with other Democrats who are potential contenders for president — Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to the company's website . Middle Seat, the firm AOC is leaving, has Sanders roots as well: It was founded by alumni of the Vermont senator's 2016 campaign. Flashback: Ocasio-Cortez's reorganizing follows several changes she made to her staff this year, as Axios previously reported . They included parting ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director, as well as bringing aboard a few former aides. The Washington Sun…

33e1d7779a:3a5558395dfd5677.title: How the midterms swing each party's economic feelings
33e1d7779a:3a5558395dfd5677.author: Emily Peck
33e1d7779a:3a5558395dfd5677.summary: Note: Figures compare average daily sentiment readings over the seven days before each election with the five days after. Election Day is excluded; Data: Morning Consult; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios There was an unusually sharp partisan mood shift in the wake of the midterms, according to sentiment data from Morning Consult that was shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: While big partisan swings in consumer sentiment are typical after a presidential election, they have been much smaller in midterm races. The latest numbers show just how tightly Americans' views on the economy are now intertwined with politics. By the numbers: Democratic consumer sentiment rose 6.5 points in the five days after the election compared with the week before, while Republicans' mood fell 6.4 points. How it works: Morning Consult's index considers survey responses from approximately 5,000 U.S. adults. They're asked five questions, including on people's personal finances and financial outlook, as well as their views on overall business conditions. Zoom in: The biggest shifts in sentiment were in respondents' feelings about the future. Republicans' outlook across all five metrics fell after the election. Their confidence in business conditions over the next five years plummeted 12 percentage points. Democrats, meanwhile, had a jump of 9 percentage points in confidence about business conditions (although they remain negative about it) and an even bigger increase — 12 percentage points — in optimism that their own finances would improve over the next year. Of note: Both sides were more negative about their own finances compared with a year ago. Zoom out: Overall sentiment, which includes Independents, barely moved — ticking up less than one point, per Morning Consult. The opposing partisan shifts appear to have canceled each other out. Reality check: It's early days, and sentiment could shift quickly. Between the lines: Consumer sentiment was once a telling measure of how people would…

33e1d7779a:c0a5ea394eabe367.title: Murders plunge 15% in America's biggest cities
33e1d7779a:c0a5ea394eabe367.author: Russell Contreras
33e1d7779a:c0a5ea394eabe367.summary: Data: Major Cities Chiefs Association (MCCA) ; Note: Tulsa Police changed crime-reporting systems, which may affect year-over-year comparisons.; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios Homicides fell 15.2% across major U.S. police jurisdictions through the first nine months of 2026, extending a retreat from pandemic-era violence that began under President Biden and continues under President Trump . The big picture: A new Major Cities Chiefs Association report found declines in all four major violent-crime categories among 66 reporting U.S. large law enforcement agencies from January through September, compared with the same period last year. Homicides dropped 15.2%. Robberies fell 9.1%. Rapes declined 3.5%. Aggravated assaults decreased 3.4%. State of play: Combined, the four categories fell 4.9% — or 13,822 fewer reported offenses. Fifty-one of the 66 agencies reported overall declines. Homicides dropped in 49 jurisdictions, increased in 15 and remained unchanged in two. Zoom in: Some of the nation's largest cities recorded striking homicide declines. Memphis: Homicides plunged 36.5%, from 156 to 99. San Antonio was down 36.5%, Indianapolis down 33.6%, Philadelphia down 21.2%, Aurora, Colorado down 65.2% and Newark, New Jersey down 59.1%. The other side: New York City was a major outlier and reported more violent crime in all four categories, including 24.5% more homicides and 14.2% more robberies. Its combined violent crime total was up 5.1%. San Diego reported 45.2% more homicides and Las Vegas recorded a 23.4% jump. Washington, D.C., saw homicides fall 29.9%, but robberies surged 41.1%, pushing its combined violent-crime total up 9.7%. The caveat: The figures remain preliminary. Houston reported no data because of a records-system transition, and Tulsa recently transitioned to a new crime reporting system, the report notes.

33e1d7779a:c7b7da7d21f0244e.title: Nvidia sinks after report implicates CEO Jensen Huang in 2nd affair
33e1d7779a:c7b7da7d21f0244e.author: Nathan Bomey
33e1d7779a:c7b7da7d21f0244e.summary: Shares in Nvidia sank Wednesday night after the New York Times reported CEO Jensen Huang had a second affair with a senior executive who reports to him. Why it matters: The report adds to mounting scrutiny of Huang, already under investigation over an affair with a purported Chinese spy. The potential impact goes beyond one man and one business, though. Huang is arguably the world's most powerful CEO at the moment, his company serving as the beating heart of the AI revolution. He also has no obvious successor . Driving the news: Huang, 63, had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, 48, Nvidia's vice president of health care, according to the Times. Both are married to other people. The two were reportedly seen being affectionate at a hotel during Nvidia's annual developer conference in San Jose in March. A bystander recorded the interaction, and Huang's security team made an offer to the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement, per the Times. The paper reported that Nvidia declined to issue a statement, and Powell did not respond to a request for comment. By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell nearly 8% in after-hours trading as of 6 p.m. ET Wednesday. The company's lost about $1 trillion in market cap since the Times first reported on Oct. 29 that Huang had a "close relationship" with a suspected spy. On the prediction market Kalshi, the odds of Huang being out as CEO as soon as this weekend skyrocketed. Zoom out: This new report comes after Huang confirmed in a company email that he had been unfaithful in his marriage. Nvidia has an independent panel investigating, and hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to handle the probe. Between the lines: Peter Jaworski, a business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said it will be hard for Huang to keep his job after this. "You can't have a relationship like this with a direct report," Jaworski tells Axios. "Does the CEO get fired? In this situation that's probably the move to make." Jaworski said the…

33e1d7779a:37e339ac5774008a.title: Scott Colom ousts Cindy Hyde-Smith in historic Mississippi Senate flip
33e1d7779a:37e339ac5774008a.author: Donica Phifer
33e1d7779a:37e339ac5774008a.summary: Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset , becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects. Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress. Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction. Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881. Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate. Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom. "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Cologne and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said. Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election." "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said. The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024. Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage. She was also outspent on TV advertising , with a flood of ads from…

33e1d7779a:60b2d1a8bfd36fca.title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
33e1d7779a:60b2d1a8bfd36fca.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:60b2d1a8bfd36fca.summary: Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations. Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures. Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records . Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats. What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X . The White House and Speaker Mike Johnson's offices have not yet provided comment. The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics. This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files. This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld. Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files. Their first…

33e1d7779a:e5b4239cdfca1062.title: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
33e1d7779a:e5b4239cdfca1062.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:e5b4239cdfca1062.summary: President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead. One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal. This report was assembled from interviews with six high-level sources who were briefed on or, in some cases, heard the discussions. Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal. The group sided with Bessent. Lutnick appeared to agree, but then muttered under his breath, "I need to check with the president." Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen. "He's stalling it out," said one official, describing how Lutnick had previously met privately with the president to change his mind about the export limit. "This is an ongoing concern with Howard and this issue," said another. This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?" Around 5pm, the group headed to the Oval Office. Trump called tech advisor Elon Musk and agreed to move forward. Musk supported…

33e1d7779a:cdf10059d309039d.title: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
33e1d7779a:cdf10059d309039d.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:cdf10059d309039d.summary: The U.S. has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent, two sources with knowledge of the matter said. Why it matters: For years, Russia has sought a European security deal that limits NATO expansion and scales back its military presence in Eastern Europe. The U.S. has rejected those demands in the past, but now appears open to them in some form as part of a broader agreement to end the war in Ukraine. But many European governments are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach. State of play: President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to reiterate the request. They also want Putin to allow European representatives to join the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. official said. From Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday night. Catch up quick: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday were the first time Ukrainian and Russian officials met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran. In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a bit of momentum. Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was detained by Russia in 2022 . Together with First Lady Melania Trump and her team, Witkoff and Kushner also brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of Oleshky. Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi started on Tuesday with Witkoff, Kushner and commander of the U.S. European Command Gen. Alexus Grynkewich mediating between the Russians and the Ukrainians. The parties agreed to a prisoner exchange deal that Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said could be the biggest since the war began. U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the exact number of prisoners to be…

33e1d7779a:aa7a6317df2b31f9.title: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
33e1d7779a:aa7a6317df2b31f9.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:aa7a6317df2b31f9.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick's actions — or lack thereof — are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huan g had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. Driving the news: At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would "look into it." Commerce Undersecretary Jeff Kessler also was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings. But Kessler deferred to Lutnick, saying "That's a decision for the secretary." Sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" efforts by other administration officials to hold Megaspeed — a company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China — accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China. Spokespeople for Treasury and Commerce couldn't be immediately reached for comment. Catch up quick: The Commerce Department is increasingly at the center of scrutiny over the broader Trump administration's handling of an intelligence memo overseen by State Department head Marco Rubio. Lutnick was among the officials who received the report in May, ahead of a trip to China, Axios first reported. On Tuesday, the New York Times reported Commerce Undersecretary Kessler abruptly stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia intervened. The Financial Times reported the department was delaying efforts to blacklist Megaspeed despite several U.S. government agencies pushing it to do so. Inside the room: White House and intelligence officials have pressed Lutnick and his top…

33e1d7779a:8ac11d2c173c24f9.title: Don Leonard isn't a House member yet. He's already rocking Capitol Hill.
33e1d7779a:8ac11d2c173c24f9.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:8ac11d2c173c24f9.summary: Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) hasn't been sworn in yet, but he's making a name for himself on Capitol Hill as one of the most outspoken anti-establishment progressives in the incoming freshman class. Why it matters: That's an unlikely position for a Democrat who represents a rural Ohio district that President Trump carried by 10 percentage points in 2024. Leonard is archetypal of a burgeoning breed of swing-district House Democrats — populist in style, receptive to left-wing policies and unbound by traditional political norms — that will be well-represented in the 120th Congress. "I'm really vibing with my class," he told Axios in a Tuesday interview on Capitol Hill. "These are everyday citizens who heard the same call I heard and stood up." State of play: Leonard, a professor of city planning who defeated Republican Rep. Mike Carey in last Tuesday's midterm elections, was turning heads on Capitol Hill before he even arrived for freshman orientation on Sunday. He told his local CBS affiliate the day after the election he will "be shopping for a new leader" unless House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) changes his pro-Israel positions. He made an even bigger splash on Tuesday with a video he posted to social media saying he met with "senior members" who warned him his life would be a "living hell" and that he would lose reelection if he opposes Jeffries for speaker of the House. The other side: House Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), asked about Leonard's video at a press conference Tuesday afternoon, told reporters, "I don't know what senior Democrats he's talking about." "I think all of us here can attest to the work, the time, the energy that Hakeem Jeffries put into helping us build this majority," Aguilar said. Aguilar predicted Jeffries will be "overwhelmingly selected" as speaker and that he doesn't "lose any sleep over that." "Members could have ideas and interests and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in…

33e1d7779a:cdeb2d3422930b7a.title: Dems put Noem on notice
33e1d7779a:cdeb2d3422930b7a.author: Brittany Gibson
33e1d7779a:cdeb2d3422930b7a.summary: President Trump fired Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March, but Democrats aren't finished with her. Why it matters: Armed with commanding House and Senate majorities, they're preparing to haul the architects of Trump's mass deportation agenda before Congress to answer for their actions. "Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what's up? Clear your schedule," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, warned on X. She was referencing current DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (who replaced Noem), White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Border Czar Tom Homan and former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino. Dems on the House Oversight Committee included former DHS Special Government Employee Corey Lewandowski in a list of people who should "lawyer up." Zoom in: Rep. Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee, said in a letter to colleagues he'd prioritize investigating every death in DHS custody and during arrests. Thompson, who is running for committee chair and the subpoena power that comes with it, also plans to investigate alleged financial corruption at the agency and oversight of spending, particularly the gargantuan budget supplied by the One Big Beautiful Bill. "I called for Kristi Noem's impeachment in January, and she was gone by March. But the questions she refused to answer are still open," Thompson wrote. "Tom Homan and Stephen Miller would not appear [for a hearing] when we invited them this spring. In the majority, they will not have that choice," he wrote. Zoom out: Democratic leaders in both the House and Senate have a lengthy list of areas for oversight, according to sources familiar with their plans. That includes: The billions spent to expand ICE detention , including Alligator Alcatraz and a warehouse buying spree. Oversight agencies have been reviewing these purchases. Noem's purchase of luxury private jets that she claimed could be used for deportation…

33e1d7779a:94eb70410daa97b6.title: The AI industry's week from hell
33e1d7779a:94eb70410daa97b6.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:94eb70410daa97b6.summary: A week of political upheaval , financial turmoil and salacious scandal delivered one final indignity to the AI industry Tuesday, as Anthropic's staggering IPO target fell short of expectations. Why it matters: The bubble is wobbling. Investors, businesses and governments need a spectacular success from Anthropic to stave off a crisis of confidence that could tear through the broader economy. Facing new political headwinds, the industry can scarcely afford another setback — much less the spectacle of AI's crown jewel losing its luster on Wall Street. Zoom in: Anthropic announced plans Tuesday to raise as much as $64.4 billion in one of the largest IPOs in history, targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. That's roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago, as slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a punishing market selloff tempered expectations. Anthropic's annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have also climbed to nearly $901 billion. Zoom out: Anthropic's valuation reset caps a punishing stretch of new challenges that began with last week's stunning midterm results: 🌊 A blue wave of AI-skeptical Democrats will arrive in Congress armed with subpoena power and an appetite for investigating the industry's safety failures and vast political influence. Voters delivered another blow at the local level, favoring restrictions on data-center development in 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide. 🤖 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the central cog in AI's global gears, was swept up in an espionage scandal after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. His board, the FBI and Congress are investigating. Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times revelations on Oct. 29, with shares plunging further Tuesday as the company faces a new shareholder lawsuit. 📉 Wall Street went into a tailspin as…

33e1d7779a:9874d6fb6c80b52b.title: House GOP bets on MAGA "fighter" Jim Jordan
33e1d7779a:9874d6fb6c80b52b.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:9874d6fb6c80b52b.summary: House Republicans are turning to one of their fiercest fighters to lead their diminished conference after one of their biggest drubbings in decades. Why it matters : Jim Jordan , 62, a founding member of the hardline House Freedom Caucus, has completed a stunning insurgent-to-establishment turn after spending much of his nearly 20 years in Congress battling Republican leaders from the right. The Ohio Republican's victory over House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) represents a bet by Republicans that they shouldn't move away from President Trump to claw their way back to power. But Republicans are divided over what went wrong in the midterms, and whether a more confrontational approach is the right answer. Driving the news: Republicans emerged from last week's defeat hungry for change , handing Jordan a 106–73 victory over long-time GOP leader Scalise. GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) survived their elections. Jordan pitched himself as a battle-tested fighter capable of defending Trump against Democratic investigations and winning back the majority. What they're saying: "I think when you take a beating like we took, you need to make some changes, and I also think we're gearing up for war," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.), who backed Jordan, told Axios. "We need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Fine said. "We just got beat bad. We can't just go in with the same step forward," Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios. McClain told Axios: "Don't count Jim Jordan out. He's a fighter. He's been able to get stuff done." Yes, but: Not all Republicans are convinced they have the right response to their losses. Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.), who backed Scalise, argued that Republicans lost too many independent and Hispanic voters, pointing specifically to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies. Asked whether Republicans should have examined their losses before electing new leaders, Gimenez…

33e1d7779a:7c4bc592c0881fcc.title: Scoop — Stephen Miller's post-midterm focus: MAGA and men
33e1d7779a:7c4bc592c0881fcc.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:7c4bc592c0881fcc.summary: Stephen Miller wants to use his new role as White House chief of staff to win back young and minority men who helped elect President Trump in 2024 but swung toward Democrats in the midterms, two people familiar with the administration's plans tell Axios. Why it matters: Miller, named last week to replace Susie Wiles, plans to focus on reviving the populist agenda that helped the president build his 2024 coalition, with an emphasis on working-class voters. Young, working-class and minority men fled the GOP in droves in last week's elections , amid high prices fueled by Trump's tariffs, the war in Iran, and concerns about AI's impact on the job market. Another key factor in last week's voting: Latino men also swung sharply toward Democrats, as the administration's hard-line immigration crackdown became an increasingly contentious political issue. Driving the news: Miller wants to spend more time highlighting administration policies he believes haven't gotten enough attention, and that will appeal to working-class voters concerned about the economy, insiders tell Axios. His priorities will sound familiar to Trump watchers: eliminating what the administration considers "woke" policies from colleges and workplaces, lowering prescription drug prices, and rooting out government and health-care fraud. He also wants to emphasize reducing the federal bureaucracy and push for permitting reform , while highlighting how those efforts could help address affordability. Sources in the business community say Miller's ideological drive makes him mostly impervious to typical Washington lobbying. Yes, but: With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, Miller will have to advance that agenda without the help of Republican majorities in either the House or Senate. Some of his plans could be pursued through executive orders by Trump. Others, including permitting reform, would require bipartisan cooperation. That could be a challenge: Miller, a political fighter who's been called…

33e1d7779a:015f73afc1ca63ef.title: The Democratic leadership revolt has a glaring problem
33e1d7779a:015f73afc1ca63ef.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:015f73afc1ca63ef.summary: The Republican leadership fights are over. For Democrats, the pain has only just begun. Why it matters: All the talk about changing party leadership is empty if no one steps up to run. Senate Republicans demanded more time and deeper conversations about their leadership, but no one stepped forward to challenge John Thune, who won by acclamation. Democrats are demanding their own conversations about the party's future and the leadership of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. Neither has a challenger. ‼️ The intrigue: Where there was a contested leadership fight, the challenger won. Rep. Jim Jordan, the Freedom Caucus founding member who spent years tormenting Republican leaders, will now lead the battered House GOP after defeating 12-year leadership veteran Rep. Steve Scalise by 33 votes. Jordan is the kind of fighter House Republicans want to take on Democrats as they enter the minority, lawmakers told Axios. "We're gearing up for war. And you're talking to a guy who's known as a hammer. You know we need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Axios. 🤺 Zoom in: No such fighter has emerged to challenge Democratic leaders from within their ranks, and Schumer said he is "confident I will be elected majority leader." The closest thing to a challenge is Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's listening to calls to run for Democratic leader while also considering a presidential campaign. It's hard to do both. Meanwhile, opposition to Schumer is building: " [T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who said she's not "actively seeking the job" but demanded a plan for change. 🏛️ Over in the House, Jeffries is dismissive of the idea that anyone would challenge him after the midterms gave him a massive majority. "You think I don't have the vote nailed down? I guess we'll find out next Wednesday," he told reporters on Monday. Some of his new members…

33e1d7779a:761b62b86126fad7.title: "Rome is burning": Incoming House Democrats prove unusually willing to defy leaders
33e1d7779a:761b62b86126fad7.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:761b62b86126fad7.summary: House Democrats' incoming freshman class is barely a week old and already threatening to defy party leaders in ways most of their incumbent colleagues wouldn't dare. Why it matters: It's a dynamic House leaders may have to learn to live with as they integrate a massive group of new members who were swept into office on a wave of populist, anti-establishment anger. "My class is huge not because of ... the Democratic Party and its brand but despite it," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "Many of us are outsiders who didn't come up through the machine, don't buy into the conventions." Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) told Axios: "Any members that are new and have just run their elections are going to be very close to where the voters are, and we know the voters are very upset." State of play: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is on track to become speaker, in part thanks to his rock-solid support among sitting House Democrats. His supporters include high-profile progressives such as Casar and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.). "There is one candidate in this race, Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday. Things get more spotty when gauging Jeffries' support among incoming freshmen, some of whom have openly declined to commit to supporting his leadership. That includes members of the informal progressive "Bloc," including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.) and Chris Rabb (D-Pa.). "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only one running," said progressive Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). "But ... I think we need to see some prioritization of some legislation, particularly around health care, foreign policy and immigration." Some incoming and sitting House Democrats…

33e1d7779a:d73ecac1b22e84a6.title: Scoop: Commerce Department received national security warning on Nvidia CEO affair
33e1d7779a:d73ecac1b22e84a6.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:d73ecac1b22e84a6.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, multiple sources familiar told Axios. Why it matters: Lutnick oversees the agency charged with keeping sensitive U.S. technology out of the hands of American adversaries. The warning raises questions about how the department weighed potential security risks as it cleared advanced Nvidia chip sales to China-affiliated entities. Driving the news : Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the memo detailing Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese intelligence agent, according to The New York Times. The memo, which drew on surveillance of Alice Huang and a chip-smuggling investigation into her company, Megaspeed, circulated before President Trump's trip to May 13–15 trip to China. Rubio also warned Trump directly aboard Air Force One before a refueling stop in Anchorage where Jensen Huang joined the delegation. He hadn't initially been invited to participate, the Times reported Tuesday . On May 14, Reuters reported that the Commerce Department had cleared around 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia's H200 chips. Some export approvals predated the warning. Nvidia disclosed in February it had received an H200 export license, and Huang told Axios' Ina Fried in March the company had licenses covering Chinese customers. Yes, but : It's unclear how those approvals ultimately translated into sales, as China's government has halted some chip-buying activity in spite of U.S. approvals. Megaspeed purchased billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips, according to multiple media outlets. What they're saying : Trump said on Monday that it was possible intelligence officials had shown it to him, but he didn't recall: "Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me." The Commerce Department did not comment. Catch up quick : Nvidia has been rocked by the…

33e1d7779a:1ea8f1a97f6f6169.title: Trump swung between war and diplomacy — then chose a third way
33e1d7779a:1ea8f1a97f6f6169.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:1ea8f1a97f6f6169.summary: When Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, he told them that President Trump had considered resuming the war with Iran or cutting a deal — but chose a third option: strangling the Iranian regime, three people who attended the meeting told Axios. Why it matters: The Iran war has become a political albatross in Trump's second term, costing Republicans dearly in the midterms. For months, the president has alternated between threatening to obliterate Iran and predicting it will capitulate and give him the deal he wants. "He's been searching for the solution, but he wasn't sure what's the best way to go," a U.S. official close to Trump said. This debate over which course to follow has led to strife between several factions within the top echelon of the administration. Each faction had the support of U.S. allies in the Middle East — namely Israel favoring renewed strikes and most Gulf countries opposing them. Driving the news: After meeting with the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump said that a new round of strikes against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary." Trump said he instead favors continuing the economic crackdown and naval blockade against Iran, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology. Behind the scenes: Rubio explained the U.S. Iran policy in a closed meeting on Tuesday with the foreign ministers of the G7 countries in Paris. "The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just return to war or sign a ridiculous peace deal. We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said, according to three people in the room. Rubio went on to say that the U.S. is imposing devastating costs on Iran's economy, making it harder for it to fund terrorist organizations or rebuild its military. And there's no end date.…

33e1d7779a:97a004069c983519.title: GOP House rejects Hegseth impeachment effort
33e1d7779a:97a004069c983519.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:97a004069c983519.summary: House Republicans voted Tuesday evening to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , shielding a top Trump administration official from a politically embarrassing rebuke. Why it matters: The vote marks a victory for Hegseth, the Trump administration and Republican leaders, who were bracing for the prospect of a rebellion within their own ranks. But the reprieve is probably short-lived: Democrats are all but guaranteed to force the issue again when they retake majorities in the House and Senate in January. The vote to refer the impeachment measure back to committee passed 211-204, with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), the measure's sponsor, the lone "no" vote. Driving the news: Massie forced a procedural vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth, alleging he has defied Congress and illegally continued the U.S. war in Iran. The Trump administration has been vehemently defending Hegseth , including through a statement opposing the impeachment effort issued shortly before the vote. "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X . "Like so much of Congress , impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements," Vance added. Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt previously reported that Hegseth is on " thin ice " with Trump officials. Between the lines : Republican leaders protected their members from having to go on record on the politically difficult issue before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent lawmakers home early to campaign. What's next: Tuesday's vote effectively kills any effort to impeach Hegseth this Congress.

33e1d7779a:25b898aa2c84a662.title: Credit card debt hits record high as Americans struggle with cost-of-living
33e1d7779a:25b898aa2c84a662.author: Julianna Bragg
33e1d7779a:25b898aa2c84a662.summary: Federal Reserve Bank of New York ; Note: Not adjusted for inflation; Chart: Axios Visuals Americans' credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, according to a new report released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Why it matters: Falling behind on credit card payments can trap struggling households in a cycle of fees, damaged credit and increasingly expensive borrowing. The latest figures show that financial pain is concentrated in lower-income communities, even as delinquency rates improve nationally. By the numbers: Consumer credit card balances rose by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7%. That's $52 billion higher than a year earlier. The figures aren't adjusted for inflation, meaning some of the increase reflects higher prices rather than greater borrowing in real terms. Total household debt, including mortgages and student and auto loans, rose $334 billion, reaching a record $19.1 trillion in the third quarter. The total is up $5 trillion since 2019, just before the pandemic. Yes, but: Fewer credit card balances are becoming seriously delinquent, a sign of some improvement in Americans' ability to keep up with payments. The rate at which credit card debt becomes seriously overdue edged down to 6.9% in the third quarter, though it remains notably above the 5.2% recorded before the pandemic. Between the lines: A separate report from the New York Fed on Tuesday showed Americans in lower-income neighborhoods are having a harder time keeping up with credit card payments relative to their wealthier counterparts. Delinquency rates remain above pre-pandemic levels across all neighborhood-income groups, with the gap between the richest and poorest areas increasing since 2022. In the lowest-income neighborhoods, 10.3% of credit card balances became seriously delinquent over the past year — more than double the 4.4% rate in the wealthiest neighborhoods. The big picture: Average credit card balance per borrower is now…

33e1d7779a:5d05e1edf79b83c0.title: Jim Jordan wins House GOP minority leader race
33e1d7779a:5d05e1edf79b83c0.author: Kate Santaliz
33e1d7779a:5d05e1edf79b83c0.summary: House Republicans elected Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as their new leader Tuesday, handing the reins of the battered GOP conference to one of its most prominent conservative firebrands. Why it matters: Jordan's victory marks a major shake-up in House Republican leadership, elevating a founding member of the hardline Freedom Caucus who campaigned as an alternative to the leaders who presided over the GOP's crushing midterm defeat . Jordan bested Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), who had served as the No. 2 House Republican since 2014, in the conference-wide secret ballot for minority leader. Scalise trailed Jordan by 33 votes. Jordan's victory signals an appetite among House Republicans for a more confrontational approach as they prepare to enter the minority. State of play: Jordan and Scalise entered Tuesday's election locked in a tight race, with both camps expressing confidence in their chances of winning. Jordan drew public support from some of the conference's most conservative members, who argued Republicans needed a change in direction after their devastating midterm losses. Scalise leaned on his longstanding relationships across the conference and his decade-plus of experience in leadership. The big picture: Jordan's ascent represents a remarkable turnaround for a conservative agitator who spent much of his career challenging the Republican establishment before becoming one of President Trump's most vocal allies. He'll be tasked with uniting a fractured Republican conference and leading the party's efforts to reclaim the House majority in 2028. Zoom out: Beyond the top job, current whip Tom Emmer (Minn.) beat back a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (Texas) to stay on as minority whip. Conference Chair: Lisa McClain (Mich.) won a three-way race with Reps. Erin Houchin (Ind.) and Greg Steube (Fla.). Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional vote results.

33e1d7779a:c6b09181af6b1b1b.title: 3 charged with plotting terror attacks in U.S., Europe
33e1d7779a:c6b09181af6b1b1b.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:c6b09181af6b1b1b.summary: The U.S. charged three individuals in connection with alleged Iranian-linked terror plots, including a September scheme against a British Royal Air Force Base that housed U.S. military personnel and aircraft, per an indictment unsealed Tuesday. The big picture: The indictment alleges that a leader of an Islamic terrorist group attempted to coordinate with his fellow defendants from jail by passing coded messages through third parties. Driving the news: Since early in the year, the three men named in the indictment worked to commit terror attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, the indictment alleges. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:5ce95021760dd1b4.title: The Atlantic can pursue FBI records in fight with Kash Patel
33e1d7779a:5ce95021760dd1b4.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:5ce95021760dd1b4.summary: A federal judge took sharp aim at FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday, ruling in favor of The Atlantic and freezing most discovery in his defamation lawsuit against the publication. Why it matters: The ruling shields The Atlantic from potentially intrusive demands for its reporting materials and confidential sources while the court weighs dismissing the case entirely. What they're saying: " Plaintiff misrepresents Defendants' argument, the court's reasoning in Moldea, and the standard applicable in this District," U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan wrote in his 16-page ruling . "The Court concludes that discovery should be stayed at this juncture because of Defendants' legitimate First Amendment concerns and because discovery may be unnecessary," Sullivan wrote. Catch up quick: Patel sued The Atlantic after the magazine reported in April that he allegedly drinks excessively and is sometimes unavailable or difficult for his staff to wake because he was seemingly intoxicated. The story also alleged that Patel had grown increasingly worried about losing his job. Patel denied the reporting and sued the publication shortly after the story aired. Zoom in: The judge paused most discovery until he rules on The Atlantic's motion to dismiss the lawsuit, but both sides may request government records. The Atlantic says it needs Justice Department and FBI records to assess the truth of its reporting and Patel's reputation. Patel complained the requests were too broad, seeking everything from his medical and travel records to his calendar and records about personnel decisions. Sullivan rejected Patel's objection that the arrangement was unfair. The intrigue: The Atlantic warned that discovery could involve "the sitting FBI Director invading Defendants' newsgathering and editorial processes," potentially exposing confidential sources to retaliation. The Atlantic called Patel a "serial defamation plaintiff" and warned that he "may seek to wield governmental power" in connection…

33e1d7779a:c4a16b66dda59344.title: Harsh new inflation reality
33e1d7779a:c4a16b66dda59344.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:c4a16b66dda59344.summary: America's inflation problem is stubborn, broadening out and showing no sign of letting up. Why it matters: October marked the third straight month of hotter-than-expected inflation , defying repeated predictions over the last couple of years that price pressures were finally about to ease. In this sixth consecutive year of steep price increases, consumers are finding there is nowhere to hide from inflation. The Iran war has added to the pain, but other factors — tariffs and the AI investment boom — have also put upward pressure on costs, complicating an affordability problem that long predates the conflict. What they're saying: "Today's inflation report is a warning shot," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, wrote Tuesday morning. "Coming just a week after the midterm elections exposed the depth of voters' concerns about affordability, the message for the Fed is uncomfortable but clear: The inflation fight is not finished," Shah wrote. Driving the news: The headline Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, down slightly from a 0.6% surge the previous month. Core CPI — which excludes volatile food and energy costs — climbed 0.3% for the third consecutive month, a sign that underlying inflationary pressures remain stubbornly persistent. The Labor Department did not calculate October's annual inflation rate since last year's government shutdown prevented it from collecting price data for October 2025. But assuming prices that month were halfway between September and November, overall inflation over the last 12 months was 4% — up from 3.7% in September. Core inflation would have risen to 2.8%, up from 2.6%. Another measure similarly paints a picture of hot inflation. Core prices rose at a 3.7% annualized pace over the three months through October, the fastest pace by this gauge all year. It also is a sharp acceleration from the summer, when underlying inflation appeared to be cooling. Zoom out: Gasoline prices advanced another 1% in…

33e1d7779a:d4e4465d957b21ab.title: Vance says Hegseth impeachment vote "isn't about Iran"
33e1d7779a:d4e4465d957b21ab.author: Julianna Bragg
33e1d7779a:d4e4465d957b21ab.summary: Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday said that the vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "isn't about Iran," but rather his willingness to take on challenges at the Pentagon. Why it matters: It's the latest instance of the Trump administration backing the embattled Cabinet member, who is facing the possibility of enough GOP members defecting for the impeachment effort to succeed. The Iran war is at the center of the allegations against Hegseth, with three of the eight articles of impeachment specifically concerning the conflict. Other allegations include that Hegseth illegally initiated military conflict in Venezuela and Yemen. What they're saying: "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X . "Like so much of Congress, impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements." Vance added that Congress was choosing to impeach Hegseth as they did President Trump. "Legislation is hard. Impeachments are easy (and ultimately, inconsequential)." "The irony is that legislators are most angry at Pete on the issues where he's most correct: repositioning forces away from Europe/Ukraine and reorganizing the general officer corps," he continued. "This isn't about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon." Go deeper: Hegseth faces impeachment resolution from GOP member with little to lose Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

33e1d7779a:bfe52dabb2b2a33e.title: Pressure builds on Thune ahead of GOP leadership elections
33e1d7779a:bfe52dabb2b2a33e.author: Stef W. Kight
33e1d7779a:bfe52dabb2b2a33e.summary: Eight Republican senators now are calling for their leadership elections to be delayed — with one even promising to walk out rather than vote Tuesday. Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is still expected to be reelected to lead the Senate GOP tomorrow. But the growing push to delay is a sign of troubles ahead. What we're hearing: Senate Republicans spent roughly two hours behind closed doors hashing out their path forward. Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisc.) led much of the conversation, arguing for a delay in the leadership elections and demanding an aggressive lame duck schedule, senators told Axios. Some senators also discussed their election losses, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine). Both were ousted last week. They will resume the discussion at 2pm ET, where leadership votes — and motions to delay leadership elections — are expected. Driving the news: Sens. ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.author: Van Reenen, John
ecbefe1924:a1112539a5399e7d.summary: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.title: The Division of Labor: Productivity, Coordination, and Learning
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.author: Xu, Yaling
ecbefe1924:48aaa5128f75aff6.summary: The division of labor is fundamental to how firms organize production. Since Adam Smith, economists have recognized that dividing tasks more finely increases productivity through specialization but also raises coordination costs—a tradeoff formalized by Becker and Murphy (1992). Yet we have little systematic evidence on how this tradeoff operates within firms. Moreover, this classical perspective overlooks a second, dynamic tradeoff: firms not only produce output, but also develop a central input into future production—their workers’ human capital. A finer division of labor allows workers to develop greater expertise through repeated performance of narrowly defined tasks, but may also reduce opportunities to learn from coworkers by limiting interactions and knowledge exchange. We study both tradeoffs using population-wide Norwegian employer–employee records, linked workplace surveys, quasi-experimental variation in coworker availability, and randomized experiments with workers and managers. We find that more specialized firms exhibit higher productivity but also greater coordination costs. Their workers report more learning-by-doing but substantially less coworker learning, resulting in lower overall learning and slower wage growth. To establish the importance of coworker learning for human capital accumulation, we exploit extended coworker absences and show that losing access to colleagues reduces subsequent wage growth, particularly in occupations characterized by greater task overlap and coworker learning. To isolate the role of the division of labor from other workplace characteristics, we conduct randomized experiments that vary task allocation in otherwise identical workplaces. Workers and managers anticipate greater coordination demands, weaker coworker interactions, and lower skill accumulation under greater specialization. The experiments then ask workers to choose their preferred workplace and managers how they would organize production. Both favor…

ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.title: AI Adoption and Employment Expectations: Evidence from a Survey of Small Business Owners
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.author: Asani Sarkar
ecbefe1924:b243d5e5a333b044.summary: There is little consensus on the effect of AI adoption on employment. Economy-wide measures of pay and headcount have moved little even as AI adoption has spread rapidly, yet narrower measures document declining hiring for workers at the start of their careers or in AI-exposed occupations. In this post, we revisit this topic for U.S. small businesses. We use data from the 2025 Small Business Credit Survey (SBCS) to examine the twelve-month-forward employment and revenue expectations of AI users. We find that firms currently using AI are significantly more likely than non-users to expect increased employment and revenues over the next year, even after accounting for firm and owner characteristics and location. Revenue expectations are most optimistic for AI users that report facing operational challenges in utilizing technology.

ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.title: Beliefs Over Contracts
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.author: Collin B. Raymond
ecbefe1924:f2a4557243c634ca.summary: We study how firms choose among incentive contracts and how accurately managers predict their effects. Using a survey of managerial beliefs and a large-scale field experiment, we randomly assign agents at the market level to several widely used, expenditure-equivalent incentive schemes. In the field, the best-performing contract increases agent output and firm revenue by over 20% relative to the status quo, despite being ranked lower by managers, whereas the worst-performing contract performs as predicted. Managers correctly identify underperforming contracts but systematically underestimate top- performing ones. We document the sources of performance di!erences—labor supply responses rather than selection or pricing and the determinants of managerial predictability: contract complexity and managerial hierarchy. Our results highlight the importance of contract design for firm performance and reveal systematic limits to managerial cognition in shaping incentives.

ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.title: Asymmetric Information in Wage Contracts: Experimental Evidence and Welfare Implications
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.author: Daniel Herbst
ecbefe1924:cc19a494a9782497.summary: Compared to self-employment or performance-based pay, fixed wages reduce earnings uncertainty but are prone to market distortions through moral hazard and adverse selection. Using a model of wage contracts under asymmetric information, I show that these distortions map to marginal treatment response functions in a marginal treatment effects (MTE) framework. I apply this framework to a field experiment in which data-entry workers choose between a randomized fixed wage and a piece rate. I find evidence of both moral hazard and adverse selection: Fixed wages reduce worker productivity by an estimated 8.74 percent relative to the mean. Meanwhile, a 10 percent increase in the wage offer attracts a marginal worker whose productivity is higher by 1.90 percent of the mean. Using semi-parametric MTE estimation, I calculate the welfare loss associated with asymmetric information and the marginal values of public funds (MVPFs) for policies aimed at recovering this loss. I find that a tax on piece rates can mitigate adverse selection into fixed wages, generating tax revenue at social costs as low as $0.88 per dollar.

ecbefe1924:ac5b1d4244cec881.title: Reliability of AI Agents: Rater Effects, Drift, and the Return to an Evaluation Program
ecbefe1924:ac5b1d4244cec881.author: Mark Esposito
ecbefe1924:ac5b1d4244cec881.summary: Firms increasingly evaluate deployed AI agents using repeated human ratings, yet observed score changes may reflect the measurement process as much as changes in the agent itself. Firms also rarely know how long an evaluation remains informative as deployed systems evolve. We study reliability as a latent state using 2, 611 rubric-scored production interviews from a deployed voice-and-video interviewing agent, overlapping human reviewers, the agent's change log, and support tickets. Reviewer severity varied substantially: two reviewers assessing the same batches differed by 0.79 standard deviations on the composite index, and a shift in reviewer composition flattened the raw trend. After adjusting for reviewer effects and smoothing batch-level estimates, evaluated reliability increased by 0.53 standard deviations from March to August 2026. Reliability also shifted materially across logged deploys. At the estimated rate of unaccounted movement, forecast uncertainty reaches the magnitude of the largest observed deploy contrast after about five weeks, although this horizon is imprecisely estimated and based on a small number of step-like changes. An independent operational outcome moved in the same direction: interview-related support tickets fell by about 10% per month relative to technical-issue tickets. These data do not identify a causal effect of evaluation on performance. Instead, they show that longitudinal AI evaluation requires three checks: comparability across raters, evidence currency under drift, and corroboration with consequential operational outcomes.

ecbefe1924:409a2dd6ca59a95d.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
ecbefe1924:409a2dd6ca59a95d.author: Christopher T. Stanton
ecbefe1924:409a2dd6ca59a95d.summary: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This in turn makes general skill firm-specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

ecbefe1924:f856f0eb7ab7cad2.title: Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
ecbefe1924:f856f0eb7ab7cad2.author: Huseyin Yildirim
ecbefe1924:f856f0eb7ab7cad2.summary: A principal designs ratings for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talents, mapping outputs into arbitrary finite-variance statistics. Peer output both benchmarks effort and signals talent, making full disclosure suboptimal under confidential ratings. Relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality yields a closed-form rating and computable effort bounds for general priors; under normality, the relaxation is exact. Optimal confidential ratings combine the full-disclosure wage with the Fisher score for effort: they are relative-performance when individual output is informative about talent and team-based when it is noisy. Public ratings must satisfy joint Bayes plausibility, weakening incentives; hence, the principal prefers confidential ratings, whereas agents prefer public ratings. A spectral decomposition characterizes public ratings under normality: small cost heterogeneity implies full disclosure regardless of the noise structure, whereas large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers can induce partial disclosure to reallocate incentives. The results bear on performance ratings and pay transparency.

ecbefe1924:37b37d42031cfba7.title: Do weekend workers like their jobs?
ecbefe1924:37b37d42031cfba7.author: Mark Wooden
ecbefe1924:37b37d42031cfba7.summary: Weekend work is a pervasive feature of labor markets that comes with both potential benefits (e.g., higher pay, flexible schedules) and drawbacks (e.g., less social time). Nevertheless, robust evidence on weekend workers’ job satisfaction is lacking. Longitudinal data from 21 waves of the annual Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey (n=211, 077; i=26, 273) are used to estimate the association between weekend work and several dimensions of job satisfaction. Estimates from fixed effects models reveal that weekend work is associated with significantly lower levels of satisfaction with working hours and flexibility, but this does not translate into lower levels of overall job satisfaction. Additional analyses were conducted to test whether results varied with employment status, occupation and parental status. In general, the main finding applied to all groups examined. There were, however, marked differences across sub-groups in satisfaction with other job domains. Overall, the results suggest that, for most workers, the benefits of working weekends offset its disadvantages.

ecbefe1924:0c76a1df3fb235f8.title: Remote Work from the Office
ecbefe1924:0c76a1df3fb235f8.author: Emma Harrington
ecbefe1924:0c76a1df3fb235f8.summary: Roughly half of in-office days are spent entirely on Zoom calls or doing solo work according to a new survey of college-educated Americans. These workers commute in just to work remotely from the office. Existing measures of remote work that focus solely on working from home miss up to three quarters of its true prevalence. We use a collage of data to unpack the drivers of working remotely from the office. The biggest driver is geographic distance, which causes teammates to work in different offices or fully remotely. Other contributors include non-compliance with in-office policies, poor coordination on in-office days, and a tendency to take Zoom calls rather than booking meeting rooms even when everyone is in the office.

ecbefe1924:620ea2fd44250f2f.title: Training Your Replacement: Worker Incentives and the Pace of Automation
ecbefe1924:620ea2fd44250f2f.author: Peter Landry
ecbefe1924:620ea2fd44250f2f.summary: Firms ask workers to train AI systems that will replace them. We model this with a worker who can shirk, cooperate with training, or obstruct training while maintaining productivity. Because training ends the job but only cooperation completes training, dismissal becomes a weaker penalty for shirking. The firm must raise the worker’s rent, and the worker gains from their replacement. AI can create jobs paying more than they produce and eliminate jobs it never automates. Firms paying only wages may slow training. A credible completion bonus equal to the worker’s rent without AI removes both the gain and the slowdown.

ecbefe1924:46524f1965373964.title: The Occupational Ladder: Implications for Life-Cycle Wage Dynamics
ecbefe1924:46524f1965373964.author: Guido Matias Cortes
ecbefe1924:46524f1965373964.summary: Some occupations pay higher wages than others, even conditional on worker characteristics, implying that occupations can be ranked on a ladder. We develop a simple decomposition to study the role this occupational ladder plays in average wage growth and in the fanning out of wages over the life cycle. We present three main findings. First, the distribution of employment shifts towards higher-paying occupations as workers gain experience. This contributes modestly to average life-cycle wage growth, with greatest impact in early career. Second, this upward movement in the occupational employment distribution is not accompanied by increasing dispersion; thus, the occupational ladder does not directly contribute to the fanning out of wages. Third, early-career workers who are well-positioned on the occupational ladder tend to earn wages far below the occupational average. However, by mid-career, workers’ relative wages within occupations (their positions on the job ladder) no longer depend on their occupation. This change in the covariance between individuals’ positions on the job and occupational ladders is a major contributor to the fanning out of wages over workers’ careers.

ecbefe1924:1c5ef94bd23acb99.title: Task Expansion with Generative AI: Experimental Evidence on Middle-Skilled, Early-Career Workers
ecbefe1924:1c5ef94bd23acb99.author: Tschoepe, Nele
ecbefe1924:1c5ef94bd23acb99.summary: Does generative artificial intelligence (AI) expand the set of tasks that middle-skilled, early-career workers can successfully perform? In a field experiment with 673 final-year IT apprentices at twelve German vocational schools, we randomly assign access to AI for completing occupation-specific tasks. To identify task expansion, we study tasks both within the apprenticeship curriculum and deliberately beyond it. AI raises productivity substantially across all task types, with gains tending to be larger on tasks where performance without AI is lowest. Crucially, productivity increases by 26â€“31 percentage points on tasks beyond apprenticesâ€™ formal training, providing direct evidence of AI-enabled task expansion. These productivity gains do not come at the cost of reduced immediate task comprehension. Treatment effects are generally larger among apprentices with above-median AI literacy.
